en: *Commentary and Praise on the Section on the Principles of Prajñā from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Scroll One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Ji of the Great Ci’en Monastery.
I prostrate to those who have transcended nature and characteristics, whose minds and speech are fundamentally empty and quiescent;
to the eternally abiding True Triple Gem, and to my own venerable teacher.
The profound Dharma of the ultimate mode of being is beyond my power to praise.
Now, relying upon the power of the Venerable One’s wisdom and compassion, and through the force of his empowerment, I shall speak.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle eighty-two, states: "When any Dharma-preacher is about to expound [the teachings], he should first praise the Buddha, either briefly or extensively."
The brief praise of the Buddha is by way of five aspects:

first, his exquisite form, which is perfectly adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and embellished by the eighty secondary signs upon his limbs, shining with radiance like a great mountain of gold.

Second is tranquility: his features are upright, majestic, and exquisite; his faculties are serene and still; his mind is at peace. He has already attained the supreme, perfectly compliant, and ultimate state of calm abiding (*śamatha*); he has already reached the foremost shore of perfect compliance and tranquility. He is well able to closely guard and subdue his faculties, being a "dragon among men" because he is free from error and transgression;
a "bull-king among men" because he leads the great assembly; and a "fine horse among men" because his mind is well-tamed.
It is pure and undisturbed like a pool of clear spring water, having already been able to forever uproot the habitual tendencies of afflictions.
Third is supreme wisdom, which means being unimpeded and unattached regarding the phenomena of the three times as well as supramundane phenomena.
Fourth is right practice, wherein the practices for the benefit of oneself and others—namely the six perfections and the four means of integration—are all fully perfected.
Fifth is majestic power, which refers to the blazing intensity of the majestic power of the Tathāgatas’ playful mastery of supernatural faculties.

Furthermore, there are six praises: because his merit is perfected; because he is free from defilement; because he is without turbidity or impurity; because he has no equal; because his sole activity is to benefit sentient beings; and because he possesses the capability for this activity. These boundless praises are extolled at length, all as previously described.
Having thus praised the Buddha, one who fulfills ten qualities is called a Dharma-preacher.
As for these ten qualities: first, being skilled in the meaning of the Dharma, which means being well able to understand the six dharmas and ten meanings.
Second, the ability to proclaim extensively, meaning that one has heard much, retained what was heard, and accumulated that learning.

Third, being endowed with fearlessness, such that when proclaiming the True Dharma amidst a great assembly, one is without timidity or dread; one's voice does not falter or become hoarse, one's armpits do not perspire, and one's mindfulness is never lost.

Fourth is skillfulness in speech, which consists of eloquent and perfect language endowed with the eight branches, such that one possesses the requisite verbal skills to teach the Dharma in the midst of an assembly.
Fifth is skillful means in teaching, which refers to the proclamation of the true Dharma through twenty kinds of skillful means, such as [teaching] at the proper time and with reverence.

Sixth, they are fully accomplished in the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma; they do not consider mere hearing to be the ultimate goal, but rather practice exactly as it has been taught.

Seventh, they are complete in their dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*); that is to say, when preaching the Dharma, their hands and feet are not disordered, their heads do not shake, their faces do not change expression, and their noses do not alter their natural state; whether advancing or retreating, coming or going, their deportment is composed and orderly.

Eighth, with courageous diligence, one always delights in hearing teachings not yet heard, further clarifying and purifying those already heard; one does not abandon yoga, does not abandon mental attention (*manasikāra*), and the mind does not depart from internal śamatha.
Ninth is the absence of weariness, meaning that when proclaiming the sublime Dharma extensively for the fourfold assembly, one feels no fatigue in body or mind.

Tenth is the possession of the power of patience, meaning that even when reviled, mocked, or rebuked, one never retaliates; even when treated with contempt, one does not give rise to anger or resentment, and so forth, as explained at length.

Regarding those who listen to the Dharma: when this Dharma-preacher expounds the true Dharma, he should establish others in a state of reverence and cause them to listen without error, by means of one cause or even up to ten.
First, listening to the Dharma with reverence brings about the realization of benefit and happiness in the present.
This consists of four points, as explained in the section on the "Dharma-base" (*dharmapada*) within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Second, first, because it skillfully establishes all phenomena, being free from all faults and endowed with great significance;
second, because the diligent efforts exerted by both the speaker and the listener yield a superior fruit.
Third, there are three aspects: first, it enables sentient beings to abandon the evil realms;
second, it leads them to attain the good realms;
and third, it can swiftly induce and gather the causes for nirvāṇa.
These three matters are obtained only through listening with reverence.
Fourth, [the teacher] is able to thoroughly understand the sūtras and other scriptures;
second, such true Dharma enables sentient beings to abandon all that is unwholesome and embrace all that is wholesome, and one who listens well is able to accept and relinquish accordingly.
Third, because through this equanimity one abandons the future suffering summoned by unwholesome causes;
fourth, because one swiftly realizes *nirvāṇa*.
Fifth [consists of five points]: first, "I shall now hear what has not been heard before."
2. Having heard it, one investigates;
3. One should sever the net of doubt;
4. One abandons and turns away from all views.
Fifth: "I shall, by means of wisdom, thoroughly penetrate all profound words and meanings.
This reveals the three types of wisdom: the first two reveal hearing (*śruta*), the next two reveal reflection (*cintā*), and the last one reveals cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Sixth: First, it is because one wishes to respectfully repay the kindness and virtue of the Great Master; that is to say, the Buddha practiced immeasurable difficult and painful austerities for my sake to seek and attain this Dharma—how could I now fail to listen and hear it?
2. Contemplating one's own welfare;
3. Ultimately being able to leave behind all feverish afflictions;
4. Skillfully conforming to correct decorum.
Fifth, it is easily perceived and understood;
sixth, it is that which is realized within by those who are wise.

Seventh, it means that I shall collect the seven kinds of true Dharma, knowing the phenomena and knowing their meaning, and so forth, up to the detailed explanation of the distinctions between the noble and the humble.
Eighth, [the Buddha’s teaching] is: first, easy to attain, as it is revealed even to those such as the caṇḍālas;
second, easy to study, as it can be practiced while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;
third, capable of inducing the fruits of higher rebirth and the definitive fruits of supreme excellence.
Fourth, good in the beginning;
fifth, good in the middle;
sixth, good in the end;
7. It brings about the fruit of happiness in the present;
8. it leads to happiness in the future.
As for the ninth, it means that it is capable of liberating one from the nine kinds of worldly afflictions.
First, because it enables one to emerge from the great prison of birth and death;
second, because it forever severs the firm bonds of greed and the like;
third, because it abandons the poverty of the seven riches and establishes the wealth of the seven riches.
4. Because it transcends and delivers through virtuous conduct, it makes hearing the True Dharma abundant, whereas without it, hearing the True Dharma would be meager;
5. Because it extinguishes the darkness of ignorance and gives rise to the light of wisdom;
6. Because it crosses over the four violent currents and ascends to the shore of Nirvāṇa.
7. Because it is ultimately able to cure the disease of afflictions;
8. Because it releases one from the snares of all craving and attachment;
9. Because it enables one to cross the dense forest of the wilderness of beginningless birth and death.

Tenth: first, by listening to the Dharma with reverence, one attains the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna-bala*); through this, one is able to receive the benefits of hearing the Dharma, seeking wealth in accordance with the Dharma rather than through unrighteous means, and using it while deeply perceiving its faults; continuing thus up to the tenth, which can induce all mundane and supramundane meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*), as explained at length therein.
The speaker and the listener must first abide in the supreme Dharma before they can speak and listen; if they do not abide therein, their efforts will be in vain and ultimately yield no great fruit.
Now, in order to praise the scriptural text, I shall briefly explain it by means of four sections:
first, the statement of the sūtra’s primary purpose;
Second, revealing the essential nature of the sutra;
third, manifesting the sublime virtues of the sutra;
fourth, explaining the main text of the sutra.

Regarding the purpose of this scripture: nine hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a great arhat named Bhāviveka. His physical bearing conformed to the conventions of the Sāṃkhya school, yet he demonstrated no attachment to sectarian factions; his mind dwelt within the principles of Śākyamuni, yet he maintained no biased or stagnant sentiments. His contemporaries called him the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī; his spiritual wonders and holy virtues are detailed extensively in other records.
In his *Treatise on the Precious Palm*, he states: "All objects of knowledge are, in brief, of two kinds:
first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and second, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Because foolish worldlings do not correctly realize the non-erroneous nature of the conditioned and unconditioned within the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), they falsely grasp at the intrinsic natures and specific characteristics of phenomena, thereby entangling themselves in various nets of false views."

It is like a certain ignorant painter in the world who creates the image of a terrifying medicinal demon or a woman; with eyes dazzled and mind confused, he takes it to be truly existent. Because he clings to it as real, he becomes terrified or gives rise to lustful attachment, engaging in numerous conceptualizations regarding that object and thereby increasing the snare of various views born of discrimination.

If one correctly realizes that the ultimate truth consists of the non-erroneous nature of the conditioned and the unconditioned, then, like a wise painter of the world who does not grasp those [forms] as having a real intrinsic nature, one is not—as previously described—bound by the distinctions between the spheres of the conditioned and the unconditioned, like a silkworm dwelling within its cocoon; because such [distinctions] do not exist, the practice of entering into non-conceptual wisdom is accomplished.
However, to realize supramundane non-conceptual wisdom, one must accumulate the añjana medicine of unerring observation of emptiness, which is capable of destroying the cataracts of all false views.

Thus, to accumulate this undistorted contemplation of emptiness, one must rely on the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), which is capable of dispelling the intrinsic nature of all objects of cognition; therefore, one should listen to this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra.

Taking what has been explained here as the fundamental tenet: True nature is empty of the conditioned, for they arise dependently like illusions; the unconditioned has no reality, for its non-arising is like flowers in the sky.
In this context, conventional reality is accepted as having a degree of existence, whereas from the perspective of ultimate truth, all things are empty.

Herein, the analogy of the painter—whether wise or ignorant—and his fear or attachment serves as a metaphor for Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*): they are drawn by their own karma and consequently give rise to aversion or attachment. The wise person, however, understands that the painting is equal [to its substrate] and thus gives rise to neither fear nor attachment.
Maitreya’s *Madhyāntavibhāga-kārikā* states: "The false imagination exists; within it, both [the grasped and the grasper] are entirely absent.
Within this, there is only emptiness; and within that, there is also this."
Therefore it is said: "All dharmas are neither empty nor non-empty;
because of existence, non-existence, and the presence of both, this accords with the Middle Way.
This takes the absence of any attachment to existence or non-existence as its thesis, as explained at length elsewhere.
Second, regarding the revelation of the essence of the sūtra, there are five aspects of Prajñā:
first, the true mark (lakṣaṇa);
second, contemplative illumination (vipaśyanā).
Third is the syllables;
fourth is the objective realm, namely the two truths of ultimate and conventional reality;
fifth is the retinue, namely all merit and wisdom.
As has already been briefly demonstrated in the introduction to the title, the essence of the sūtra is twofold:
first, the words; second, the meaning.
The letters are the *vyañjana* (the expression), while the four kinds [of wisdom] are the *artha* (the meaning).

The true aspect (*dharmatā*) is the nature of *prajñā*, contemplative observation is the characteristic of *prajñā*, the letters are the cause of *prajñā*, the objective realm is the object of *prajñā*, and the retinue is the companion of *prajñā*; therefore, these five kinds are all named *prajñā*.

Nāgārjuna explained: "In terms of ultimate truth, all things are empty; thus, as for the teaching, there is neither teaching nor non-teaching, and as for its essence, there is neither essence nor non-essence."
"Within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), it may also be said that the teaching has as its essence phrases, words, chapters, treatises, and sounds.
This is explained at length in Bhāviveka’s *Prajñāpradīpa*.
Dharmapāla explains, saying:
There are four aspects of the essence of the teaching (*śāsana*).
First, the essence that subsumes characteristics into their fundamental nature (*dharmatā*).

The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The emanated and transformed [bodies] are not the true Buddha, nor are they the speakers of the Dharma. When the teaching is expounded, there is no dualistic grasping; it is without speech, transcending the marks of language."
This sutra further states: "All sentient beings and all phenomena are themselves suchness; therefore, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also suchness."
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states: "The nature of syllables is detached; that which is without syllables is itself liberation.
The characteristic of liberation is precisely all dharmas," and further: "All dharmas are also suchness."
Therefore, one knows that the nature of the teaching's substance is precisely *tathatā*.
Second, because all else is subsumed within the substance of consciousness:

the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states, "The triple world is mind-only," and the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states, "Because of the differentiation of the consciousnesses in other continuums, it causes the differentiated consciousnesses in other continuums to arise; since they act as mutual dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for one another, the minds of both speaker and listener constitute the substance of the teaching."
3. Subsuming the provisional according to the substantial entity.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The sound that is 'produced by what is brought about' (*naimittika*) refers to that which is spoken by the Noble Ones. Thus, we know that it takes sound alone as the substance of the teaching, subsuming provisional dharmas such as names (*nāman*), because these are spoken in accordance with the actual sound.
Fourth, the distinction between characteristics and functions regarding the essence [of the teaching]:

that which manifests upon the consciousness of the speaker—namely, sounds, names, phrases, and syllables—is taken as the essence of the teaching, because both the provisional and the real constitute the essence of the teaching.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Both the speaker and the listener attain completion through two things:
first, sound; second, excellent syllables.

Due to the power of habitual perfuming and the power of the transformation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), these manifest and assemble within the cognitive mind of the one preaching the Dharma."
As explained in a separate chapter, I shall not cite it here at length.

Third, regarding the manifestation of the sutra’s superior merit: the general title of this sutra is *Prajñā-naya* (The Principle of Wisdom). According to its specific meanings, there are fourteen distinct titles:
first, "This Dharma-gate of all phenomena that is profoundly deep, subtle, and pure."
If, having heard this, one believes and accepts it, one shall obtain eight supreme fruits:

first, until one sits upon the sublime seat of Bodhi, no obstacles or hindrances whatsoever can defile one; that is to say, although afflictive obscurations, karmic obscurations, and dharma obscurations may have accumulated extensively, they cannot defile one;
second, although one may commit various kinds of extremely grave evil karma, it is easily extinguished.
Third, one will not fall into the evil realms;

fourth, if one can receive and uphold [this teaching], reciting it daily with diligent and uninterrupted application and reflecting upon it according to the principle, one will certainly attain the vajra-samādhi of the equality of all phenomena in this very life;
fifth, one will attain mastery over all phenomena.
Sixth, they will constantly experience all supreme and wondrous joys;
seventh, after passing through sixteen births as great bodhisattvas, they will certainly attain the nature of the Tathāgata-Vajradhara;
eighth, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Second is the gateway of manifesting perfect awakening to the nature of phenomena that is quiescent.
If there are those who, having heard this, believe, understand, accept, uphold, recite, and cultivate it, they shall obtain two supreme fruits:

first, until they sit upon the sublime seat of bodhi, even if they commit all manner of most grievous evil karmas, they will be able to transcend all evil destinies; second, [they shall attain] the state of non-retrogression.
Second, one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Third, it is the Dharma-door of universally overcoming all evils through subjugation.
If anyone hears this, believes, understands, accepts, upholds, recites, and practices it, they shall attain four supreme fruits:

First, even if one were to kill all sentient beings throughout the three realms, one would not thereby fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts, because one is able to subdue all afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and evil karma;
second, one will always be born in the happy destinies (*sugati*) and experience supreme and wondrous bliss.
Third, cultivating the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
fourth, swiftly realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Fourth is the Dharma-door of the Purification of the Seal of Equalizing Wisdom.
If there are those who, having heard this, believe, understand, accept, uphold, recite, and practice it, they will obtain three supreme fruits:

first, although they dwell amidst the accumulation of all adventitious afflictions and defilements such as greed, hatred, and delusion, they remain unstained by any adventitious dust, defilement, or fault, just as a lotus flower is not soiled;
second, they are constantly able to cultivate the supreme practices of a bodhisattva.
Third, the swift realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Fifth, the empowerment dharma-gate, which attains two superior fruits.
Sixth, the Tathāgata-jñāna-mudrā-vajra dharma-gate, which attains five superior fruits.
Seventh, by means of the dharma-gate of the wheel of syllables free from all conceptual proliferation, one attains two superior fruits.
Eighth, by means of the dharma-gate of the equality of the vast wheel, one attains two superior fruits.
Ninth is the Dharma-door of Truly Pure Offerings to the Unsurpassed, through which one attains two supreme fruits.
Tenth is the Dharma-door of the Treasury of Wisdom that Skillfully Subdues, through which one attains six kinds of fruits.
Eleventh is the supreme dharma-gate of the nature of equality, which attains three superior fruits.
Twelfth is the supreme treasury dharma-gate of the pervasive sustenance of all sentient beings, which attains two superior fruits.
Thirteenth is the Vajra Dharma-gate of the Ultimate Principle of Boundlessness and Limitlessness, which attains three supreme fruits.
Fourteenth is the Most Supreme Dharma-gate of the Profound Principle.
Those who are able to receive and uphold it possess eighteen supreme virtues:
first, the extinction of all obstacles;
second, the unfailing accomplishment of whatever one desires according to the mind.
Third, it is the mother of all Buddhas;
fourth, all transgressions of those who can recite and uphold it are extinguished;
fifth, one constantly beholds all Buddhas.
Sixth, they attain the knowledge of past lives;

seventh, there are classes of sentient beings who have not yet planted various roots of goodness under many Buddhas nor long since made great vows, and thus are unable to hear, write, read, recite, honor, revere, contemplate, or practice this profound principle and supreme Dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā*; only those who have planted various roots of goodness under many Buddhas and long since made great vows are able, regarding this profound principle and supreme Dharma-gate, at the very least to hear a single phrase or a single syllable, let alone being able to fully read, recite, receive, and uphold it.

8. If sentient beings were to offer worship, respect, honor, and praise to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in eighty *gaṅgā* rivers, multiplied by *koṭi-nayuta*, they would then be able to fully hear this profound principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*, up to and including the fact that the fourteen classes of devas will constantly follow and protect them;
14. they shall never suffer an untimely death;
15. they shall not unjustly encounter misfortune or affliction.
Sixteenth, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will constantly protect and sustain them, causing virtue to increase and evil to diminish at all times;
seventeenth, they will be reborn in various Buddha-fields according to their vows;
eighteenth, until they reach enlightenment, they will not fall into the evil realms.
All classes of sentient beings who uphold this sutra will certainly obtain boundless benefits and merits; I shall now briefly explain a small portion thereof.
Fourth, the explanation of the main text of the sutra.
The Sūtra says:
"Thus have I heard.
The Commentary states:
In this sutra, there are briefly three parts:
first, from "Thus have I heard" up to "the perfectly pure and white holy life," is the introductory section (nidāna);

second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of the bodhisattvas, spoke of all dharmas as profoundly deep and subtle" up to "briefly explaining such a small portion," is the main body of the teaching (śarīra).
"Then the Bhagavat... [and so forth] until 'practiced accordingly'" constitutes the section on circulation (*pariṇāmanā*).
The three-part topical outline of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* differs from those of antiquity, as explained in that treatise itself.
Now, the three distinctions are explained:
first, the section on the introductory context preceding the text;
second, the section on the extensive exposition according to the capacity of the audience.
Third, the section on awakening through realization and practice.
Regarding these three categories, their names—both ancient and modern—should be understood in full according to their respective meanings.
Within the first category, following the verses of Master Vasubandhu’s *Pradīpa-śāstra*, it is divided into six parts.
He said: "The first three clarify the disciples; the latter three testify to the Teacher’s teaching.
First, 'Thus' refers to the disciple's faith.
These words 'Thus' now declare that [the teaching] is not false."
Second, "I have heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*) indicates that this was not received through hearsay.
Third, "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) indicates that there was a specific occasion for hearing the Dharma.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The time, place, and person are mentioned so as to inspire faith."
There are four masters, five locations, and six capacities.
Now, following the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the first section has five parts:
first, the general manifestation of what has been heard, namely, "Thus have I heard."
There are two times, three masters, four locations, and five capacities.

Now, based on this sutra, these are expanded into six: the first five are as described in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, while the sixth praises the Dharma for possessing ten superior virtues, such as the teaching of the sublime Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.
However, this preface, which describes the establishment of the Buddhist teachings, is also the word of the Buddha.
The *Dharmasaṃgraha Sūtra* states: "Ānanda asked about four matters:
'Who shall be our teacher?'"
Upon what dharma does it rely for its abiding?
How is an evil nature subdued?
What words are placed at the beginning of the sutra?
The Buddha said:
"Precepts can instruct and admonish, and thus may serve as a teacher.
The foundations of mindfulness destroy perversions; one should abide by relying upon them."
The Brahma-dharma of silence subdues those evil persons.
At the beginning of all sutras, six matters are indicated:
first is right practice; second is right understanding; and last is the discernment of the conditions for cultivating understanding and practice while remedying obstacles.
However, these three gates must necessarily rely upon the sacred teachings; therefore, there are exactly four questions, neither fewer nor more.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Anuruddha instructed Ānanda to request four matters, while the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* speaks of Upāli’s instruction; thus, it is said here that both individuals provided the same instruction.
Furthermore, the causes and conditions for the compilation [of the scriptures] are explained in detail, as recorded in a separate transcription.
Paramārtha states:
"The *Vinaya-sūkṣma* (Subtle Vinaya) clarifies this."
"When Ānanda ascended the seat to bring forth the Dharma-treasury, his body was like that of the Buddhas, endowed with all the marks and signs.
Examining the *Jí zàng zhuàn* (Biographies of the Compiler of the Canon) today, it also makes this same statement.
When he descended from his seat, he resumed his original form.
The assembly had three doubts:
first, they doubted that the Buddha’s compassion had arisen from nirvana to further preach the wondrous Dharma.
2. Doubting that a Buddha has come from another direction and is dwelling here to preach the Dharma;
3. Doubting that Ānanda has transformed his body to become a Buddha and is preaching the Dharma for the sake of the assembly.
Therefore, the sūtra begins by stating, "Thus have I heard," in order to inspire faith.

Regarding the term "thus" (evam), the *Fahua zhu* states: "Such are the auspicious signs of response and resonance; 'thus' is a name derived from conforming to the capacities [of beings], and therefore there is nothing that does not establish this designation."
Sentient beings respond through non-action, while the Tathāgata responds by acceding to their capacities.
Since those who transmit the scriptures maintain that the teaching of names arises from this principle of resonance and response, they say: "Thus" (evam).
This should be understood according to Master Sengzhao’s interpretation.
Furthermore, the *Commentary on the Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings* states: "The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is solely for the purpose of manifesting the Suchness (tathatā).
Since only Suchness is what is true, it is called 'Thus' (evam)."
Master Yao said:
"To be free from the five types of slander is what is meant by 'thus' (*tathā*).

The first four phrases are free from the slanders of superimposition (*samāropa*) and so forth; the fifth, 'thus,' refers to this sutra’s cause and effect being neither non-existent nor non-non-existent, which is called the slander of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); and the fourth phrase is called the slander of delusion (*moha*)."
Guangzhai said:
"In this way, he transmits what he has heard; the preceding title cites a single section of the scripture.
That the meaning of such a scripture was personally heard by me from the Buddha serves as a thorough invocation of 'I have heard'."
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty said:
"Such and so-like words are what the Buddha taught; therefore, one says 'Thus' (evam).
The five preceding interpretations are all cited by Master Jizang.
Paramārtha and Chang-er both state:
"In this way, there are three [meanings]:
first, with respect to the Buddha, the fact that the Buddhas of the three periods of time all teach without difference is called 'tathā' (thus); because they teach in common, it is termed 'is' (so)."
Because it is thus, it is trustworthy, for it is taught in the same way.
Second, from the perspective of principle, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is shown to be no different between the past and the present; therefore, it is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*).
It is called "is" (*iti*) because it is spoken in accordance with reality (*tathatā*).
Since it is an expression that accords with principle, being neither increased nor diminished, it is decisively trustworthy; therefore, it is called "thus" (*evam*).

Third, regarding the person: from the perspective of Ānanda, because what he transmits does not differ from the Buddha's teaching, it is called "as it is" (*tathā*); because there is nothing that is not so, it is called "is" (*iti*).
The three interpretations above are those cited by Master Jing and others.
Furthermore,
another interpretation holds that these words indicate the profound essence of a specific section of the scripture, namely the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional.
The ultimate is "as-it-is" (tathatā) and the conventional is "correct" (satya), because it is intended to reveal that the referent is not distinct from these two.
Furthermore, that which accords with principle is called "as-it-is," while the negation of its being false is termed "correct."

Furthermore, it is revealed that the teachings which express the two types of knowledge serve as the causes for those two knowledges: the nature of things as they are (*yathāvad-bhāvikatā*) constitutes "as it is" (*yathā*), and the nature of things in their full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) constitutes "that which is" (*idam*).
Therefore, it is stated below: "They are the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
Furthermore, merit and wisdom are presented as the causes for the two adornments: merit is "thusness" (tathatā), and wisdom is "this" (idam).
Moreover, teaching that accords with principle is called "thusness," while practicing according to that teaching is "this."
Furthermore, the object is the "thusness" (tathatā) and the wisdom is the "is-ness" (tathatva); the contemplation of the true nature of the vehicle and the rider is set forth as the primary heading.
Moreover, the term "thus" (tathā) is an auspicious word.
This phrase is placed at the beginning of all sutras to distinguish them from the scriptures of non-Buddhists and others, which place the two characters "A-yu" at their outset.
Furthermore, the term "thus" (evam) is a demonstrative word that points to what is elucidated in the following section of the text.
The eight explanations above are all the traditional interpretations transmitted by the former masters of this land.
Furthermore, the term "thus" (*evam*) functions according to four meanings:
first, based on analogy.
As it is said: "Such wealth and nobility are like those of Vaiśravaṇa;
such teachings as have been transmitted and heard are like the words of the Buddha, and are certainly the cause for the skillful means of benefit and happiness."
First, it may be that the words and phrases spoken are exactly as I have heard them in the past.
Second, it relies upon the instruction;
as it is said:
"You should recite and study the sūtras and śāstras in this manner.
In this context, 'distant' refers to the instructions of the Buddha, while 'near' refers to the instructions of those who transmit the Dharma."
Or he may address the assembly:
"Listen thus to what I have heard in the past.
Third, [the section] based on questions and answers.
Thus have I heard; thus it was proclaimed.
That is to say, there may be one who asks:
"Did you previously hear what you are about to speak?"
Therefore, he replied:
"Thus have I heard.
Fourth, [the phrase is used] based on permission.
As it is said:
"I shall for your sake contemplate thus, act thus, and speak thus.
This refers to when the assembly of bodhisattvas collectively made this request at the time of the compilation: [Please do so].
"As you have heard, so should you speak.
The Bodhisattva who transmits the Dharma then gave his consent, saying:
"So shall it be spoken, just as I have heard it."
Or one may have faith such that it can be said:
"This matter is thus;
that is, I have heard this Dharma in the past."
This matter is thus; it should be explained up to this point, for there is certainly no difference.
The four interpretations presented above are all the explanations of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* by the Bodhisattva Prabhāmitra and others.
Furthermore, "thus" (evam) is a term of faith and compliance.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "'Thus have I heard' gives rise to faith;
'faithfully receiving and practicing' gives rise to wisdom."
Faith is that which enables entry; wisdom is that which enables transcendence.
Faith is the primary foundation for entering the Dharma; wisdom is the profound art of ultimate realization.
When faith accords with the principles of what is taught, the Way of teacher and disciple is perfected.
"Because of faith, the Dharma that is taught can be followed accordingly.
Because of this following, the relationship between teacher and disciple is established for both the speaker and the listener.
Regarding this faith, there are briefly ten explanations; therefore, it is necessary first to cause faith to arise.
First, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Faith is like the water-clearing jewel, capable of purifying turbid water," for it can remedy the inherent turbidity of lack of faith.
Therefore, among the three essentials—military force, food, and faith—faith must not be abandoned.
2. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Faith is the basis for desire; desire is the basis for diligence. Therefore, the desire for all phenomena is the root.

It is produced by attention (*manasikāra*), accumulated by contact (*sparśa*), sustained by feeling (*vedanā*), dominated by concentration (*samādhi*), supreme in wisdom (*prajñā*), firm in liberation (*vimukti*), and culminates in renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*)."
Since faith is the basis for desire, it is mentioned first.

Third, those who study the Buddha-dharma are like great dragon-elephants: they take faith as their trunk, relinquishment as their tusks, mindfulness as their neck, and wisdom as their head; upon their two shoulders, they carry and gather all wholesome dharmas.
This is the teaching of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
Fourth, the Dharma is the hand of the Buddhas, and faith is the hand of sentient beings.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that [the Buddha] "extracts sentient beings from the mire of birth and death."

Since the main body of the scripture is the Buddha’s hand and the introductory section that engenders faith is the hand of sentient beings, the joining of these two hands allows one to reach the other shore and emerge from the mire of birth and death.
The following two interpretations reflect the intent of the *Sūtra of King Suvarṇabhāsa*.
Fifth: Just as one crosses the vast, deep ocean by employing a boat, so too must one cross the river of birth and death by relying on faith to give rise to wisdom.
Sixth, when wandering through a vast wilderness, one uses a staff held in hand to ward off a multitude of bandits;
when wandering through the source of birth and death, one uses the hand of faith to hold the sword of wisdom to ward off the bandits of affliction.
Seventh, while rare treasures and jewels are seen and can be gathered by hand, the jewel of the Dharma is obtained only through provisional faith.
Eighth, because faith is the foremost of the noble riches, it is made to arise first.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "The seven noble riches are faith, ethical discipline, learning, renunciation, wisdom, shame, and dread. Therefore, one first causes faith to arise.
9. Faith is the ladder for ascending to the stage of the noble ones; therefore, among the forty minds, faith is placed first, consisting of the faculty of faith and the power of faith.
Because there is the faculty of faith, all myriad virtues arise from it;
because there is the power of faith, the four māras cannot subdue or overcome one.
Tenth, various treatises state:
"Faith enables one to transcend the evil realms and abandon the causes of poverty and low status; therefore, there are four indestructible faiths.
For this reason, the words "Thus have I heard" are placed at the beginning of all sūtras in order to inspire faith.
Regarding the phrase "I have heard": the Bodhisattva who transmits the Dharma refers to himself, stating that he personally heard this Dharma from the Buddha; therefore, it is called "I have heard."
The "self" (ātman) refers to that which is conventionally designated upon the aggregates (skandhas).
However, there are three types of self:
first, the self as falsely grasped, which refers to the arbitrary conceptions of self held by non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings—conceived either as being like space or as small as a mustard seed.

Second, the provisionally designated self (*prajñaptātman*): this refers to the [provisional] permanence, bliss, self, and purity; it is the designation of a "self" within non-self (*anātman*) for the sake of leading those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), so that they may relinquish the fruit of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
This refers to what is said in the sūtras: "The Buddhas sometimes speak of a self, and at other times speak of non-self.
Within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is neither self nor non-self.

This means that for the sake of śrāvakas, [the Buddha] taught impermanence and so forth to eliminate the four inversions (*viparyāsa*) imagined by ordinary beings, and thus spoke of the absence of a sentient being or a self.

However, because phenomena possess causes, the Buddha later taught the Bodhisattvas that they are permanent and blissful, in order to eliminate the four faults that arise when [the truth] is withheld from those of the Two Vehicles.
Since the intrinsic nature of all these phenomena is fundamentally free from both self and non-self, they are described as "permanent" and "self"; thus, these are merely provisional designations.

Third, the "self conventionally renowned in the world" refers to the self commonly transmitted in the world through surnames such as Zhang or Wang, and personal names such as Devadatta; this is the self that circulates in the world.

Now, those who transmit the Dharma follow worldly convention when they refer to themselves using the term "I. This differs from the previous two types [of self], for it is not a false attachment and is not a mere provisional designation; nevertheless, its essence is precisely the "self" that is non-self (*anātman*).
Question:
Since the Buddhas’ teaching of the Dharma fundamentally aims to eliminate the grasping at a self, why did Ānanda not refer to himself by name, but instead use the word "I"?
Answer:
From the perspective of principle, it should also be called by its specific name; however, for three reasons, it is generally referred to simply as "self" (ātman).
First, to show that one does not deviate from worldly convention:

although the fundamental tenet reveals the ultimate truth, the words do not deviate from the conventional. Although there is no self, the name "self" is nevertheless established, because one wishes to demonstrate that the ultimate truth is not separate from the conventional.

Second, "I" (Aham) signifies the sense of mastery and sovereignty. Ānanda has heard much and retained what he has heard; his hearing has been accumulated, and he is fully equipped with the three types of wisdom, maintaining both the words and their meanings. Thus, within the holy teachings, he possesses sovereign mastery as a dhāraṇī-holder.
If one were to say "Ānanda heard this Dharma," although it would refer to his own person, it would lack the sense of having attained mastery over the Dharma.
To manifest the meaning of attaining mastery over the Dharma, he says "I heard" rather than "the Joyful One."
Third, the word "I" (aham) carries the sense of intimacy; it is commonly said in the world that when one says, "I saw this" or "I heard this," it serves as personal testimony.
If one were to simply say in general terms that "Ānanda heard it," it might imply that he did not hear it directly from the Buddha but received it through transmission from another.
Now, because Ānanda heard this directly from the World-Honored One and did not hear it through another’s transmission, he refers to himself as "I.
For these three reasons, he does not call himself "Ānanda," but simply says, "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam).
"Was heard" (*śruta*) means that consciousness arises from the ear-faculty (*śrotrendriya*) to listen to and receive what is spoken.
Here, setting aside the specific faculty of the ear, we refer to it collectively as "I," hence the phrase "heard by me.
Regarding the term "was heard," the various schools (*nikāya*) hold differing views.

Now, according to the Mahāyāna, it is only when the sense organ (*indriya*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), mental factors (*caitta*), and the object (*viṣaya*) come together in harmony that it is termed "hearing.
Nevertheless, because the sense organ possesses five superior characteristics compared to consciousness and the other factors, it is designated as "hearing."
Both the *Abhidharma* and Nāgārjuna state this:

if one merely hears a sound, it occurs only in the ear; however, when it also takes names and so forth as its object, it occurs within the mind. Therefore, it is the mind alone that should be designated as "hearing."
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Hearing refers to inference (*anumāna*).
That which is called "hearing" by means of the ear serves as the gateway for the mind through its direct hearing of sounds.

Furthermore, because those who hear the teachings do so by means of the ear, that which is accomplished based on hearing is collectively termed "hearing"; and because it is obtained through the ear, the ear itself is designated as "hearing."

However, the ear cannot directly apprehend the specific names and other attributes of phenomena; as explained in the *Śrutamayībhūmi* regarding the discourse on skillful means, because one accomplishes the Dharma through hearing, both [the process and the result] are termed "hearing with the ear. This is like seeing a second moon or a whirling firebrand. For instance, when King Virūḍhaka spoke in order to kill the Śākyas, all those words were functions of the mental consciousness alone, as his own ears did not perceive them.
Question:

At that time, Ānanda personally saw the Buddha speak and personally realized and understood what the Buddha spoke. Why did he not say, "Thus have I seen, thus have I realized, thus have I known," but instead simply say, "Thus have I heard"?
Answer:
There are three reasons.

First, because one who wishes to realize profound principles and awaken to the essential meaning of what is expounded must rely upon hearing the teachings; seeing, awakening, knowing, and so forth are not the primary means for attaining realization of these principles. Although these may also constitute actual seeing and so on, one can only say, "I have heard it."
Second, the Sahā world takes sound as its Buddha-work; because it seeks to distinguish itself from other Buddha-lands, it speaks only of "hearing.

In other Buddha-lands where Buddha-work is performed through light, exquisite fragrances, flavors, and so forth, the beginning of the sutra could likewise speak of "I see," "I perceive," or "I cognize";
however, to distinguish this land from those, it speaks only of "hearing."
Third, it is intended to show that the awakening of wisdom and enlightenment can only be attained through the process of perfuming (*vāsanā*).

If one does not hear the true Dharma, the three types of wisdom cannot arise. Therefore, the sūtra begins with the word "hearing" (*śruta*), so that the perfuming of both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) states may increase; as these mutually reinforce one another, they are able to produce supramundane and mundane fruits and so forth. For this reason, it speaks only of "hearing."
Question:
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and other sutras, the Buddha himself stated:
"From the time I attained enlightenment until my final nirvana, I did not speak a single word during that interval."
"For what reason does Ānanda misrepresent the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma by claiming 'I have heard it'?
Furthermore, the *Śīṃśapā-leaf Simile Sūtra* states: 'The teachings already spoken by me are like the leaves in my hand; the teachings not yet spoken are like the leaves in the forest.'"
It is clear that the Buddha preached the Dharma.
Now, you say "I heard," yet you also say it was not preached; how can these two statements be so contradictory?
The answer is as follows:

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "According to one interpretation, through the dominant power of the Tathāgata’s compassion and original vows as a contributing condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the aspects of word and meaning arise within the consciousness of the listener.

Although these aspects of word and meaning arise directly dependent on the power of the listener’s own roots of virtue, they are termed 'the Buddha’s teaching' with respect to their predominant condition."
"Because it is manifested by one's own mind through the power of the auditory faculty, it is called 'I heard.

This master’s intention is to say that the Buddha possesses three qualities—namely, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*jñāna*), and compassion (*karuṇā*)—and that these three qualities constitute his essence; in reality, he does not preach the Dharma.

Because of his original vow to benefit sentient beings within the causal stage, his great compassion arises constantly; when the virtuous karma of sentient beings—who have long practiced and now encounter a Buddha—reaches maturity, it appears as if they hear the Buddha preaching the Dharma upon their own conscious minds, manifesting as if through instruction, yet in reality, he does not speak.
It is like the mother of Zeng Shen, who bit her finger; Zeng Shen felt pain in his heart and, knowing his mother was calling him, returned home.

His mother had indeed said nothing, but merely harbored the thought of longing for her son; through the mutual resonance of wind and clouds, his son’s heart pained him as if it were the appearance of his mother calling, and he hurried back exactly as she had described.
Now, the Buddha is like a mother and sentient beings are likened to guests; whether words are spoken or not, the principle remains the same.
It is also like a woman who invited a bhikṣu to preach the Dharma, yet the bhikṣu departed privately without actually preaching for her.
When women attain the Way, they say it is due to the kindness of the bhikṣus.
Taking the bhikṣu as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), their minds become weary of birth and death and they subsequently realize the fruits of the path.

Sentient beings take the Buddha as the dominant condition; thus, their own minds transform and arise in the semblance of the teachings of the Three Vehicles. From the perspective of this powerful condition, it is called "the Buddha's teaching," yet in reality, the Buddha has no words.
This statement, "I have heard," has the same meaning. According to one interpretation:
by the power of the superior conditions of the roots of merit and the original vows of the hearer, the aspects of word and meaning arise within the consciousness of the Tathāgata.
The characteristics of the meaning of this text arise from the Buddha’s roots of goodness for the benefit of others; thus, it is called "spoken by the Buddha.

Although the consciousness-mind of the listener does not directly perceive them, they appear as if those characteristics were being clearly and distinctly proclaimed; therefore, it is said, "I have heard."

The intention of this master is as follows: The Buddha possesses the five aggregates, the eighteen elements, and so forth, and performs the actual work of teaching the Dharma for the benefit of others. Although he lacks the conceptual differentiation that gives rise to cognitive grasping (*ālambana*), he spontaneously and eternally teaches the Dharma according to the capacities of beings, bringing about great benefit and happiness—just like a *maṇi* jewel or the drum of Śakra. Though these lack the intention to rain down various jewels or to speak or remain silent for the sake of Śakra, they nonetheless perform their functions.
Because the Śakra-devendra’s wholesome karma evokes that power, the drum sounds spontaneously; hearing it, the Śakra-devendra becomes naturally alerted.

Now, the Buddha is likewise: though he has no intentional discrimination regarding whether to speak or not to speak, when the causes for sentient beings’ wholesome karma to hear the Dharma have matured, the Tathāgata spontaneously manifests the act of preaching the Dharma.
The teaching herein is like a phantom person preaching the Dharma to another phantom person; names are by nature detached and devoid of syllables, which is itself liberation.

It is not as one falsely clings to—namely, that names are fixedly attached to phenomena, or that there truly exist a speaker, a listener, and something spoken. Therefore, the Buddha said that not a single word was preached.
Now, as for those who preach the Dharma, there is neither preaching nor demonstrating; it is like a phantom person preaching to a phantom person, which is not non-existent.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The preaching of the Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent; all phenomena are established in dependence upon causes and conditions."
Since the Buddha had preached the Dharma and Ānanda personally heard it, it is called "Thus have I heard.

Regarding this, there are two interpretations: the first is the explanation of a class of masters such as Nāgasena and Asvabhāva; the latter is the doctrine of masters such as Dharmapāla and Prajñākaragupta.
One should understand that the statement "Thus have I heard" is intended to avoid the faults of addition, subtraction, or deviation from the original.

That is to say, it shows that this Dharma was heard by me directly from the Buddha and not through successive transmission from others; it demonstrates that the hearer is capable and that everything heard is free from the faults of addition, subtraction, or deviation.
It is not like the foolish who lack capability, who—upon hearing anything—might be unable to avoid adding to, subtracting from, or distorting it.

When the Dharma was being compiled, those transmitting the Buddha’s teachings uttered these words at the outset of the Tathāgata’s instruction: "In order to inspire reverence and faith in sentient beings, I say: 'Such is the Dharma as I have heard it from the Buddha. Its phrasing and meaning are definitive, with nothing added and nothing subtracted. Therefore, having heard it correctly, those who hear it should reflect upon it according to reason and constantly apply themselves to diligent practice.
The Sūtra says:
"At one time.
The Commentary states:
Second, the clarification of the time of the teaching, which refers to the auspicious moment of transformation.

On the day the Dharma King inaugurates his transformative work, at the time of the great assembly’s joyful gathering, this—considering the continuous succession of moments without interruption until the teaching and listening are complete—is collectively termed "at one time" according to its respective state.
It is not so; since the letters and other elements differ between the time of speaking and the time of listening, how can they be called "one"?

Herein, "one time" is not defined by a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), nor is it defined by a continuum (*saṃtāna*), nor is it defined by the four periods, the eight periods, or the twelve periods, including the time after the attainment of enlightenment; rather, a certain duration of time is designated as "one time."
However, when the two parties—the speaker and the listener—meet together so that the teaching and the listening reach their conclusion, this is collectively termed "one time.
This is because the speaker has attained *dhāraṇī*, such that when pronouncing a single syllable, he has already expounded all others;
or because the listener has attained the pure faculty of hearing, such that when understanding one syllable, they are able to comprehend all others.
The speaker may speak for many *kṣaṇas* or even for many *kalpas*, and the listener likewise may listen for as long as many *kalpas*.
Therefore, it cannot be fixed that the duration is either a single moment or many *kalpas*.

Because the faculties of those present at a single assembly vary—some being sharp and others dull—the Tathāgata’s supernormal power extends a short moment into a long kalpa and contracts a long kalpa into a short moment. Due to these distinctions of time, there are two interpretations in the treatises:
first, "time" as a conventional designation for the temporal states established upon conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).

For those who speak and listen, the five aggregates and all conditioned formations arise and perish moment by moment, lacking any fixed temporal essence. There exists a provisional dharma that responds to what precedes and induces what follows in the present; it is these dharmas that respond to and are induced by [past causes] which are conventionally designated as the "past" and the "present."

It is said that when the sequence of the provisional phenomena of the two disciples and the five aggregates reaches its conclusion, it is conventionally designated as "time"; therefore, they are collectively termed "one time.

This is like a mathematician who, using a single counting-bead, passes it through various positions and names them one, ten, hundred, thousand, ten-thousand, and so forth; in reality, it is a single object, yet because its horizontal and vertical orientations differ, the names assigned to it vary.

This teaching shows that for a listener, the phenomena of the five aggregates—those that have already existed are called the past, those yet to exist are called the future, and those currently existing are called the present; these are what constitute time, and are thus designated as the three periods.
Now, the complete sequence of events across these three periods of time is collectively termed "one moment" (*ekasamaya*).

Second, within the cognitive consciousness of both the speaker and the listener at this time, the phenomenal aspects (*ākāra*) arise as the substance of the three times; this is the consciousness of time, which—whether referring to a single thought-moment or many eons—is conventionally designated as "one moment" once the sequence of events has reached its conclusion.

It is like a person who, within a dream, dreams of many lifetimes and the cycle of birth and death as the flux of the three periods of time; yet upon awakening, there is only a single deluded mind, and one realizes that the three periods of time do not exist.

Now, to explain this by way of principle: the substance of time is likewise so. There is only the deluded mind that transforms and appears as the three periods; when the sequence of events reaches its conclusion, it is collectively termed "one period.

Because this is explained according to its meaning, it is solely the object-condition (*ālambana*) of the mental faculty (*manas*), subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Why not speak separately of the twelve periods and so forth?
For example, regarding pure and impure locations, or the divisions of day and night, the directions are not fixed.
Since a location has fixed directions, one speaks of it as simply "one" within the context of time.
Question:

Since the intermediate states (*antarābhava*) involve both purity and impurity and are not fixed, why do you speak of them as being only one? Furthermore, since directions and times differ, what prevents us from speaking of them as being fixed as well?
Ordinary beings perceive impure places, while we know that the Sages dwell in pure lands.
Why not discuss this separately and state that it refers to a different time, as one does with other cases?
Answer:

It cannot be definitively stated whether it is a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) or many eons (*kalpa*), because it is understood according to the context; therefore, it is spoken of in general terms simply as "at one time."

Regarding the expansion or contraction of the duration of kalpas: it may be through consciousness alone that they are contracted or extended; or through the dual negation of what is grasped as real; or through false phenomena based on the other-dependent nature; or through equality in terms of the true nature; or through the empowerment of the power of the sages; thus, there is expansion and contraction.
There is no need for weary doubt; the meaning should be explained according to the standard principles.
The Sūtra says:
"The Bhagavat."
The commentary states:
From here on is the third section, which specifically discusses the Teacher.
Desiring to praise the excellence of the Dharma by way of its source in a superior person, it follows that the Dharma must itself be superior.
Within the section on manifesting the Teacher, there are two parts:
first, the designation of his name; second, the praise of his virtues.
This is the designation of his name.
The ancient name is Bhagavat, which corresponds in meaning to the title "World-Honored One" (Shizun).
However, its full significance remains incomplete; thus it is not translated [into Chinese], as the Han language lacks this term.

The eighty-third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Sitting serenely and at ease upon the sublime seat of Bodhi, he spontaneously crushes and destroys all demonic armies; because of his great power, he is called Bhagavān."

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The term *bhagavat* operates according to six meanings: sovereignty (*vaśitā*), brilliance (*tejas*), majesty (*saubhāgya*), renown (*yaśas*), auspiciousness (*śrī*), and nobility (*gurutva*)."
One should understand that these six kinds of distinct meanings are collectively designated by the term *bhagavat*.
The intended meaning here is that whoever is referred to by this sound "Bhagavat" must necessarily possess these qualities.
All such qualities are possessed by all Tathāgatas in every respect and can never be separated from them; therefore, a Tathāgata is called Bhagavat.
This is because all Tathāgatas are forever unbound by any afflictions, and thus possess the sense of mastery.
Because it is refined and tempered by the fiercely blazing fire of wisdom, it possesses the sense of being "blazing.
Because it is adorned with the thirty-two excellent marks of a Great Man, it possesses the sense of being "majestic."
Because all supreme qualities are perfected and there is nothing he does not know, it possesses the meaning of "renown.
Because all those in the world draw near to him, make offerings, and praise him, it possesses the meaning of "auspiciousness."

Because he possesses all virtues and constantly exerts skillful means to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings without weariness or fatigue, he possesses the sense of being "venerable" (*bhaṭṭāraka*).
Alternatively, because he is able to destroy the four Māras, the enemies, he is named Bhagavān.

The four māras and adversaries are the māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), the māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), and the māra of the Lord of Heaven (*devaputra-māra*).
They are called "māras" because they destroy the roots of virtue and other wholesome qualities cultivated by sentient beings.

Entering the third eon, one destroys the death-māra of afflictions; as one approaches the diamond-like mind, one seizes and destroys the celestial māra; and with the arising of the path of liberation, one destroys the aggregate-māra.

If one discusses their characteristics: at the time of the adamantine mind, he destroyed the demon of afflictions; beneath the Bodhi tree, he destroyed the demon of Māra the Lord of Heaven; by relinquishing the fifth portion of his lifespan and entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, he destroyed the demon of the aggregates; and by further remaining for three months, he destroyed the demon of death.
In its ultimate sense, all that disturbs and agitates a bodhisattva is termed "affliction" (*kleśa*); both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) constitute this.
When the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) arises, it permanently destroys the demon of afflictions (*kleśamāra*).

Because the seeds of the two obstacles still exist, when the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) arises, it permanently destroys the two demons of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*) and death (*mṛtyumāra*).
This treatise is composed based on the two types of death;
as for the subduing of the celestial Māras, it is not mentioned in the text.

Now, according to one interpretation, a Bodhisattva of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) should have already subdued the celestial Māras upon achieving the eightfold manifestation of enlightenment (*aṣṭa-lakṣaṇa-buddhatva*).
Alternatively, it is at the sixth mind of the tenth stage that one first subdues the celestial Māras;
because at this point one is eternally free from birth and death and has emerged from the triple world, one is able to subdue the celestial Māras.
Alternatively, upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), one immediately subdues the celestial Māras.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that from the first bhūmi upward, one is free from the four coarse māras, which are abandoned or retained according to circumstance;
thus, one who destroys the four māras is named Bhagavān.
Question:
The Buddha is endowed with the ten titles; for what reason does the Buddha instruct Ānanda to recite these names at the beginning of the sūtras?
Answer:
Because all people in the world universally revere this single name, all non-Buddhists likewise address their own teachers as Bhagavān.
Furthermore, this single name subsumes all virtues, whereas other names do not; for this reason, this name is placed at the beginning of every sutra.
Although the Teacher is designated at the head of each sutra, these designations differ from one another.

For example, in the newly translated *Sūtra on Praising the Merits of the Mahāyāna*, it is stated that [the Buddha] dwells within the Dharma-nature land—the Great Palace of Adorned Merits, which is the treasury of the dharma-realm and the sphere of practice for all Buddhas—and there he speaks from the perspective of the dharma-body.

As for that *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, it was taught by the Saṃbhogakāya within the great palace established upon the king of great jewel-flowers, situated amidst eighteen perfectly pure buddha-fields, and adorned with the seven treasures in the most supreme radiance, as extensively described therein.

Although the opening of this sutra proclaims the Buddha’s true virtues, it differs slightly from other sutras in that the setting is within the mani palace of the Heavenly King Vaśavartin in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations, where the teaching was delivered by an emanation body.
However, although the Land of Dharma-nature is inhabited solely by Buddhas, Bodhisattvas such as Biao-de-yang-hua are also present in that assembly.
Furthermore, although that Pure Land consists only of bodhisattvas, the sūtras also state that there are various devas and nāgas therein.

Although this sutra speaks only of the assembly arrayed in the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, it specifically designates the great bodhisattvas who have perfected the ten stages; these collectively clarify how a single substance is perceived differently by various beings.
The *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* states: "The manifested transformation body is not the true Buddha, nor is it the speaker of the Dharma.

In the teaching of the Dharma, there is no dualistic grasping; there is no speaking, as it is free from the characteristics of words. Thus, it attributes all merit to the source, taking the *dharmakāya* as the true body, while other bodies are not the [true] body.
The Dharma-body is explained as having two aspects: speech and non-speech.
"Body" (kāya) is a collective term for the meanings of substance, support, and accumulation.

The Dharma-body serves as the general support for the body and the fundamental basis for speech; only from this do the [other] two bodies arise. It is neither a permanent body nor is it impermanent speech.

The *Prajñā* takes the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as its primary tenet, with the intention of eliminating all marks (*nimitta*). Since both the two bodies and the two teachings possess marks, they are termed "non-body teachings.

In reality, these two bodies also possess body-teachings; however, because one must realize the principle of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*) in order to understand the profound meaning of the Mahāyāna name and its significance, the marvelous land is provisionally employed to manifest the profundity of this sutra.

Regarding the statement that within the *dharmatā*-realm (*dharmatā-kṣetra*) there is verbal praise extolling the merits of the Mahāyāna: in reality, the *vyūha-puṣpa* (adorned flowers) reside only in the pure land (*śuddhakṣetra*), not in the *dharmatā*-realm.
Within the *dharmatā*-realm, there is neither body nor speech; by what means, then, could Bodhisattvas have hearing and so forth?

Furthermore, there is no fault in explaining that the correct wisdom (samyag-jñāna) which internally realizes true emptiness (śūnyatā) is said to "dwell in the Dharma-nature land" (dharmatā-kṣetra), while the subsequent wisdom (pṛṣṭha-labdha-jñāna) that gives rise to compassion and transformation is said to "dwell in the Pure Land" (viśuddha-kṣetra), and so forth.

The eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, behold this dwelling in the transformed land (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*). The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* seeks to reveal the characteristics of the eighteen kinds of perfectly pure lands; it explains the five dharmas as the actual virtues of the Tathāgata, employing the discourse on the pure land to manifest the profundity of the sūtra.

In reality, when Bodhisattvas’ correct wisdom accords with the truth, they likewise abide in the Dharma-nature; when devas and nāgas hear the Dharma, they likewise abide in the land of transformation.

When this Prajñā-pāramitā contemplates and realizes the true mark (dharmatā), all Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas take the absence of marks as their foundation; they truly all abide in the Dharma-nature body while manifesting in the Pure Land. Nevertheless, to manifest the profundity of their compassion and the thickness of their kindness, and to extol the virtues of the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya), it is said that they abide in the land of transformation to preach.

Regarding those who hear the Dharma, they are likewise merely designated as "superior persons" to correspond with the Buddha’s actual virtues, manifesting them by means of the transformation land (*nirmāṇakāya-kṣetra*).
The specific intention will be explained below.

Now, when it is said that the Bhagavān should preach according to what is appropriate, this reveals that all three bodies (*trikāya*) are capable of preaching the Dharma, and that the retinues all have the sense of dwelling in the three lands; it is simply the virtues of the recompense body (*sambhogakāya*) that are being designated here.

That being so, since the scriptural text does not explicitly state that [the Buddha] resides in his own land of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*), one should infer the nature of the Buddha-land by analogy with the Buddha’s virtues and his dwelling place.

Here, the Bhagavat, based on the specific virtues described below, resides in the actual land of retribution of the *saṃbhogakāya*. This is a land of transformation (*nirmāṇakṣetra*) that manifests the excellence of the body to reveal the supremacy of the Dharma; it cites the location of the transformation to reveal the profundity of the sutra. This is intended to show that both compassion and wisdom are produced through the cultivation of phenomenal dharmas (*dharmas as objects*), and do not refer to the body and land of the *dharmatākāya* (the body of reality).
The Sūtra says:
First, the wondrously virtuous accomplishment of the various rare and supreme merits of the Wisdom of Equality that sustains the vajra-state of all Tathāgatas.
Second, having already been able to skillfully obtain the jewel-crown of consecration of all Tathāgatas, one transcends the three realms.
Third, he has already been able to skillfully attain the Great Avalokiteśvara of the Pervasive Vajra Wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
Fourth, he has already attained the Great Seal of Wondrous Wisdom that definitively realizes all dharmas of all Tathāgatas.
Fifth, they have already perfectly realized the seal of the ultimate emptiness, quiescence, and equality of all Tathāgatas.
Sixth, they have attained skillful mastery in accomplishing all activities, both those to be performed and those already undertaken, without exception.
Seventh, they are able to fulfill all the various aspirations of all sentient beings according to their wishes, provided those are blameless.
Eighth, they are already well-established in the equality of the three times, which is eternally uninterrupted, inexhaustible, vast, and universally illuminating.
"The nine [aspects of] body, speech, and mind are like vajras, equal to all Tathāgatas, immovable and indestructible.
Commentary:
Herein, these nine phrases praise the virtues of the Tathāgata.
Based on various sūtras and śāstras, I shall provide a brief threefold explanation.
First, I will explain according to the text of this sūtra itself.

The first line offers a general praise of the Tathāgata while encompassing his secondary virtues; the remaining eight lines offer specific praises of the Tathāgata, enumerating the distinct varieties of his virtues.
However, the main body of the text below consists of fourteen sections, which manifest the fourteen true virtues of the World-Honored One.
Now, this first sentence provides a general indication of all these virtues, while the subsequent sentences specifically assign them to their respective gates of merit (*guṇa-dharmamukha*).

Regarding "the Vajra-holding Wisdom of Equality," this refers to the virtue of surpassing the three realms through the second consecration of the precious crown; it corresponds to the third section among the fourteen sections.
The Dharma-gate of the Universal Victory that Subdues All Evils is also manifested by the fifth Dharma-gate, the Treasury of Wisdom for the Empowerment of the Dharma Kings.

To cite one virtue and two types of Dharma-gates as examples of their various rare and supreme merits is to refer collectively to all the excellent virtues contained within the remaining seven phrases; it is because it would be impossible to fully enumerate each and every Dharma-gate found throughout the twelve subsequent sections.
This concludes the general explanation.
To explain it specifically: "sublime" (*praṇīta*) refers to its qualities being subtle; "excellent" (*śubha*) refers to the fact that no one other than a Buddha can fully fathom it.
Furthermore, what the followers of our own tradition do not understand is called "sublime," while what those of external paths do not know is called "excellent."
Furthermore, wisdom that is profound and difficult to fathom is called "wondrous" (miao), while merit that is subtle and beyond recognition is termed "good" (shan).
As for the term "accomplishment" (chengjiu), it signifies the sense of being able to manifest [the result] spontaneously and with mastery.
Moreover, the actual attainment of perfection is what is meant by "accomplishment."
"All Tathāgatas" is used to manifest that the virtues of the Buddhas are shared among all Buddhas; because they are shared, these Buddha-virtues are worthy of veneration and constitute true virtue.
In the Sanskrit language it is called *tathāgata*; formerly it was translated as *duōtuó'jiādù*, which here is translated as "Tathāgata."

The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "Because he is without falsehood, he is called the Tathāgata. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "'Tathā' means that because he does not change or alter the sūtras and other teachings as taught by the Buddhas of the past, he is called 'Tathā. 'Gata' means that because he has come from the pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eleven kinds of emptiness to nirvāṇa, he is called 'Gata.'"

This means that, just as the Buddhas and others preach the sublime Dharma, proceeding from the cultivation of the myriad practices to the attainment of nirvana, it is therefore said that they are not false; this is the meaning of "Tathāgata."
Furthermore, because his words are never false and he always practices truthful speech, he has arrived at the state of Buddhahood; thus, he is called the Tathāgata.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Among the ten titles, the first is the general introduction."

If one abides within birth and death, yet by practicing sublime conduct proceeds to the state of Buddhahood, they are named Sugata, titled the Well-Gone; in ancient times this was called Xiugeda (Sugata).
If one abides on the other shore through causes such as those of a Buddha, one is called a Tathāgata.
The term *tathā* signifies both "coming" and "going," while *āgata* signifies both "leaving" and "arriving"; the same applies here.
"Vajra" is a metaphor.
Because the wisdom of equality can harmonize all evils, subdue afflictions, and universally triumph over everything—just as a vajra is capable of crushing and destroying—it is called "vajra."

Regarding "sustaining" (sthiti-dhara): upon reaching the rank of Dharma King, one is able to become the supreme sovereign of all the three realms; all the sublime dharmas existing in the world are sustained by this wisdom.
That which prevents them from being destroyed is called "abiding" (sthiti), and that which assists their growth is called "sustaining" (dhṛti).
Furthermore, this wisdom of equality is the treasury of all wisdoms; all merit and wisdom take this as their cause.

This is able to sustain all the virtues of the Buddhas and is able to extinguish all delusions; it is named "Vajra Sustenance" (Vajradhara), and this is the function of the Wisdom of Equality (Samatājñāna).
Internally it is able to maintain [the state], and externally it is able to destroy [adversaries].

As for the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), it is not the second of the four wisdoms; rather, it is the wisdom that can realize the ultimate empty and quiescent nature of equality, which is named the wisdom of equality. This is precisely the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*), the correct wisdom within the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), which is truly able to sever afflictions as the path of uninterrupted continuity (*ānantaryamārga*), like a vajra.

If it serves as the foundation for abiding in all virtues and acts as the fundamental wisdom capable of destroying [delusions], it is the wisdom of equality within the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
If it is able to destroy attachment to both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa and abides in non-abiding, it is the wisdom of equality realized by the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manas*).

If one can destroy all afflictions of the two vehicles and ordinary beings, and abide in the merit of compassion and benefiting others, this constitutes the wisdom of equality of the nature of accomplishment.

Now, by means of right principle, among all forms of wisdom, each according to its appropriate application, realizes the equality of intrinsic nature; this is capable of destroying conceptual construction, the two obstacles, and so forth.
This foundation of all virtues is called the Vajra-Abiding Wisdom of Equality.
It is the fundamental pursuit of all bodhisattvas, like a jeweled crown in the stage of consecration.
Its nature is untainted, free from the bonds of the triple world, and forever devoid of conceptual discrimination.
This passage concludes the first quality mentioned below.
The remaining qualities are not limited to one, hence they are called "various.
Having been unattainable since beginningless time, they are called "rare"; being accomplished by the Buddha alone, they are called "supreme."
The accumulation of the power of the path is termed "merit" (*guṇa*).
This term generally encompasses what follows, which one should understand for oneself.
