The second phrase, "Having already been well-granted the precious crown of initiation by all Tathāgatas, one transcends the triple world," is manifested in the thirteenth [section] among the fourteen subsequent sections, namely the Dharma-gate of Universal Victory in Subduing All Evil, and the fifth, the Dharma-gate of the Treasury of Initiation Wisdom.
The commentary on the lower sutra states: "If one bestows the worldly consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one shall obtain the fruit of the supramundane consecration.

In the Western Regions, when a prince of the Kṣatriya caste is about to receive the position of king, he first invites virtuous Brahmins and others to serve as his preceptors. He mounts a thousand-li elephant and takes water from the four great oceans; using auspicious *kuśa* grass, he moistens that ocean water and sprinkles it upon the crown of the prince’s head to purify him. Having performed this great auspicious rite, once the four quarters have submitted, he then receives the royal throne.
The ancient translations referred to him as a "Kṣatriya water-sprinkled king," while the new translations call him a "Kṣatriya lineage consecrated great king.
The king's person must necessarily be of the Kṣatriya lineage.

He requested a brahmin to serve as preceptor and perform the consecration upon his crown; because the brahmins are a lineage that cultivates the holy life and pure precepts by nature, the kṣatriya requested them to consecrate him. This was the ritual for emulating and receiving the position of Dharma King.

This refers to the Bodhisattva at the ultimate stage of the tenth ground, who is born in the Great Maheśvara Palace within the Form Realm. Seated upon the center of a lotus pedestal, he is about to enter the Vajra-samādhi and receive the rank of Buddha. Surpassing all other bodhisattvas, he is the most honored among them; as the eldest son of the Buddhas, he is called the Crown Prince (*kumārabhūta*). The Buddhas of the ten directions serve as his preceptors and teachers, each extending their hand of wisdom and their right arm to pour the pure Dharma-water of the Buddhas of the three periods over his crown. "Crown" here refers to both the heart-crown and the head-crown. This removes the defilements of the two obstacles and the tainted impurities accumulated since beginningless time, and fills him with the position of a supreme Dharma King—pure, untainted, immaculate, and sublime.

Just as a worldly crown prince, having been consecrated, is about to receive the royal throne, donning the king’s crown, wearing the king’s robes, and occupying the king’s palace; so too is the Crown Prince of the Buddha-Dharma.

He is about to receive the position of Dharma-King and Lord of Dharma, donning the Buddha’s crown—namely, the Knowledge of All Things (*sarvajñā*) and the Knowledge of All Aspects (*sarvākārajñā*). Because these are worn and upheld upon the head of the Buddha’s mind, they are the Perfection of Insight (*prajñāpāramitā*). This dharma of merit is a truly precious jewel; among the seven noble riches (*saptadhanāni*), it is called the "riches of wisdom. Therefore, this crown is named the "Jewel Crown."
One dons the Dharma-robe of the merits of the Buddhas of the two limits; this is the superior garment of shame, modesty, gentleness, and patience.
This crown of wisdom is a treasury of great knowledge, for all wholesome dharmas arise because of it.

Abiding in the empty and tranquil jeweled palaces of the Buddhas of the ten directions, because they wear such crowns, robes, and so forth, the water of afflictions poured by beginningless evil associates upon their hearts and crowns—the crown of ignorance and ugliness worn upon the heads of the minds of birth and death, and the harsh, stubborn, and wrathful evil garments of shamelessness and lack of remorse to which birth and death cling—are all completely extinguished and forever abandoned. They shall never again enter the prison of the triple world; therefore, this is called the Dharma Gate of Subduing All Evils and Universal Victory, and it is also called the Dharma Gate of the Treasury of Wisdom for Consecration.
Because of this, he is the lord of the three realms; having emerged from the bonds of birth and death associated with outflows (*āsrava*), he transcends the three realms.
His own essence being without outflows is termed "pervasive" (*vibhu*).
Therefore, the subsequent scripture states: "If one bestows the worldly position of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one shall attain the fruit of the supramundane position of the Dharma King.

Regarding the third phrase, "The All-Vajra Wisdom Great Avalokiteśvara," this refers to the twelfth among the fourteen sections below: the Dharma-gate of the Supreme Treasury Pervading and Sustaining All Sentient Beings. This means that because the Buddha has fully realized that all sentient beings are the *tathāgatagarbha*, and because the essential body of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is omnipresent, he is able to realize that the *tathāgatagarbha* pervades all sentient beings.
This realizing wisdom is called the "Pervasive Vajra Wisdom" because it utterly destroys all obstacles of birth and death.

Nevertheless, out of compassion, one observes the physical, verbal, and mental activities of sentient beings and manifests [oneself] at the appropriate time for those who may be rescued and delivered.
Therefore, all sentient beings are the treasury of the vajra, because they are consecrated by the vajra-treasury;
they are all the treasury of the true Dharma, because everything proceeds in accordance with the correct word;
they are all the treasury of sublime activity, because all undertakings and applications depend upon them.
Because he initiates the three types of action by observing sentient beings, he is called Avalokiteśvara.
Because he provides benefit and happiness according to the needs of those who seek his mindfulness—without fail regarding time, place, the Dharma, and so forth—he is the Great Avalokiteśvara.
This is like the events manifested by the venerable Bhikṣuṇī of Kucha.

As for the fourth phrase, "The Seal of the Great Sublime Wisdom that Resolutely [Comprehends] All Dharmas," it refers to the second among the fourteen sections below: the Gate of Manifesting Complete Enlightenment through the Prajñā-principle of the Tranquil Dharma-nature.
All phenomena in their entirety do not exceed two categories:
first, wisdom; second, objects. Wisdom refers to vajra-wisdom, and objects refer to all phenomena.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
First is that which expresses (the signifier), and second is that which is expressed (the signified). The signifier refers to phenomena (dharma), and the signified refers to their meaning (artha).

Now, it is revealed that the World-Honored One has attained definitive realization regarding these two pairs of phenomena, such that he is free from all doubt; the wisdom capable of knowing this is called the Great Seal of Wondrous Wisdom.

This Seal of Wisdom (jñānamudrā) stabilizes two pairs of dharmas; being free from the net of all doubts, it is called "sublime" (praṇīta) as it cannot be fathomed by the foolish and ignorant. Because its divine function is inconceivable, it is further called "great" (mahat). That is to say, through contemplation, the Seal of Wisdom stabilizes all dharmas so that there is no doubt.
Regarding the fifth phrase, "The Seal of the Ultimate Emptiness, Quiescence, and Equality of All Tathāgatas," this refers to the five dharma-gates within the fourteen subsequent sections.

First, the Dharma-gate of the Profoundly Subtle and Pure Nature of All Phenomena; Fourth, the Dharma-gate of the Purification of the Seal of Equal Wisdom; Seventh, the Dharma-gate of the Wheel of Letters Free from All Proliferation; Eighth, the Dharma-gate of Entering the Equality of the Vast Wheel; and Eleventh, the Dharma-gate of the Supreme Equality of Nature.

This means that whereas in the past one falsely conceptualized all phenomena as existing, now one is free from such false conceptualization and grasping, which has been forever eliminated. Since that which was grasped no longer exists and that which is realized is fully perfected, the permanent abandonment of all delusions is called "purity."

These various deluded thoughts are ultimately empty in essence; all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane realms, whether defiled or pure, are without exception empty and quiescent. The essential nature of this emptiness and quiescence is True Suchness (tathatā), which is the equal nature of all phenomena.
This principle is determined to pervade all phenomena and is therefore termed a "seal" (*mudrā*).
Because the Buddha has attained this suchness (*tathatā*) in its entirety, he is called "one who has well-realized it.

However, the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*, in its explanation of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) among the twenty kinds of emptiness, states: "It is called ultimate emptiness because one contemplates emptiness for the sake of constantly benefiting sentient beings."
This means that for the sake of sentient beings, one contemplates emptiness specifically, or contemplates the sentient beings who are the objects [of that concern] as empty.
This contemplation—that sentient beings and so forth are ultimately unapprehendable and ultimately empty—is called "ultimate emptiness" (atyanta-śūnyatā).
This ultimate emptiness and quiescence is entirely equal within all sentient beings and all phenomena.

This nature of equality among persons and phenomena seals all dharmas as being ultimately empty; for whether it be that which is conceptually grasped or the principle of the two kinds of emptiness, all are ultimately empty.
This interpretation is precisely the primary meaning of the first gate, the profound, subtle, and pure Dharma-door of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
The remaining four gates should be understood accordingly based on what follows; however, for fear of excessive prolixity, they are not explained here in full.

The sixth phrase, "He attains skillful accomplishment without remainder in all tasks to be performed by all causal agents," reveals the merit manifested in the tenth Dharma-gate among the fourteen sections below, titled "The Treasury of Wisdom for Skillfully Subduing."
That which is to be subdued refers to the faults of the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), defilements (*mala*), anger (*krodha*), resentment (*pratigha*), and so forth.

This means that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is himself able to subdue such faults as anger and resentment, and is likewise able to subdue all sentient beings' losses, such as the entanglements and defilements.

Whether they be great or small, virtuous or non-virtuous, arising from conditions, or consisting of fetters and defilements—the Tathāgata is skillfully able to subdue them all; having perfected this wisdom, he has exhausted everything without exception or remainder.

Therefore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, having perfected his own wisdom, has subdued all afflictions and calamities; he is likewise able to subdue the afflictions such as the fetters and impurities of all sentient beings, and causes them to attain even the Bodhi of a Buddha. This is called skillfully accomplishing everything without remainder.

However, because all skillful means capable of subduing the various entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), defilements (*mala*), and so forth, are fully accomplished, it is said that they are "skillfully accomplished without remainder.
Skillfulness in wisdom is called the "activity to be performed," while the anger and other afflictions subdued are called the "tasks to be performed."

Furthermore, wisdom and skillful means are called "the capacity to perform the task," while the subduing of the activities of body, speech, and mind so that they are freed from the stains of entanglements is called "the task performed.

This praises the Blessed One for being fully endowed with wisdom and skillful means, and for being exceptionally capable of subduing all afflictions such as anger in both himself and others, leaving none remaining.

The seventh sentence, which states, "All sentient beings' various aspirations are able to be fulfilled according to their being free from fault," reveals the fourteenth profound principle, the most excellent dharma-gate, among the fourteen sections that follow.

This means that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, by virtue of possessing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), establishes supreme knowledge; he skillfully discerns all pure activities and is able to bring all states of existence (*bhava*) to complete purity.

Furthermore, by means of greed and other [afflictions], one subdues the world; universally and at all times, even throughout all states of existence, one brings about purification and spontaneous subdual.

Moreover, through great greed and other [afflictions], one attains pure great bliss and great wealth, achieving constant and firm benefit for sentient beings with sovereignty over the three realms, all by virtue of this dhāraṇī.
This divine mantra is taught through esoteric terminology; for those who can receive and uphold it, all obstacles are extinguished, and whatever they desire will be accomplished without fail.

It is explained at length that if one is free from afflictions and evil karma, then whether regarding worldly or supramundane aspirations—whether in this life or in the future—all shall be fulfilled because of being free from transgression.
If afflictions or evil karma arise, because their root is sinful, such vows as these shall not be granted.
Therefore it is said that the World-Honored One does not deprive sentient beings of any of their vows;
yet he does not grant them all, for only those that are free from fault are to be fulfilled.
If one gives rise to afflictions or forms evil vows, then even if there is utmost sincerity, [the wish] will certainly not be granted.
It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel: whatever wholesome vows one makes, all shall be attained.

The eighth phrase, "already well-established in the equality of the three times, eternally uninterrupted, vast, and all-illuminating," reveals the thirteenth of the fourteen subsequent sections: the Vajra Dharma-gate of the Boundless, Limitless, and Ultimate Principle.
This intention generally reveals that whether in essence or function, the Prajñāpāramitā is vast and profound, no different from the most supreme.

Therefore, the Tathāgata is boundless and limitless, of a single flavor, and ultimate. Because he can contemplate the vastness of the essence and function of prajñā, he is boundless; because he can universally illuminate, he is limitless; because it is uninterrupted, it is of a single flavor; and because it is inexhaustible, it is most supreme. Thus, the wisdom that contemplates can wondrously know the three periods of time; knowing the past and future as if they were the present is called "equality."

Furthermore, the wisdom of observation and illumination is boundless and limitless, reaching a single flavor of ultimate perfection; it can observe the principles and phenomena of the three periods of time, clearly discerning each and every phenomenon with thorough understanding, and is therefore called "equality."
The principle of this single characteristic is also termed "equality.
Since one is able to thoroughly comprehend both principle and phenomena, the term "equality" applies to both.
Being eternally uninterrupted and exhaustively pervasive, it is the function of wisdom.
One who is well-established is so called because their wisdom that can contemplate [reality] has skillfully penetrated the three periods of time;
thus they are named "well-established. Because there is no error or confusion regarding either principle or phenomena, they are named "well-established."
The meaning is that at all times, the function of wisdom is all-pervasive.

The ninth line, which states, “The nature of body, speech, and mind is like vajra, unmoving and indestructible like all Tathāgatas,” reveals the sixth section among the fourteen subsequent sections—the Vajradharmamudrā-gate of Tathāgata Wisdom—and reveals the ninth section—the Unsurpassed Gate of Truly Pure Offering.

The Buddha fully possesses and embraces the vajra-body seals of all Tathāgatas, and is able to realize the dharma-body of all Buddhas; he fully possesses and embraces the vajra-speech seals of all Buddhas, and attains sovereign mastery over all phenomena.
Possessing the complete integration of all Buddhas’ Vajra Mind-Seals, one shall attain mastery over all meditative absorptions.

Possessing the complete integration of all Buddhas’ Vajra Wisdom-Seals, one is able to attain the unsurpassed, sublime body, speech, and mind, which—like a vajra—is immovable and indestructible; it cannot be stirred by afflictions, nor can it be destroyed by external paths or Māras so as to cause the three karmas to waver or be ruined.
With the wisdom of the Buddha’s three karmas as its precursor, it is free from all faults and cannot be destroyed or caused to give rise to faults; therefore, it is immovable and indestructible.
Being immovable and indestructible, it is no different from the merits of all Buddhas, and is thus called "equal" (samatā).
The "All Tathāgatas" refers to the sublime meaning of all Tathāgatas as explained in the aforementioned gates.

This is like a vajra, immovable and indestructible; it is the excellence of the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind]. Because in former causal stages one made offerings to the Buddhas through the three karmas performed according to the Dharma as a "Dharma-offering," one attains this fruit upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood.
Because it is the retribution obtained through true and pure offerings, it cannot be moved or destroyed.

Alternatively, these three karmas cannot be moved by non-Buddhists or evil associates, nor can they be destroyed by celestial Māras or heterodox companions; thus, like a vajra, they shatter all three karmas associated with birth and death.
The nature of the three karmas is the very essence of the three karmas; there is no other meaning.
Herein, these nine phrases manifest the virtues revealed in the fourteen subsequent sections of the sutra concerning the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

Now, by extolling the Buddha’s virtues, I wish to cause sentient beings to know that the Buddha is fully endowed with these qualities, so that they may give rise to a heart of profound respect and reverently accept what is taught; or, having heard this, they shall develop a superior resolve to joyfully seek its realization.

Alternatively, it may be to reveal that the Blessed One possesses these various qualities and thus transcends all others; therefore, the profound principle he has taught is most excellent and worthy of being relied upon for study and practice.
A second interpretation is as follows:
Based on the various sūtras which state that the Buddha possesses twenty-one virtues, these nine phrases are specifically assigned [to them].

Regarding the scriptural passage on "the adamantine sustaining of the wisdom of equality" (*samatā-jñāna*): it refers to the Buddha’s supreme merit of non-dual manifestation and absolute unobstructedness, as well as manifesting the attainment of the equality of all Buddhas and the supreme merit of attaining activities identical to those of all Buddhas.

In this way, this single phrase generally reveals two virtues: namely, that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is free from the active manifestation of the various defilements of ordinary beings who dwell with attachment in saṃsāra, and free from the active manifestation of the nirvāṇa of those of the Two Vehicles who dwell with attachment in nirvāṇa by unilaterally abandoning the work of benefiting and gladdening others. Because the World-Honored One lacks those active manifestations of the two obstacles, he is said to be "one whose non-duality is manifest."
Because compassion and wisdom are all-pervasive, one dwells in neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa; therefore, it is called "equality.
Because it can shatter these two obstacles, it is metaphorically likened to a vajra.
Abiding in non-abiding—that is, in *apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*—it is called "abiding support" (*sthiti-dhara*).

Because it abides in compassion and wisdom, it further attains the equality of all Buddhas; that is to say, the principle realized is equal, the wisdom that realizes it is equal, and the bodies accomplished are equal, such that the mental activities and compassionate deeds are entirely equal.
Because this equanimity can destroy birth and death, it is called "vajra" (diamond).
Because it serves as the basis for sustaining all virtues through equanimity, it is called "abiding support.
Here only one aspect is mentioned, though such qualities are very numerous; therefore, they are termed "various and preeminent merits."
The second phrase of the sutra states: "The crown jewel of empowerment transcends the three realms," which refers to the three virtues of a Buddha:
first, the wisdom that is the true object of pursuit for all bodhisattvas;
second, its ultimate extension throughout the dharma-realm.
Third, their practice is unimpeded.
Herein, the first phrase establishes the excellence of the skillful means for ensuring that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed.

This means that bodhisattvas diligently cultivate preparatory practices (*prayoga*) specifically so that the lineage of the Buddhas remains uninterrupted; this is not the case for those of the two vehicles (*yāna*). Therefore, the wisdom of the Buddha is precisely what bodhisattvas alone should seek.

By virtue of this empowerment, the rank of a Dharma Prince belongs exclusively to the tenth stage; one dons the precious Buddha-crown and succeeds to the position of a Buddha, which is not the case for those of the two vehicles.

This means that causing sentient beings to seek out and listen to the profound Prajñāpāramitā sūtras is intended for the realization of the awakening of a Buddha, and it is also the succession to the position of the Dharma King. Therefore, if one obstructs and destroys these [beings] and prevents them from practicing and studying the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, one severs the seeds of all Buddhas.
This second phrase refers to the distinguished merit of attaining the fruit, namely, the attainment of the utterly pure *dharmadhātu*.
This pure *dharmadhātu* is the fruit of the path of cultivation; because it constantly manifests before the mind of contemplative observation, it is likened to a jeweled crown worn upon the head.
The jeweled crown is the supreme ornament of the body, and the dharma-realm is likewise the root of all merit; therefore, it is metaphorically compared to a jeweled crown.
This third phrase concerns the preeminent merit of subduing demonic adversaries, referring to the objects of practice, namely form and so forth.
Because these objects of engagement disturb the mind and thus obstruct the wholesome, they are called "Māra, the Enemy.

Even the minds of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, which dwell in perfect composure within the most delightful of objects, cannot be disturbed; all their virtues are perfectly fulfilled, and no adverse object can create an obstacle.

Because they are able to subdue all objective spheres, and because they cannot be constrained or obstructed by any activities—being dharmas free from fetters—they reach the stage of Buddhahood and transcend the three realms.
This second phrase concerns the virtues of the Blessed One: that which was not accomplished from the beginningless past but is attained for the first time at this moment is termed "acquisition.
The third phrase states, "The All-Pervading Vajra-Wisdom, the Great Avalokiteśvara," which refers to the three virtues of a Buddha:
first, the unalterable Dharma; second, abiding in the Buddha-abode; and third, achieving great enlightenment regarding all modes of conduct.

Among these, the first phrase concerns the supreme merit of subduing non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). This means that the Buddha’s True Dharma cannot be overturned by any non-Buddhist; having subdued them, he reveals his own Right Path. Because he has accomplished the all-pervading vajra-like wisdom, he preaches the profound Dharma to subdue the non-Buddhists;

furthermore, because he has accomplished the wisdom that pervades all phenomena, he is able to preach the deep Dharma and overcome all non-Buddhists. Therefore, this wisdom is said to be like a vajra.
"Omniscience" (*sarvajña*) refers to the all-encompassing knowledge that thoroughly understands all phenomena.
This second phrase contemplates the sublime qualities of those to be converted, namely, that [the Buddha] dwells in great compassion and observes the world during the six periods of day and night.

This third phrase refers to the ability to manifest one's own sublime qualities in accordance with the needs of sentient beings to be converted by all vehicles; that is, because one thoroughly understands the differences in the dispositions and conducts of all sentient beings and manifests one's own body accordingly, one is called Mahā-Ārya-Avalokiteśvara.
If one observes that the mental activities of sentient beings are not autonomous, they cannot manifest their bodies in accordance with those types;
because the Buddha is able to manifest accordingly, we know that he possesses universal knowledge and great sovereign mastery.
Furthermore, the first phrase, "all-pervading vajra wisdom," refers to the wisdom of the twenty-one qualities; it is the general term for the most pure awakening.

It is called all-pervading vajra wisdom because it correctly awakens to all objects of awakening, whether conditioned or unconditioned, and because it correctly awakens to that which is pure, sublime, and perfect;
furthermore, it is so named because it correctly awakens to the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāva*) and the full extent of things (*yāvadbhāva*).
Among these, the two virtues now manifest as newly perfected, and are thus termed "attainment.

Regarding the fourth phrase, "the seal of the great, wondrous wisdom that definitively [comprehends] all phenomena": this wisdom has already been partially attained during the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and is now manifested in its fullness.
This reveals two kinds of virtues:
first, having no doubt or obstruction regarding knowledge of all phenomena; second, having no uncertainty regarding knowledge of all phenomena.

Herein, the first phrase refers to the preeminent merit of severing all doubts, meaning that one has already attained the definitive knowledge capable of eliminating all uncertainty concerning all phenomena.

This second phrase refers to the supreme merit of the wisdom that thoroughly and excellently understands all phenomena, which is able to provide constant and correct instruction as appropriate; for those who harbor doubts regarding various phenomena lack the power to provide such instruction accordingly, whereas the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has realized and seen all phenomena with a wisdom that is perfectly determined, and is thus able to provide unerring instruction as appropriate, without ceasing or failing.
If one were not certain regarding all phenomena, the principle would be untenable.

Furthermore, one attains the three seals of the Dharma: the specific seal that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are impermanent; the specific seal that nirvāṇa is the tranquility of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); and the universal seal that all phenomena are without self (*anātman*). These three sublime principles are called "seals" because they definitively characterize all phenomena. When the Buddha attains this wisdom, it is termed the "seal of wisdom."
The fifth phrase, "the seal of the ultimate emptiness, quiescence, and equality," reveals two kinds of virtues:
first, attaining the supreme other shore of the Buddha’s non-dual dwelling; second, realizing the equality of the Buddha-ground, which is devoid of middle or extremes.
Among these, the first phrase concerns the excellence of the constituent parts of its intrinsic nature.

The Buddha’s non-dual abiding has the *dharmakāya*, which is *tathatā* (suchness), as its essence; it is a state without differentiated characteristics, wherein all conceptualizations of dualistic marks do not manifest.
Because he relies on that supreme concentration and dwells eternally within it, it is called "abiding.
This very non-dual abiding is named the "supreme further shore" (*pāramitā*); because the Buddha has already reached its ultimate limit, it is called "attainment."

This Dharmakāya is the common, equal nature shared by all Buddhas; it is only through the elimination of the two selves and the contemplation of the emptiness and quiescence of these two selves that one can fully realize it.
This second phrase refers to the preeminent merit of realizing the characteristics of True Suchness (Tathatā).

This means that the characteristic of suchness is because it is far removed from all characteristics of the conditioned and the unconditioned, as well as the characteristics of center and periphery; and because it is far removed from the characteristics of spatial direction, center, and periphery. It is precisely the equality of the dharma-nature of the Buddha-ground.
By realizing this, one thoroughly knows all phenomena and remains unstained by them.
This principle of *tathatā* seals all phenomena, accords with ultimate emptiness, and only through this can one realize that the Buddhas have fully realized it all.
Regarding the sixth phrase, "being skillful in all tasks to be performed by all causal agents and accomplishing them without remainder," this reveals two kinds of merit of the World-Honored One:
first, his body pervades all worlds; second, that which he establishes is inconceivable.
Among these, the first phrase refers to the sublime merit of descending from the Tuṣita heaven.

This means manifesting a transformation body that simultaneously descends into the wombs of mothers across all worlds and continents; that is, the manifestation of the eight phases culminating in the attainment of enlightenment. This constitutes the Blessed One’s mastery in performing all his enlightened activities.

Since this is the case for the nirmāṇakāya, the principle by which the sambhogakāya and other bodies manifest accordingly is likewise; this second line establishes the sublime qualities of the established Dharma-teachings.

This refers to the Buddha’s establishment of the teachings on all phenomena, which transcend the sphere of all discursive thought; this is what is called being skillful in all activities to be performed.

Having cultivated the causes for three kalpas originally for the sake of manifesting bodies and preaching the Dharma for sentient beings to bring about great benefit and happiness, now that this is fully perfected, it is called "skillful accomplishment without remainder."

The seventh phrase states that the Blessed One is able to fulfill all the various aspirations of sentient beings according to their needs, provided they are blameless; this reveals two kinds of qualities of the World-Honored One:
first, his inclination toward signless phenomena (*animitta-dharma*), and second, his state of being unmixed with other characteristics.
The Tathāgata’s liberation is the ultimate perfection of wondrous wisdom; herein, the first phrase refers to the sublime merit of the skillful means of subduing.
That which is the signless dharma is precisely nirvāṇa.

The Buddha thoroughly understands sentient beings of the three vehicles and, according to their respective capacities, teaches them with appropriate means of subduing as they truly are, so that they may proceed toward the realization of the signless Dharma.
This means that all sentient beings who seek liberation from birth and death shall all attain nirvāṇa;

because the sublime vows of the three vehicles are free from fault, the Buddha is able to fulfill them all. This second phrase refers to the excellence of the merit of the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
This means that the enjoyment bodies (saṃbhogakāya) do not intermingle, because the enjoyment bodies of all Tathāgatas are each distinct.

Because the sublime wisdom (prajñā) of the Tathāgata can bring liberation to all sentient beings, it is called the "sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata’s liberation"; the Buddha has attained the ultimate perfection in this wisdom.
This wisdom of the Tathāgata is not intermingled; likewise, the manifestation of the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) in pure buddha-fields is also not intermingled.
Within great assemblies, the manifestation of various bodies and the bestowing of the dharma-joy upon the bodhisattvas are likewise not intermingled.

The Tathāgata has also reached the ultimate consummation regarding this body manifested through wisdom; this meaning reveals that both the wisdom of the Tathāgata and the body he manifests have already attained the ultimate consummation.

In accordance with all the aspirations and wishes of sentient beings that are free from fault, one is able to manifest skillful means to rescue and deliver them, causing them to leave birth and death; therefore, it is called "fulfillment."

The eighth phrase states: "Having already well established oneself in the equality of the three times, which is eternally uninterrupted, inexhaustible, vast, and all-pervading. This reveals the three kinds of qualities of the World-Honored One:
first, wandering within the dharma-nature of the equality of the three times; second, exhausting the nature of space; and third, reaching the limits of the future.

Among these, the first phrase records the distinguished merits of the three periods of time; that is to say, because one records the events of the past and future just as one does the present, without any obstruction.

This refers to the prophecy that Prajñāpāramitā will flourish for the last time in the northeast and then first perish, continuing until the time when the True Dharma (saddharma) is completely extinguished.
It also records that the Dharma shall perish in the kingdom of Campā, as the characteristics of this event are to be explained in detail in the *Saddharmavipralopa-sūtra*.
Furthermore, it was recorded that when the bodies of the two stone Bodhisattvas by the Bodhi tree were submerged up to their necks, the True Dharma would come to an end;
now they have sunk to the level of their chests, and this matter may be verified.
The account of Aśoka becoming a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) is precisely the evidence for this.

The latter two lines concern the inexhaustible and preeminent merit of the two virtues of self-benefit and benefiting others; that is to say, just as the nature of the kalpas of formation and destruction is eternally inexhaustible like space, so too are all the Tathāgata’s true merits eternally uninterrupted and inexhaustible, having no end as long as the limits of the future.

The merit of benefiting others is likewise thus: reaching the limits of the future, it constantly performs deeds for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings; therefore, its vast and pervasive illumination is the very function of the unceasing and inexhaustible light of true merit.
The ninth phrase, "The nature of the body, speech, and mind is like a vajra; all Tathāgatas are immovable and indestructible," reveals two kinds of qualities of the Bhagavān:
first, his arrival at the state of non-obstruction; second, that whatever bodies he manifests are beyond conceptual differentiation.

Regarding this, the first phrase refers to the excellence of having cultivated the remedies for all obstacles and fetters; that is, having practiced the noble path that serves as the remedy for both types of obstacles, one has reached the state of liberation from all obstacles.
Because they are that which is relied upon and that which is approached, they are called "bases" (*āyatana*).
By virtue of this, all three types of action of the Tathāgata are wholesome and untainted (*anāsrava*), like a vajra;
for no other Buddha can move or destroy them. This second phrase correctly encompasses the supreme qualities of his own undefiled body.
This means that the Buddha’s own body does not arise from false conceptual construction (*abhūta-parikalpa*), because it is free from the defilements of afflictions, karma, and birth.
This is because the Tathāgata’s body does not arise from defiled conceptualization and is beyond conceptual differentiation.
The Buddha’s three karmas, being free from faults, are as indestructible and immovable as a vajra, equaling those of all Buddhas.
Within this passage, nine phrases—through the combination and expansion of their textual meanings—collectively praise twenty-one virtues.

In this context, for now, I shall rely on the first interpretation from the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*; fearing that the text would become overly prolix, I have not recorded the views of later masters.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises explain these matters extensively as appropriate; it is impossible to cite them one by one.
Third, another interpretation:
regarding these nine phrases of the sutra, the first four praise the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body).
The first phrase offers a general praise of the true virtues of the *saṃbhogakāya*, wherein the four wisdoms are perfectly complete and subtle, without yet discussing the *dharmadhātu*.
The second line praises the excellence of the Path and the sublimity of the state;
the third line praises the profundity of compassion and the universality of wisdom, wherein the two fruits are equally perfected;
the fourth line praises the vastness of insight and the virtue of knowledge.
This summarizes all matters of existence and emptiness, as well as principle and phenomena, because it realizes them without error.
The fifth phrase praises the virtue of the cessation of both illumination and quiescence;
this praises the Dharmakāya.
The following four lines praise the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body):
the sixth line praises its skillful merit of grace;
the seventh line praises its wheel of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-cakra*) as being able to fulfill supreme vows.
The eighth phrase praises the wheel of the mind of knowledge (*jñānacakra*) for its ability to preach the Dharma;
the ninth phrase praises the wheel of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayacakra*) for its ability to manifest instructions and admonitions free from defilement.

Within the first phrase, which provides a general praise for the true virtues of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*)—the subtle and perfect realization of the four wisdoms—the term "vajra" serves as a general metaphor for the nature of *tathatā* (suchness), the basis of the four wisdoms, because it is capable of destroying [all obstacles]. All are termed "vajra," yet this does not mean that they all possess the actual functional activity of destruction.
That which is called "abiding and maintaining" (sthiti-dhara) is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; it is that which abides in and maintains the adamantine True Suchness (vajra-tathatā).
Because this is the foundation of all mundane and supramundane virtues, and because it is the root of the other wisdoms, it is termed "abiding and maintaining."
According to the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, there are nine metaphors for the mirror:

first, just as various images appear in dependence upon a round mirror, so too do the images of all sense-bases, objects, and consciousnesses appear in the mirror of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. For this reason, he is called the "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*), and thus all the virtues of the Buddha-body are sustained by this [wisdom].

Furthermore, because all supramundane and mundane wholesome states, as well as the bases, objects, and consciousnesses within other continuums, arise in dependence upon the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna), it is called "sustaining" (sthiti-dhara).
Second, it is also like a perfect mirror that is neither moving nor shaking.
When sentient beings observe their own gains and losses, they desire to preserve virtue and abandon all faults.

This is analogous to the Tathāgata’s Mirror-like Wisdom, which, being suspended as the banner of the *dharmadhātu*, is without interruption and thus remains unmoving; for countless sentient beings observe defilement and purity, desiring to preserve purity and abandon all defilements.
Third, it is like a mirror that reflects well; its reflection is pure and stainless, and its radiance shines everywhere.

This is analogous to the Tathāgata’s Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), which is free from the stains of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*). Having been perfectly polished and refined, and being sustained by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is clear, pure, and stainless; it performs deeds of great benefit and bliss, and is thus called "shining everywhere with radiance."

4. Just as various reflected images arise in a mirror depending upon conditions and the essential nature [of the objects], so too do the images of wisdom arise from the Mirror-like Wisdom of the Tathāgata, which constantly depends upon conditions.
5. Just as a mirror, with its surface polished and bright, serves as the universal basis and condition for the arising of all reflected images in every place.

It is like the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata, which is polished by the uninterrupted cultivation of immeasurable virtuous deeds and serves as the supporting condition for the reflected images of the wisdoms of the three vehicles.
Sixth, it is like a mirror in which great reflections of the earth, great mountains, and palaces can be perceived, yet the mirror itself is not equal in size to those great reflections.

It is like the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) of the Tathāgata, which manifests the reflections of all mundane and supramundane virtues of the ten stages; yet this wisdom does not share the same limitations as those reflections.
Seventh, it is also like a perfect mirror, which is not the causal condition for the arising of reflections from obstructed objects.

For example, the Tathāgata’s mirror-like wisdom is not encompassed by evil friends; it is not the condition for the arising of the reflections of wisdom in sentient beings who hear incorrect teachings, because they are not suitable vessels.
Eighth, furthermore, it is like a round mirror which is not the condition for the arising of reflections from objects situated in darkness.

It is like the Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata, which does not serve as the causal condition for the arising of the wisdom-reflections of sentient beings who delight in evil and are ignorant, for they are not suitable vessels.

Because their ignorance is so profound, although there exists the "excellent field" of the Triple Gem from which all wholesome dharmas grow, they have no desire to hear or receive the teaching, nor do they rejoice in taking refuge; instead, they return to external paths—is this not the most grievous obscuration of delusion?
Therefore, it is said that they are not "vessels.
Ninth, it is also like how a round mirror is not a condition for the arising of reflections from objects located at a great distance;

likewise, the mirror of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is not a condition for the arising of the reflection of wisdom within sentient beings who lack faith due to karma that results in impurity and deprivation of the Dharma, because they are not vessels.
Because they slandered the True Dharma in their previous lives, they have not heard the True Dharma for immeasurable eons due to the obstruction of their own karma.
Alternatively, because they lack the spiritual disposition and do not believe in causes and conditions, they are not vessels for the Noble Ones; therefore, it is not due to those conditions.

Based on these nine similes, as appropriate to each case, because they serve as the causes and conditions for one's own body and the bodies of others, for existence and non-existence, and for mundane and supramundane virtues, they are termed "sustaining" (sthiti-dhāraṇa).
Regarding equality, it refers to ten kinds of equality:
first, the equality of the dharma-nature through the superior love and joy for all marks.
This means that because one generates love and joy toward the primary and secondary marks, one now realizes that the dharma-nature is entirely equal.
2. The equality of the dharmatā of all dependent origination as it is experienced, namely internal and external dependent origination.
3. The equality of the dharmatā that is free from distinct characteristics and non-characteristics.

Because the various phenomena such as form possess dissimilar characteristics, such as the characteristic of transformation and decay, they are called "distinctive characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). To be free from these individual distinctive characteristics is the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Such a common characteristic, taking non-characteristic as its characteristic, is the equality of all phenomena (*dharma-samatā*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "All dharmas have but one single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of non-characteristic.
Fourth, the great compassion that universally delivers others through the equal nature of reality (dharmatā).
There are three types of loving-kindness (*maitrī*):
first, that which has sentient beings as its object (*sattvālambana*), which takes sentient beings as its cognitive domain and is cultivated by bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds;

second, that which has phenomena as its object (*dharmālambana*), which takes the true Dharma as its cognitive domain and is predominantly cultivated by bodhisattvas engaged in correct practice, because it arises from taking the teachings as its object.

The third is the objectless [compassion] (*anālambana*), which takes *tathatā* (suchness) as its objective sphere; it is primarily cultivated by Bodhisattvas who have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Although this compassion has an objective referent in that it takes the *dharmadhātu* as its object, it is nonetheless called "objectless" because it is free from conceptual discrimination (*nirvikalpa*).

The Buddhas all possess equal meritorious karma, which has been practiced for a long time without interruption, with profound earnestness and without exception; therefore, it is called "vast salvation.
Fifth, there is the impartial dharma-nature of non-referential great compassion.
The compassion of the followers of the two vehicles does not uproot all suffering; it uproots only that of the desire realm and functions only temporarily.

The Tathāgata’s compassion uproots universally, taking all three realms as its object, and functions at all times. Without depending on anything else, he constantly rescues and never abandons sentient beings afflicted by the three types of suffering. He regards them all equally as his only child, without giving rise to discrimination between "this is my child" and "this is not," or between those who are uprooted and those who are not.
Having realized great enlightenment, the Tathāgata constantly reflects:
"I shall always establish all sentient beings in the roots of all that is wholesome; those who have not yet awakened, I shall cause them to awaken."
This also has three aspects, which should be explained by analogy with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Sixth, [the Tathāgata] manifests the equal nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) according to the inclinations of sentient beings.

Although the Tathāgata abides in a state free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), through the sovereign power of his wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), the pure consciousness associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) manifests subtle physical bodies, such as those of lapis lazuli, causing the roots of virtue of all sentient beings to reach fulfillment. These beings perceive such bodily forms as transformations of their own minds, thinking that they see the body of the Tathāgata outside of their own minds.
Seventh, all sentient beings respectfully receive the teaching on the equal nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

As they experience joy through such verbal activity arising in accordance with their inclinations, the Tathāgata immediately manifests; out of compassion and vow, he speaks in a way that necessarily accords with their capacities, never failing or being in vain.

Although there may be sentient beings who do not comply with the Buddha’s words, these are merely emanations; they may yet be of benefit and will certainly come to believe and accept [the teaching] later.
Eighth, the tranquility of the world is entirely of one flavor, the equal nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The five aggregates with outflows are called the world (*loka*); their cessation is called tranquility (*śānti*).

Because both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equal, they are termed "of one taste" (*ekarasa*). Furthermore, because the intrinsic nature of the clung-to world does not exist, it is called tranquility; this very absence of differentiation in suchness is what is meant by "one taste."
9. The Dharma-nature of the equality of the single flavor of suffering and pleasure regarding all worldly phenomena.
There are eight worldly conditions, namely: gain and loss, defamation and praise, renown and insignificance, suffering and pleasure.

Obtaining agreeable things is called gain (*lābha*); losing agreeable things is called loss (*alābha*). To disparage someone behind their back is called defamation (*nindā*); to fail to praise them behind their back is called dispraise (*praśaṃsā*). To praise someone in their presence is called fame (*yaśas*); to disparage them in their presence is called infamy (*ayaśas*). That which afflicts the body and mind is called suffering (*duḥkha*); that which gratifies the body and mind is called pleasure (*sukha*).

The Noble One abides in the center, ever of a single flavor: not elated by gain, nor depressed by loss; even when encountering suffering, he is without affliction, and when encountering pleasure, he is without craving; he should be like space, equal and of a single flavor.
Tenth, the cultivation and planting of the ultimate equality of the dharma-nature of immeasurable merit.
"Merit" refers to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) and so forth; the perfuming of seeds, their nurturing, and their maturation leading to liberation is termed "cultivation and planting."
Possessing these ten virtues is called the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of equality: the equality of all sentient beings and the equality of all Buddhas.
As explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts, this is attained through the transformation of the seventh consciousness.
Because there was formerly a self, this and that were unequal;
now, because one is free from the self, they are called equal and impartial.
As for the various rare and sublime qualities, these refer to the wisdom of wondrous observation and the wisdom of accomplishing activities, each of which has ten causes.
Regarding the ten causes of the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*): first, the cause of establishment.
This wisdom sustains all *dhāraṇī*-gates and *samādhi*-gates, and provides unimpeded eloquence in expounding the sublime Dharma of the Buddhas, namely the ten powers (*daśabala*) and so forth.
Second, the cause of arising.

This wisdom can serve as the causal condition for the various, immeasurable marks of consciousness that arise simultaneously as the unimpeded, sublime wisdom regarding all objects of knowledge; that is to say, all-encompassing wisdom can instantaneously cognize all objective marks, serving as the generative cause for the simultaneous arising of all objective marks.
Third, the cause of joy:

This wisdom is worthy of contemplation; adorned with the perfections (*pāramitā*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the ten powers (*daśabala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), it is exceedingly delightful.
Fourth, the analysis of causes:

within this wisdom, one thoroughly observes, with exquisite and alternating adornment, the mundane and supramundane causes and effects of decline and prosperity, as well as the complete and exhaustive realization of the three vehicles.

In the mundane world, the evil realms and the happy realms are regarded as the causes and effects of decline and prosperity; in the supramundane, the two vehicles and the Great Vehicle are regarded as the causes and effects of decline and prosperity.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation, as found in the fifth fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*.
Fifth, the cause of enjoyment (*saṃbhoga-hetu*).

This wisdom acts as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the wisdom of equality, striking and activating the pure consciousness associated with the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) to manifest the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*). It displays various assemblies with blazing majesty and rains down the great Dharma rain, so that the great Bodhisattvas of the ten stages may experience the great joy of the Dharma. Furthermore, it assists in the manifestation of the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), even extending to enabling those to be converted who are prior to the stages to enjoy the Dharma bliss.
Sixth, the cause for the differentiation of destinies (*gati-vibhāga-hetu*):
within this wisdom, the boundless causes and effects that fully manifest the differentiation of the five destinies appear.
Seventh, the cause for the differentiation of realms (*dhātu-vibhāga-hetu*).
Upon this wisdom, the infinite causes and effects and the various distinctions of the three realms appear fully and clearly.
Eighth, it is the cause for raining down the great Dharma rain;
upon this wisdom, the vast and profound teachings brought forth by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can be attained.
9. The cause for subduing enemies and adversaries.
Beyond this wisdom, one cannot be shaken by any celestial Māras, externalists, or heterodox arguments; the profound teaching of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) can be attained.
Tenth, the cause for severing all doubts:

because the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (the wisdom of wondrous observation) is not deluded regarding anything, as it is surrounded by both specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), the nature of these specific and general characteristics is extensively analyzed herein.
The characteristics of these ten causes are explained in detail in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
Regarding the ten kinds of causes for the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), they refer to the transformations of the three types of action (*trividha-karman*).
I. Transformation of the bodily action (*kāyakarma*).
This has three types:
first, transformation by manifesting supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

For this reason, the Tathāgata manifests in various fields of arts and crafts to subdue those sentient beings who are arrogant regarding their skills; by means of such power of skillful means, he leads all sentient beings to enter the holy teaching, bringing them to maturity and liberation.
Second, manifesting birth and transformation.
By this means, the Tathāgata goes to the various places of birth of sentient beings, manifesting birth as one of their own kind while occupying a position of supreme authority.
Because he manifests birth as one of their own kind, he subdues all sentient beings of different kinds.
Third, the manifestation of the ripening of present karma.
By means of this, the Tathāgata manifests the experience of various difficult practices from his past lives and previous births, as stated in the sūtras.
For example, it is said that in a former life during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the Tathāgata spoke these words of abuse:
"In what place could a śramaṇa who has shaved off his hair and beard possess great bodhi?
For unsurpassed bodhi is extremely difficult to attain.
Due to that evil karma, he now undergoes such a fruit of suffering that is so difficult to endure.
These words are also intended to stop the evil conduct manifested through supernatural transformations.

Otherwise, how could there be such agitated speech and evil conduct arising from a bodhisattva bound to a single lifetime—one who has already personally served immeasurable Tathāgatas, planted all manner of roots of virtue, and possesses the nature of recollecting past lives?

It should be understood that these words are intended to transform and deliver those who are suitable to hear them and thereby attain liberation, so that they may depart from such speech in the presence of the Buddha.
Second, the transformation through verbal action.
This also has three types:
first, transformation through words of consolation and encouragement.

By means of this, the Tathāgata eloquently expounds various teachings according to what beings delight in, with such skillfulness in both phrasing and meaning that even sentient beings of limited intelligence will believe them upon first hearing.

It is said that the Buddha’s vocal utterances possess sixty qualities; even when ordinary, foolish beings hear them for a brief moment, they give rise to faith and understanding, let alone those with other forms of discerning wisdom.
Second, transformation through skillful means.

By this, the Tathāgata establishes the correct precepts, censures all forms of negligence, and praises non-negligence; furthermore, he establishes those who follow by faith and those who follow by dharma, and so forth.

Out of great compassion, he establishes precepts for all sentient beings, causing them to subdue all evils and cultivate worldly virtues; he establishes the various stages of the noble path, leading them to enter the right path and transcend the three realms.
Third, the analysis of the transformative activity of speech.

Thereby, the Tathāgata severs the immeasurable doubts of all sentient beings; that is to say, the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) manifests transformative verbal karma according to the differences in the inclinations of sentient beings, expounding various meanings to sever all doubts.
This means that by uttering a single sound, all meanings are expressed, enabling all sentient beings to obtain benefit according to their respective types.

When the Buddha expounds all dharmas with a single voice, sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind; this is brought about by the inconceivable power induced by the Tathāgata’s original vows.
If one manifests a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), a single substance is seen differently by various beings, thereby accomplishing the task of benefiting and bringing happiness.
Third is the transformation of mental action (*manas-karma*). This has four types:
First, the determination of mental transformations.

By means of this, the Tathāgata determines the eighty-four thousand distinctions in the mental activities of sentient beings; that is to say, there are eighty-four thousand distinctions in the mental activities of the various afflictions and defilements of sentient beings, which are able to obstruct the eighty-four thousand pāramitās, dhāraṇī-doors, samādhis, and so forth.

As explained in detail in the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra*, there are three hundred and fifty perfections (*pāramitā*), beginning with the first, the practice of the perfection of Dharma, and ending with the final, the perfection of distributing the Buddha-body; each and every one of these is fully endowed with the six perfections.

Thus, there are two thousand one hundred in total; when applied to the eight thousand four hundred distinctions in the mental activities of sentient beings—namely, those characterized by greed, hatred, delusion, and their equal combination—and excluding the faults arising from the four great elements and the six sense objects, the total number reaches eighty-four thousand through tenfold multiplication.
By practicing this, one subsequently attains the accomplishment of eighty-four thousand dharanī-doors, samādhis, and so forth.
This is but a brief explanation; were it to be expanded, it would be immeasurable.
Second, the manifestation through mental construction (*nirmāṇa-manas-karman*).

By means of this, the Tathāgata observes the conduct of sentient beings—whether they act or do not act, and whether it be virtue or fault—and constructs remedial countermeasures (*pratipakṣa*) to induce them to adopt or abandon [those qualities].
That is to say, one observes the conduct of all sentient beings: if they engage in unwholesome actions, there is a fault in their failure to practice virtue;
if they engage in wholesome actions, there is a fault in their failure to practice them. Thus, practicing brings virtue, while failing to practice brings fault.

Observing in this way, one desires to cause them to adopt virtues and abandon faults; regarding virtues, one applies the remedy of cultivation and maintenance, and regarding faults, one applies the remedy of distancing and abandonment.
Third, the transformation through the arousal of intention.
Because the Tathāgata desires to proclaim the remedies for those [afflictions], he manifests the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables that accord with what they delight in.
That is to say, he teaches the Dharma according to the inclinations of sentient beings, causing them to give rise to love and joy, thereby producing the remedies.
Fourth, the acceptance of the mental transformation.

Because the Tathāgata provides explanations through definitive, non-definitive, counter-questioning, and setting aside, he accepts the meanings of the past, future, and present as appropriate to each case.
These four are the four modes of discourse: categorical, analytical, counter-interrogative, and setting aside. They refer, for example, to the nature of the Triple Gem as a field of merit.
These three types of karmic transformation are the three miraculous powers (ṛddhi-prātihārya): namely, the miracle of supernormal power, the miracle of mind-reading, and the miracle of instruction.
For this reason, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is called the Great Sage of Wisdom-Medicine, for he is able to eliminate all diseases of affliction (*kleśa*).
The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done each possess ten causes; therefore, they are termed "various rare and marvelous virtues."
This sentence generally reveals the actual virtues of the *saṃbhogakāya*; therefore, it is extolled by means of the initial gateway of the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*).
This is because all other conditioned virtues, whether material or non-material, are subsumed within the categories of these four wisdoms.
The second line states: "The consecrated jewel-crown transcends the three realms. This praises the supreme status of the path.

Having emerged from the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the tenth bhūmi, one wears the Buddha’s jewel-crown; with a body of sublime and wondrous wisdom that is pure and untainted, one is free from all fetters and is not subsumed within the realms. Therefore, it is called "transcending."

Because the stages of the two vehicles, ordinary beings, and non-Buddhists are all inferior by comparison, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "There is this Pure Land that transcends the three realms, wherein Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage shall be born."
That land and its locations are not separate from the triple world; it is called "transcendent" because it is free from fetters, not because it is not included within them.
The body of the Tathāgata is likewise: it is called "transcendent" because it is not subject to outflows (āsrava), not because it is born in a place distinct from the triple world.

The third phrase, "Pervasive Vajra Wisdom, Great Avalokiteśvara," praises the perfection of both the profundity of compassion and the vastness of wisdom, wherein the two fruits are simultaneously fulfilled.
During the causal stage, one practices for the benefit of oneself and others; thus, compassion and wisdom serve as the path through which the fruition is brought to completion.
Since the fruit consists in the thorough knowledge of all phenomena as being pervasive vajra-wisdom—
which is able to realize universal gnosis and destroy the two obscurations— it is likened to a vajra.
Alternatively, because the two obscurations to be destroyed are firm and difficult to shatter, they too are likened to a vajra.
The sublime wisdom that realizes the universal destruction of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations—like a vajra—is called the "Universal Vajra Wisdom.
Having attained the awakening of this wisdom, one is able to compassionately rescue and liberate all sentient beings.
One whose wisdom for self-benefit is perfected and whose compassion for benefiting others is fulfilled is named Avalokiteśvara.
Because he is able to compassionately rescue sentient beings according to their aspirations arising from the three karmas—without exception—he is named Mahāvalokiteśvara.
This demonstrates that no other of the Buddha’s virtues surpasses these two, as they encompass all phenomena exhaustively and provide a comprehensive inclusion according to their respective natures.

The fourth line, "The seal of the great, wondrous wisdom that definitively [perceives] all phenomena," praises the virtue of vast wisdom; it serves as a general seal for all matters of existence and emptiness, as well as principle and phenomenon, because it realizes them without error.
Wisdom is of two kinds; since both types of non-wisdom have been completely eradicated, one attains these two wisdoms.
Conventional wisdom can know that conditioned phenomena are definitively impermanent, while unconditioned wisdom can know that the unconditioned is definitively quiescent.

These two seals of selflessness (*nairātmya-mudrā*) are definitively certain; there must be no hesitation. Therefore, they are called the seal of great and sublime wisdom (*mahāmudrā*) due to their vast renown.
Without this wisdom, one cannot give rise to decisive knowledge regarding phenomena.
The fifth phrase, "the seal of the ultimate emptiness, quiescence, and equality," praises the virtue of the cessation of illumination.
This praises the essential nature of the *dharmakāya*, which is realized only after severing the two obstacles and thereby attaining the two kinds of emptiness.

The principle of the two emptinesses seals and determines all phenomena; that all phenomena are equal arises entirely from these two emptinesses. By means of the gateway of the two emptinesses, one realizes this dharmatā, which is termed the "nature of equality."
However, ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) merely serves as an entrance; it is not the state of equality (*samatā*).
As for the state of equality, the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is neither empty nor existent.
Now, it is designated as "ultimate emptiness" by way of expedient means, because it is that which is realized through observing sentient beings as being ultimately empty.
Because the Buddha has already attained perfection, it is called "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*).

The sixth line states that he has attained skillful mastery in accomplishing all activities, both those to be performed and those that have been performed, without exception; the following four lines praise the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), while this [sixth line] praises the excellence of his skillful grace.

This means that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, being impelled by the six periods of time through the permeation of great compassion, manifests expedient means—the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*)—for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; he teaches the Dharma as appropriate to bring benefit and joy to bodhisattvas, those of the two vehicles, and others.

That wisdom of equality strikes forth the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), manifesting for all bodhisattvas the reward body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of others; meanwhile, the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) preaches the Dharma therein, severing the web of doubts of the multitudes.

The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done strikes and activates the mirror-like wisdom to manifest transformation bodies, appearing in the forms and speech of emanations for the sake of those of the two vehicles and others; meanwhile, the wisdom of wondrous observation preaches the Dharma therein to sever all nets of doubt.

The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) manifests the transformations of the three karmas; in total there are ten types, as explained in the commentary on the first phrase regarding general qualities.

This wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done and the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*) are called "the agency that performs activities," while the ten types of transformations produced by the wisdom of equality and the others are called "the activities performed."
The Blessed One is skillful and fully accomplished in all that is to be done and has been done here, because he has attained complete mastery in everything.

Regarding the seventh phrase, which states that "he can fulfill all the various aspirations of sentient beings according to their faultless [desires]," this praises the wheel of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-cakra*) for its ability to fulfill supreme vows.
Because the Buddha possesses the power of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*), he is able to fulfill all blameless worldly and supramundane aspirations of sentient beings.
Nevertheless, he does not grant them all; thus, he is said to be "capable" [of granting them], for fear that sentient beings might otherwise increase their unwholesome karma.

This means that when one sees a poor person constantly seeking wealth, one should indeed give it to them; yet, having obtained wealth, they increase their unwholesome karma, which is why one does not give it.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "It would be better for them to remain destitute of wealth and status than to distance themselves from the evil deeds of the miserable realms, lest they give rise to transgressions that disturb their faculties and become vessels for the manifold sufferings of the future."
One should understand that cases such as those with impaired faculties are to be treated similarly.
If one seeks a gateway to wisdom that involves neither sin nor merit, it shall nevertheless be granted.
This is like Queen Mallikā, who wished to become a queen consort and later attained the fruits of sainthood.
Five hundred members of the noble lineage wished to behold the Buddha’s body and hear him recount his past lives.
Kāśyapa and his wife wished to become husband and wife as practitioners of the Way, and later attain the fruits of sainthood.
The daughter of King Aśoka wished to obtain money for almsgiving and later became the king’s own daughter.
Such wishes as these are all blameless and can all be fulfilled.
This is unlike the case where parents grant their children a sinful wish; a blameless aspiration cannot be granted if it is not so.
Furthermore, he manifests supernatural powers (ṛddhi), appearing as a Buddha according to what is appropriate for each being so as to fulfill their specific aspirations.

For instance, he manifested miraculous feats for the three disciples of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and others; likewise, he displayed great supernormal powers to subdue Kapphiṇa and others, leading them to enter the Path. In all such cases, he fulfills their supreme vows.

Regarding the eighth phrase, "well-established in the equality of the three times, eternally uninterrupted, vast, and universally illuminating," this praises the Buddha, the World-Honored One, for his ability to expound the Dharma through the power of his mind-wheel.
The divine eye perceives the present world, just as one knows when a cow among humans gives birth to a calf.
The knowledge of birth and death perceives the future, knowing that after the Brahmins and others have slandered him with the Jāṭila-plot, he will subsequently overcome them.
He also knew that after Udraka Rāmaputra had been reborn in heaven, he would later fall into hell due to becoming attached to a winged fox;

with his knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), he knew that a beggar from below had long since planted roots of goodness, so he preached the Dharma for him to deliver and benefit him, preaching the Dharma by prophesying the three periods of time.
To perform acts of benefit and happiness without distinction is called "equanimity.

Being able to contemplate this wisdom so that it manifests in continuous succession, always without interruption or exhaustion, such that there is nothing it does not know and it shines universally and extensively—this is its nature.

The ninth phrase, "The body, speech, and mind are like vajra, equal to all Tathāgatas, unmoving and indestructible," praises the wheel of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), which is able to manifest the instructions and teachings free from defilement.

Among the three bodies, because both delusion and karma have been completely exhausted, they are equal to all Buddhas like vajras; they cannot be disturbed, corrupted, or caused to give rise to evil karma by any heterodox paths, celestial Māras, or evil companions of birth and death.

Because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted through the three types of action (*karman*), one is able to admonish and instruct sentient beings; therefore, it is called "exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣaya*).
This is as explained in the first commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
Furthermore, the fourth interpretation is as follows:

among these nine phrases, the first phrase generally praises the Dharma-body and Reward-body of the four wisdoms; the next two phrases praise the sublimity of his station and the vastness of his virtues; the following three phrases specifically praise the three excellences; and the final three phrases specifically praise the three kinds of miraculous transformations.
It is because he wishes to cause sentient beings to hear of the Buddha’s merits, thereby giving rise to supreme joy, listening to the Dharma with profound reverence, and initiating the quest for it.
The Buddha possesses these virtues and thus extols them at the beginning of the sutra, so that they may know what is being taught is most excellent and sublime.

The Sūtra says:
"The Bhagavat dwelt in the palace of the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, at the summit of the Desire Realm."
The commentary states:
From this point downward is the fourth section, clarifying the location where the teaching was spoken.

Within the land of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya-bhūmi*), the four virtues are briefly manifested to reveal the excellence of the sutra; by citing the superior site of transformation, it is shown that the lands of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *dharmakāya* likewise contain actual virtues.
First, it is supreme in location, for it is situated within the Palace of Controlling Others' Emanations in the Heaven of Ultimate Desire;
second, it is supreme in its communal excellence, for all Buddhas have once wandered through its great jewel palaces;
third, it is supreme in its magnificent adornment, for it is embellished with various jewels and priceless mani-gems.
Fourth, it is superior in terms of being cherished and esteemed, for it is that which is delighted in by the noble ones, sages, and celestial beings;
thus, this text is preeminent in its position as the foremost.
The term "Bhagavān" refers to the Teacher who expounds [the doctrine], namely, the person who abides in [that state].
"Abiding" (sthāna) means the sense of a place of reliance or residence.
"Desire" (kāma) refers to craving; it is specifically the craving for sexual contact and edible food.
"Realm" (dhātu) carries the meaning of a class or a boundary.
The realm arises from desire and is capable of producing desire; thus it is called the "Desire Realm" (*kāmadhātu*), like a pepper drink or a diamond ring.
"Summit" (*mūrdhan*) refers to the crown of the head, signifying the highest point.
This is the highest and most excellent place among the six heavens of the desire realm, and is called the "Pinnacle of the Desire Realm" (*kāmadhātu-śikhara*).
Although it is described as a superior place, its specific name has not yet been revealed; therefore, the name of the heaven is now made explicit.

The sutra subsequently states that for the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), whatever is required according to their desire appears immediately as appropriate through the power of their merit.

However, since the karma of the fifth heaven is particularly sublime, they do not manifest objects in accordance with their desires in such a manner; rather, they simply employ the power of transformation acquired at birth to transform various necessary implements and enjoy them.

Now, the karma of the sixth heaven is even more sublime; although various requisites appear immediately according to their desires, they are also able to personally transform them into requisites without using them themselves, but must wait for other deities to transform them into objects of pleasure before they themselves may enjoy them, because the power of their karma is superior.
Based on this meaning, it is called the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).

Within this heaven, there are indeed distinctions such as noble and base, ministers and lords; however, one now dwells where the noble lords reside, rather than in the inferior, base, and evil abodes of the ministers. Therefore, the Sūtra further specifies "within the palace of the Heavenly King" (*devendra-bhavana*), intending to manifest the dignity of the Dharma; it is taught that [the teaching] must rely upon the most supreme and excellent locations, and not upon other inferior ones.

Just as the realization of *bodhi* requires the Vajrāsana, it is taught that this supreme Dharma must be expounded in the Tuṣita Heaven (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), following the principle of the "excellent location" (*viśiṣṭadeśa*) as set forth in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*.

This indicates that the *saṃbhogakāya* resides within the stainless pure land, and it also indicates that the *dharmakāya* dwells in the ultimate, most sublime state of the pure *dharmadhātu*, free from all desire.
Because those who realize this Dharma are able to perform the supreme deeds that benefit others, they also abide in the Pure Land and the Dharmatā for the sake of benefiting others.
The unimpeded and manifold miraculous activities of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) are called "mastery" (*vaśitā*).
This is the palace where the Dharma Kings of the various heavens once resided; therefore, other sutras state that ultimate emptiness and stillness constitute their dwelling.
Consequently, as the three bodies benefit sentient beings in distinct ways, the lands in which they reside are likewise distinct.
