Nevertheless, in the present text, that which obstructs liberation from the afflictions is termed the obstacle of affliction (kleśāvaraṇa).

The *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra* defines the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) as such acts as destroying stupas and defiling monasteries; the *Saddharma-vyākaraṇa-saṃdeha-vinodana-sūtra* speaks of seven heinous crimes, yet these do not deviate from the five types described in the *Nirgrantha-sūtra*, which are termed karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the "obstruction to the Dharma" (*dharmāvaraṇa*): the aforementioned obstruction of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*) is also termed an obstruction to the Dharma.
Karma that results in the failure to encounter the remaining teachings is called an obstruction to the Dharma.

Alternatively, at the time of passing away, one obstructs the True Dharma or hinders others from practicing meditative concentration, thereby failing to plant the seeds for hearing the Dharma; consequently, in this present life, one does not hear, believe, or realize the Dharma—this is called the obstruction to the Dharma.
"Accumulating" means creating; "piling up" means amassing and constructing.

Although there may be much accumulation, one cannot be defiled because, through understanding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), one takes no pleasure in birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Even if afflictions arise that heavily obstruct the Dharma, by the power of this sutra, they certainly cannot cause defilement.
That which defiles and causes one to experience bitter fruits and the like is called "defilement" (*saṃkleśa*).

Furthermore, although one may commit various extremely heavy evil karmas, because the nature of afflictions is empty and they are not solid, they are easily extinguished; because they are easily extinguished, one does not fall into the evil destinies.
Since karma is easily lost, how could its evil fruits arise?
Because the true principle of all phenomena is empty by nature and their actual substance is profoundly perceived, the three obstacles are thereby dissolved.
As the Sūtra says:

If one can receive and uphold this, reciting it daily with diligent and uninterrupted application, and contemplate it according to the principle, then in this very life one will certainly attain the vajra-samādhi of the equality of all phenomena; one will gain mastery over all phenomena and constantly experience all supreme and wondrous joys.
The commentary states:
The following clarifies the fruits of diligent upholding and so forth.

"Upholding" (*dhāraṇa*) means to cherish, treasure, and receive [the teaching] within one's heart, maintaining it without forgetting—just as one remembers a child and does not forget them from the heart.

Day after day, those who read shall unravel the text; those who recite shall internalize it through silent contemplation; the refined shall apply themselves with single-minded focus; and the diligent shall exert their bodies and minds with courageous resolve.

Without interruption throughout the six periods of the day and night, they should contemplate with profound discernment according to its underlying principles. As a result of this, they will receive the fruit of manifest retribution in this very life, and will certainly attain the principle of *tathatā*, the equality of all phenomena.
Regarding "vajra-samādhi," *samādhi* refers to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). "Vajra" is a metaphor for that which can shatter the afflictions of conceptualizing and clinging to signs.

This means that the samādhi pertaining to the true principle of emptiness—the suchness (*tathatā*) and equality of all phenomena—is so named because it can shatter the perversions of conceptualizing and clinging to signs; therefore, it is called "vajra."
Furthermore, the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is called "vajra" (diamond/thunderbolt); the meditative concentration that takes this as its object is termed "vajra-samādhi.

This means being able to uphold it within the mind without forgetting, and by diligently reciting and contemplating such a nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) day after day, one attains this concentration. One should then give rise to superior wisdom to shatter all conceptual constructions, inversions, and attachments to signs; at this stage, one realizes this vajra-samādhi, which is the concentration corresponding to the stages of hearing and reflection.

In this context, there are only five kinds of Dharma-practice, namely: hearing, receiving and upholding, reading, reciting, and contemplating—these five being presented in brief because the other five, such as writing, making offerings, giving to others, expounding, and practicing, are mutually implied by them.
In truth, by practicing the ten dharma-practices, one attains this fruit.
If even mere recitation can achieve it, how much more so for those who can expound upon them and engage in their cultivation?

Regarding "attaining mastery over all dharmas": one who has not yet realized true emptiness remains obstructed regarding both principle and phenomena; however, because one who realizes the truth possesses far-reaching insight and has already mastered principle, they attain mastery.
"Master" (*vaśin*) means the sense of being unimpeded.

Regarding "constantly experiencing all supreme and wondrous joy and bliss": when one is attached to phenomena, there is sorrow and anger; yet, because one realizes emptiness in the ultimate truth and understands the falsity of the essence in the conventional truth, one is free from sorrow and anger, and thus attains the constant experience of wondrous joy and bliss. This is because, upon hearing the true joy of the *dharmatā*, one experiences what has never been attained before.
The Sūtra says:
"When these sixteen great bodhisattvas are born, they will certainly attain the nature of the Tathāgata Vajradhara and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The praise says:

The World-Honored One himself declared that one who has well cultivated the bases of psychic power can abide for an eon or even more than an eon; thus, the sixteen great births of a Bodhisattva correspond in meaning to sixteen eons.
Regarding "vajra-nature": the nature of suchness (tathatā) is called "vajra" because it is capable of shattering the faults of birth and death.
Because it is the essence of all phenomena, it is termed "nature."
"Grasping" (執) has the meaning of receiving.
Because one receives it directly and intimately, it is called "grasping"; that is, the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is able to take emptiness as its object.
Alternatively, the nature of the Vajra-grasper is itself *tathatā* (suchness), for one attains this true nature after sixteen lifetimes.
Because the practice prior to this sutra enables one to transcend birth and death without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) after sixteen kalpas.

Since the principle of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) elucidated in this sutra possesses great spiritual efficacy, hearing this Dharma allows one to transcend the measure of boundless kalpas of birth and death; being thus, one is able to swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi.

What is described here is that by attaining the present samādhi of the vajra, one gains mastery over all phenomena and experiences supreme joy and bliss; subsequently, no obstacles can defile one, nor will one fall into the evil realms. By the power of this sūtra, one attains the nature of a vajra and swiftly achieves bodhi.
Commentary on the Section on the Principles of Prajñā, Volume Two, End.
Eulogy on the Commentary of the Section on the Principles of Prajñā from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Volume Three.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Ji of the Great Ci’en Monastery,
the Sūtra says:
At that time, the World-Honored One again relied upon the marks of the Tathāgata Samantaprabha.
The praise states:
The preceding section was first, clarifying the realm of the true nature (*dharmatā*).

From here below is second, the gateway of the manifest perfect awakening to the quiescent nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is precisely the objective realm of the essence of contemplative correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*).
The true nature of the preceding gate is here understood as the characteristic of wisdom.
Within this, there are also three parts:
first, an account of the title of the Buddha’s teaching gate.
This section has two parts:
first, clarifying the characteristics of the Tathāgata who serves as the basis; second, enumerating the names of the Dharma-gates that are taught.
This is the first part.
The preceding gate clarifies the nature (*dharmatā*); the dharma of the fundamental essence is not described as a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The subsequent gate concerns its meaning; therefore, it is termed a characteristic.
While the Tathāgata’s unified essence possesses manifold capacities, here we rely on a single meaning, which is precisely the characteristic of the All-Illuminating Tathāgata.
"Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refers to the characteristics and manifestations of meaning; it is not the characteristic of having characteristics as conceptualized by discrimination.

Now, regarding the dharma that is without characteristics, the characteristics of meaning are subsequently explained because of the two kinds of wisdom—the wisdom that abandons delusions and the wisdom of contemplative observation—namely, all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) and knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñā*).
To be able to fully comprehend all phenomena is called "universal illumination" (samantaprabha); the wisdom of universal illumination is itself the characteristic of the Tathāgata.
Since this Dharma-gate is now taught based on this essential characteristic, it is named "Based on the Characteristic of Universal Illumination."
The Sūtra says:
"For the sake of all bodhisattvas, he proclaimed the gate of manifesting equal enlightenment into the profound principle of the tranquil dharmatā of all Tathāgatas, which is the Prajñāpāramitā."
The praise says:
This enumerates the names of the dharma-gates that have been taught.

Regarding "the profound principle of the quiescent dharmatā of all Tathāgatas," this refers to the wondrous Dharma of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) previously described, which is the profound principle of the quiescent dharmatā of all Buddhas.
Regarding the gate of manifesting perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*): "manifest" (*abhi*) means to appear, to be clearly present before one, and to be directly realized.
"Perfect" (*sam*) means universal or all-pervasive. "Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) means the sense of illumination.
This meaning reveals that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) clearly and directly has the capacity to universally illuminate the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The essence of manifest perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) is precisely this non-conceptual wisdom.
"Gate" (*mukha*) carries the sense of a passage through which one enters and proceeds.

Because the teachings that express the Dharma and so forth serve as the means for universally entering and approaching the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and because non-conceptual wisdom can enter into manifest perfect enlightenment by means of these profound teachings and so forth.
The Sūtra says:
"It is called the gateway of the manifest perfect awakening to the equality of the vajra, because Great Bodhi is firm, solid, and indestructible like a vajra.
The Praise says:
Below this is the second section, which consists of four gates.
First: it can sever birth and death because its nature is firm and solid.

One who attains manifest complete enlightenment regarding the adamantine equality (*vajrasamatā*) is able to shatter birth and death. This manifest complete enlightenment is like a vajra; because the *bodhi* of the *dharmatā* realized by wisdom is firm, true, and difficult to destroy—indeed, more indestructible than a vajra—the realizing wisdom is called "adamantine wisdom" (*vajrajñāna*).
The name *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is "Vajra"; its meaning is likewise the same.
Because the nature of suchness (*tathatā*) realized therein is firm and solid, the wisdom that realizes it is also like a vajra, capable of shattering birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The Sūtra says:
"The gateway to the manifest awakening to the equality of meaning, for its meaning is one with Great Bodhi.
The Praise says:
This is the second wisdom that observes the referents [of language]:
all phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, are entirely equal, because the meaning of the dharmadhātu, suchness, and bodhi is one and their nature is without distinction.
The Sūtra says:
"The gateway to the manifest perfect awakening to the equality of phenomena, because the intrinsic nature of great enlightenment is pure.
The Praise says:
This is the third wisdom that observes the expressive designations.
Because the nature of great enlightenment—the reality realized—is pure by its very essence, one awakens to the equality of the teachings that express it.
The Sūtra says:
"The gateway to the manifest perfect awakening to the equality of all phenomena, because Great Bodhi is non-conceptual with respect to all phenomena.
The Praise says:
This is the fourth supernormal knowledge, the wisdom that realizes all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
"All phenomena" refers to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Within all phenomena, one attains manifest perfect enlightenment; because the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena is without differentiation among them, the realizing wisdom is likewise non-discriminative when realizing all phenomena. Therefore, the intrinsic nature of phenomena is also equal in its essence.

It is like various clouds and mists in the sky, or various forms and images upon a screen; while both the sky and the screen remain devoid of discrimination, the various appearances of the clouds and the painted images arise.
The Sūtra says:
After the Buddha had thus attained manifest perfect awakening to the principle of the Prajñāpāramitā, the nature of phenomena which is such tranquility,
he spoke this praise:
From here below is the third section, which concludes by extolling the virtues of the Dharma;
this is the conclusion itself.
The Sūtra says:
He addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and the others, saying:

"If there are those who hear these four kinds of gateways to the manifest perfect awakening of the principles of Prajñā, and who believe, understand, uphold, recite, and practice them, even until they sit upon the sublime seat of bodhi, then although they may have committed all manner of most grievous evil deeds, they will be able to transcend all evil destinies and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The praise says:
This is an eulogy of virtues.
However, according to the sūtras, there are ten modes of Dharma practice (*dharmaparyāya*), whereas here only six modes of Dharma practice are mentioned:
First, hearing; second, faith and understanding; third, receiving and upholding; fourth, reading; fifth, reciting; sixth, practicing.

From this day forward, when first undertaking these ten dharmic practices, until the future time when one sits upon the Bodhi seat and attains Buddhahood, even if one commits all manner of most grievous evil karma—namely, among views, holding wrong views; among actions, mental action; and among the heinous crimes, breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha—even if one commits them all, because of this awakening and understanding, one will not be defiled by them and shall be able to transcend all evil destinies.

Through the great majestic power of hearing the sūtras, walking meditation, and so forth, these various evil karmas will not increase; consequently, one will not fall into the three evil realms and will swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi.

The calculation of this merit should be the same as that previously mentioned; however, it is stated separately here because the specific, superior function of the sutra is being praised individually.
The sutra says:
At that time, the World-Honored One again relied upon the characteristics of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, who subdues all evil dharmas.
The commentary states:
From here below is the second section, which consists of two parts of scripture clarifying the dharmas that are the objects of practice.
Within this, there are two [subsections]:
The first section is the Dharma-gate of Universal Victory in Subduing All Evils, which subdues all evils through the contemplation of the true nature of reality;
the latter section is the Dharma-gate of Purification by the Seal of Equal Wisdom, which illuminates through the contemplation of the wisdom of observation and insight.
Now, within this first section there are three parts;
first is the clarification of the title of the Dharma-gate being taught.
Within this, there are two [subdivisions]:
First, the characteristics of the Tathāgata, who is the basis [of this teaching], are clarified;
this constitutes the beginning.
As for "all unwholesome dharmas," it means that one is able to eliminate the two obstacles, the discrimination of cause and effect, and the discrimination between defilement and purity.

"Śākya" means "able," and "Muni" means "silent. Being able to subdue all evils and remain free from all clamor and agitation—whereby "clamorous and agitated phenomena" refers to the phenomena of birth and death—it is therefore called the mark of the Tathāgata, the Able Silent One.
Relying on this, all unwholesome dharmas are subdued, and the Tathāgata’s mark of tranquility is realized; thus, he proclaims this dharma-gate.
The Sūtra says:
"For the sake of all Bodhisattvas, he extensively expounds the profound principle of the equality of all dharmas, which is subsumed within the Prajñāpāramitā—the universally supreme dharma-gate."
The praise says:
This states the name of the dharma-gate being taught.

"Embracing the equality of all phenomena" means that all causes and effects of defilement and purity are subsumed within the dharma-realm of equality; because of this, one is able to universally overcome all evils, and thus this dharma-gate is named the "Universally Victorious Dharma."

The Sūtra says: Because the nature of desire is without conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the nature of hatred is also without conceptual proliferation; because the nature of hatred is without conceptual proliferation, the nature of delusion is also without conceptual proliferation; because the nature of delusion is without conceptual proliferation, the nature of doubt is also without conceptual proliferation; because the nature of doubt is without conceptual proliferation, the nature of all views is also without conceptual proliferation; and because the nature of all views is without conceptual proliferation, the nature of pride is also without conceptual proliferation.
The praise says:
Below this is the second section, the formal exposition of the Dharma-gate.
Within it, there are three parts:

First, it separately explains that the nature of birth-and-death, afflictions, karma, and suffering is free from conceptual proliferation; next, it sets forth that the nature of all defiled and pure phenomena is free from conceptual proliferation; and finally, it states that even prajñā is free from conceptual proliferation, thereby concluding with a return to the profound intent.
The first part, concerning the beginning and middle, is further divided into three:
first, clarifying that the nature of afflictions is free from conceptual proliferation; second, clarifying karma; and third, clarifying the fruit.
Within the section on afflictions, there are two parts:
The first part clarifies the root [afflictions], and the latter part clarifies the derivative afflictions.
This refers to the roots.
There are six roots, from which all afflictions grow and develop; these are the nature of desire-attachment (*rāga*).

"Absence of conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*)" means that the nature of defiled and delusive phenomena is itself *tathatā* (suchness), and the essence of the dharma of *tathatā* is free from conceptual proliferation.
"Conceptual proliferation" refers to the characteristics of discrimination, the characteristics of names and words, and the characteristics of discursive thought.
Due to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), one clings to and discriminates between defilement and purity; because of such discrimination, birth and death arise.

When one knows there is no conceptual proliferation, defilement and purity vanish; when defilement and purity have vanished, their nature is non-discriminative. Because it is non-discriminative, birth and death are extinguished, and thus one is able to eliminate evil.
The subsequent cases should be understood by analogy.
Of the first three, the "three poisons" are as follows:
"hesitation" refers to doubt.
The various views refer to the five views, which are erroneous investigations.
Pride refers to arrogance and negligence.
Conceit refers to the seven types of conceit; relying on oneself to look down upon others is termed conceit.
These six fundamental true thusnesses are by nature free from conceptual proliferation; because they are free from conceptual proliferation, they are able to transcend discrimination.
By realizing this fundamental nature, one transcends discrimination and is free from conceptual proliferation, thereby being able to subdue all unwholesome dharmas.
The Sūtra says:

Because the nature of pride and arrogance is without conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the nature of the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) is also without conceptual proliferation; because the nature of the envelopments is without conceptual proliferation, the nature of the defilements of affliction (*kleśamala*) is also without conceptual proliferation.
The commentary states:
This clarifies the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
"Envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*) refers to those that repeatedly increase in intensity and manifest to entwine the mind; therefore, they are called envelopments.

These consist of eight kinds: namely, lethargy, torpor, and sleep are obstacles to serenity (*śamatha*); restlessness and remorse are obstacles to exertion (*pragraha*); envy and avarice are obstacles to equanimity (*upekṣā*); and lack of shame and lack of dread are obstacles to ethical discipline (*śīla*). Therefore, only these eight are established.

There are six kinds of defilements (*mala*), namely: enmity (*āghāta*), resentment (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāsa*), as well as guile (*śāṭhya*), deceit (*māyā*), and arrogance (*mada*). They are called "defilements" because they corrupt sentient beings.
These six are coarse in their characteristics and involve severe reproach; thus, they are established under the name of "defilements."
The Sūtra says:

Because the nature of the defilements of affliction is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the nature of all evil karmas is also free from conceptual proliferation; because the nature of all evil karmas is free from conceptual proliferation, the nature of all karmic retributions is also free from conceptual proliferation.
The Praise says:

The higher afflictions are without conceptual proliferation, and the same is true for karma and its results; collectively, these are termed the "dharma-nature of birth and death without conceptual proliferation.
Because one realizes this absence of conceptual proliferation, one is liberated from all evil dharmas of birth and death.
The Sūtra says:

Because the nature of all karmic results is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the nature of afflicted phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) is also free from conceptual proliferation; because the nature of afflicted phenomena is free from conceptual proliferation, the nature of purified phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*) is also free from conceptual proliferation; and because the nature of purified phenomena is free from conceptual proliferation, the nature of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) is also free from conceptual proliferation.
The commentary states:
This second section clarifies that the nature of all defiled and pure phenomena is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
"Defilement" (*saṃkleśa*) comprehensively encompasses all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena, as they are mixed with defilement.
"Purity" (viśuddhi) comprehensively encompasses all untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) without exception.
"All phenomena" (sarva-dharma) comprehensively encompasses all tainted and untainted, conditioned and unconditioned, as well as the cycle of birth and death and sentient beings.
The sequence follows the order of meaning: first the defiled and then the pure, first the specific and then the general.
The Sūtra says:
"Because the nature of all phenomena is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise free from conceptual proliferation."
The praise says:

Because the nature of the observed object is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), the observing wisdom is likewise free from conceptual proliferation, for it knows things as they truly are.
Since both this object and this wisdom are entirely free from conceptual proliferation, one is liberated from all discriminations of saṃsāra, and all evil dharmas are subdued and utterly exhausted.
The Sūtra says:
After the Buddha had spoken this Dharma of Universal Victory, the Prajñā-principle for Subduing All Evils,
he uttered this praise:
From here below is the third section, which extols the virtues of this sutra; the intent of this has already been concluded by the preceding summary.
The Sutra says:
He addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and the others, saying:

If there are those who hear such a profound principle of the Prajñāpāramitā, and having faith, understanding, receiving, upholding, reciting, and practicing it, were even to kill all sentient beings included within the three realms, they would not fall as a result into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts, because they have been able to subdue all afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and evil karma.
The praise says:
Because the power of the sutra can subdue all evils, these sins of killing are all eliminated.
Since this supreme practice arises from awakening to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), this great sin does not bring about an evil retribution.

Because the power of this sutra is capable of thoroughly subduing all afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and evil karma, even if such transgressions exist, they will not bring about evil retribution.

Sentient beings are bound by the fetters of the marks (*nimitta-bandhana*), and they are likewise bound by the fetters of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*). Only after cultivating both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* together can one be liberated from both.

All evil karma arises from afflictions (*kleśa*), and all afflictions arise from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). Now, by departing from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and severing all discrimination, once discrimination is exhausted, delusion and karma also perish; therefore, upon hearing this sutra and attaining faith and understanding, these great transgressions will certainly be extinguished.
The Sūtra says:

"They shall constantly be born in the happy realms and experience supreme and wondrous bliss; they shall cultivate the practices of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The praise says:
Above, it is able to eliminate evil; below, it is able to gather what is wholesome.
Within this, there are two fruits:
There are two kinds of fruits: first, mundane fruits; second, supramundane fruits.
The Sūtra says:

At that time, the World-Honored One again, relying upon the characteristic of the Tathāgata of Innate Purity, proclaimed for the sake of all bodhisattvas the profound principle of the Seal of the Wondrous Wisdom of Avalokiteśvara—the contemplation of the equality of all phenomena within the Prajñāpāramitā—a Dharma-gate of purification.
The commentary states:
This fourth section reveals the sphere of practice by means of the illumination of the wisdom of contemplation through contemplation.
There are three parts within the text, all of which are explained as previously.

Because the wisdom that contemplates realizes that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure, the wisdom that discerns characteristics is said to be "naturally pure" (prakṛti-viśuddha); this is now termed "attainment of purity."
The equality of all phenomena is the compassionate activity of the Tathatā-Avalokiteśvara.
The Seal of Wondrous Wisdom is his wisdom activity.
Furthermore, this Avalokiteśvara is himself the Seal of Wondrous Wisdom, because he seals all phenomena with equality.
The remainder of the text may be understood by itself. The Sūtra says:

"Because all greed is intrinsically pure and supremely luminous, it can cause the world’s anger to become pure; because all anger is intrinsically pure and supremely luminous, it can cause the world’s delusion to become pure; because all delusion is intrinsically pure and supremely luminous, it can cause the world’s doubt to become pure; because all doubt is intrinsically pure and supremely luminous, it can cause the world’s views to become pure; because all views are intrinsically pure and supremely luminous, it can cause the world’s pride to become pure."
The commentary states:
This passage consists of three parts, as explained in the preceding text.
The preceding text concerns the object (*viṣaya*), while this text concerns wisdom (*jñāna*), because it illuminates the former.

This means that because it provides ultimate illumination within the realm of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the intrinsic nature of desire, that which is capable of illuminating is wisdom (*jñāna*).
This is because hatred and other afflictions arise with desire as their root.
The Sūtra says:

Because all pride is by nature pure and supremely luminous, it can cause the fetters of the world to become pure; because all fetters are by nature pure and supremely luminous, they can cause the defilements of the world to become pure.
The commentary states:
This clarifies that the nature of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) is intrinsically pure and supremely luminous.
The meanings of "entanglements" (*paryavasthāna*), "impurities" (*mala*), and so forth are all to be understood as explained previously.
What are called "fetters" (saṃyojana) are the nine fetters, namely: attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, views, grasping at views, doubt, envy, and stinginess.
These fetters (saṃyojana) are bonds that can conjoin one with suffering; because they are difficult to untie, they are called "fetters.
As the Sūtra says:

"Because all defilements are by nature pure and supremely luminous, they can cause the unwholesome dharmas of the world to become pure; because all unwholesome dharmas are by nature pure and supremely luminous, they can cause the birth-and-death (saṃsāra) of the world to become pure."
The commentary states:
The preceding section clarified delusion; this section clarifies karma and its fruit.
Because the karma of birth and death compels one toward the fruit of karma, it is termed "unwholesome dharmas" (akuśala-dharma).
What is called "birth and death" refers to the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), that is, the fruit of suffering summoned by prior unwholesome karma.
As the Sūtra says:
"Because the intrinsic nature of all birth and death is pure and supremely luminous, it can cause all worldly phenomena to be pure."
The commentary states:
"The various phenomena of the world are precisely the defiled phenomena (saṃkleśa-dharma), which collectively subsume all that is with outflows (sāsrava).
From this point downward is the second section, which collectively subsumes all phenomena."
The Sūtra says:
Because all phenomena are by nature pure and supremely luminous, they are able to bring about the purification of sentient beings in the world.
The Praise says:
Because sentient beings are constituted by contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), it is after discussing the contaminated that sentient beings are explained.
The Sūtra says:
"Because the intrinsic nature of all sentient beings is pure and supremely luminous, they are able to bring about the purification of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) in the world."
The praise says:
Within the supramundane, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is the foundation; by citing this, all other pure phenomena are subsumed.
The wisdom that universally contemplates the selflessness of all three vehicles is termed "omniscience."
The Sūtra says:
Because the nature of all-knowledge is intrinsically pure and supremely luminous, it is able to bring about the most excellent purity of the profound Prajñāpāramitā in the world.
The praise states:
This is the third purity of prajñā.

Because it can illuminate the fact that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is fundamentally pure, the wisdom of contemplation is supremely pure, being in perfect correspondence with its objective referent.
The Sūtra says:
After the Buddha had thus taught the pure Dharma of the Prajñā-principle of the Seal of Equal Wisdom,
he uttered this praise:
From here below is the third section, which sets forth the superior qualities of the sūtra.

Regarding the "seal of the wisdom of equality" (*samatājñānamudrā*): it refers to the wisdom that is able to contemplate the nature of all phenomena as being free from conceptual proliferation; this is called the seal of the wisdom of equality.
The Sūtra says:
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and the others, saying:

"If there are those who hear this pure principle of the Prajñāpāramitā, and who believe, understand, uphold, recite, and practice it, then even while dwelling amidst the mass of defilements of adventitious afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, they remain unstained by any of these adventitious defilements or faults, just as a lotus flower is not stained by any adventitious impurities."
The praise says:

Because one observes with the wisdom of contemplation that the intrinsic nature of both defiled and pure phenomena is fundamentally pure, one dwells amidst afflictions without being defiled, for one has realized their fundamental nature.
This explains the elimination of faults.
The Sūtra says:
"One who can constantly cultivate the supreme practices of a bodhisattva will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The praise says:
This commentary attains wholesome fruits.
Because one awakens to true wisdom through the practice of the Dharma, one constantly cultivates the supreme conduct of a bodhisattva until, at the end of life, one swiftly realizes enlightenment.
The Sūtra says:
At that time, the World-Honored One again, relying upon the marks of the Tathāgata, the Supreme Lord of all the Three Realms,
praised, saying:
Among the six sections clarifying the objective realm, this is the third from the beginning, which consists of two segments of scripture clarifying the objective realm of the resultant dharmas.
Within these two segments, the first segment—the Dharma Gate of the Wisdom-Treasury of the Dharma-King’s Empowerment—reveals that the fruit of wealth and status is attained through two practices;
the second segment—the Dharma Gate of the Tathāgata’s Wisdom-Seal Vajra—reveals that the fruit of one's own essential body is attained through two practices.
This first section contains three parts,
which should be explained according to the preceding model.
Within the initial heading that indicates the title of the Dharma-gate being taught, there are further two sections:
First, the characteristics of the Tathāgata, who is the basis, are clarified; subsequently, the names of the Dharma-gates he teaches will be clarified.
This is the first [section].

The abode of the three realms is turbulent and lacks peace; it is beset by the immeasurable afflictions of insect-like beasts and the fires of various sufferings, which press upon one with infinite urgency. These manifold terrors cause sentient beings to experience simultaneous perils.

Because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for all beings like a great elder rescuing his children through skillful means, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is called the Lord of the Three Realms.
As the Buddha is the King of Dharma, he is called the Supreme Lord; relying upon this honored position, he expounds the Dharma-gate.
The Sūtra says:

"For the sake of all bodhisattvas, he proclaimed the Dharma-gate of the Treasury of Wisdom, the Profound Principle of the Unified Empowerment of All Tathāgatas, which is the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā)."
The praise says:
This clarifies the title of the Dharma-gate being taught.

When reaching the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) and about to receive the position of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions unite and consecrate his crown with water, just as a Kṣatriya receives the ritual for ascending the throne.
Now, as this Bodhisattva receives the exalted station of a Buddha, by what water of Dharma shall his crown be sprinkled to bring about auspiciousness?
It is said that the water of Dharma of the wisdom of all Buddhas possesses supreme knowledge; it gives birth to all virtues and contains all virtues, like a treasury.

By sprinkling this water of wisdom upon the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head, the stains of the two obscurations accumulated since beginningless time are completely exhausted, and all the auspicious merits of all Tathāgatas are fully perfected.
Now, this teaching is explained so that one may rely upon it for entry; therefore, it is called a "gate.
The Sūtra says:
"By bestowing the worldly stage of consecration, one shall attain the fruit of the rank of Dharma King over the three realms."
By practicing the gift of the unsurpassed supramundane meaning, one shall attain the fulfillment of all aspirations.
By practicing the gift of the unsurpassed supramundane Dharma, one shall attain mastery over all phenomena.
If one gives gifts of worldly wealth, food, and so forth, one shall obtain happiness of body, speech, and mind.
If one gives various gifts of material wealth and the Dharma, one will be able to swiftly bring the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) to full completion.
The commentary states:
From this point downward is the second section, which correctly reveals the dharma-gates being taught.
As the six perfections differ, they are divided into six segments accordingly.
There are five kinds of giving: first, the gift of position; second, the gift of meaning; third, the gift of Dharma; fourth, the gift of material wealth; and fifth, the gift of total fearlessness.
In reality, each of these five gifts individually yields manifold fruits; here, however, we shall briefly discuss their five corresponding fruits.
If one renounces positions of honor and nobility to cultivate the True Dharma, one shall attain Buddhahood and become the Dharma King of the three realms.
Because the gift of the flavor of meaning accords with principle, all future aspirations shall be fully satisfied.
By giving the gift of Dharma, one shall be able to penetrate and understand all Buddha-dharmas.
Because the giving of wealth and food fulfills and benefits the three karmas, one shall obtain the happiness of the three karmas in the future.

If one practices various forms of giving, whether material wealth or the Dharma, it means gathering in sentient beings through material gifts and the Dharma so that they are free from fear; this is called the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*).

The *Bodhicitta Sūtra* states that there must be five requirements for the practice of giving material wealth: [1] a pure intention, [2] a respectful attitude, [3] a joyful mind, [4] the absence of regret, and [5] the dedication of the merit toward supreme enlightenment.
First, single-mindedness; second, faith; third, timeliness; fourth, using one’s own hands; fifth, according to the Dharma. As a verse says:
"The donor, being endowed with excellence such as faith, should give with respect, at the proper time, and with their own hands," and so forth.

Furthermore, there is a verse that says: "In the application of altruism toward sentient beings, one makes no distinction between those who are capable and those who are not; at all times, one gives everything, extensively teaching the Dharma according to one's ability to provide benefit."
There are five things that should not be given as gifts:
one should not give wealth that is improperly acquired, because it is impure;
nor should one give alcohol or poison, because they give rise to disorder.
One should not give snares, nets, or traps, for they cause distress to living beings;
one should not give swords, staves, bows, or arrows, for they harm living beings;
and one should not give music or female forms, for they corrupt the pure mind.

There are five benefits of giving: first, one constantly draws near to the worthy and the holy; second, sentient beings delight in seeing one; third, one enters assemblies with honor and respect; fourth, one's good reputation spreads far and wide; and fifth, it serves as the cause for attaining bodhi.
The Bodhisattva Asaṅga stated: "It refers to the cultivation of six kinds of intention:
first, vastness; second, duration; third, joy; fourth, gratitude; fifth, great resolve; and sixth, pure goodness."
Regarding these six, one gives rise to three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*):
first, cherishing; second, sympathetic joy; and third, joyful aspiration.

If merely hearing these six kinds [of teachings] can cause even a single thought of faith to arise, it is still able to produce immeasurable masses of merit and cause all evil karmic obstructions to be extinguished; how much more so for a Bodhisattva!
The Sūtra says:
By upholding various kinds of pure prohibitive precepts, one can cause the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) to be swiftly fulfilled.
By practicing and training in patience toward all matters, one can cause the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) to be swiftly fulfilled.
By practicing diligence at all times, one can swiftly bring the perfection of diligence to fulfillment.
By practicing meditative concentration regarding all objects, one can swiftly bring the perfection of meditative concentration to fulfillment.
One constantly cultivates sublime wisdom regarding all phenomena, thereby enabling the swift perfection of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
It is praised thus:
"The three types of ethical discipline are all brought to fulfillment; like a lotus stalk or a swan's pearl, they remain unimpaired."
Because the three types of restraint are not one, they are called "various.
Because one is able to endure in every matter and is able to be diligent at all times without slackening or weariness;
because one is able to practice meditative concentration regarding all objects, being free from a distracted mind.
Because the wisdom cultivated regarding all phenomena is capable of discerning them all, one who practices these six perfections attains six fruits of retribution:

first, nobility; second, a great birth; third, a great circle of followers; fourth, the accomplishment of great undertakings; fifth, freedom from affliction, bondage, and defilement; and sixth, mastery of the five sciences.
It is capable of performing beneficial purposes, as its characteristics are explained in detail in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
The Sūtra says:
After the Buddha had taught this Dharma-gate of Empowerment, the Prajñā-principle of the Treasury of Wisdom, he addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

If there are those who hear this Dharma gate of the treasury of wisdom—the profound principle of empowerment—and believe, understand, uphold, recite, and practice it, they will swiftly fulfill all bodhisattva practices and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The praise says:
Through hearing, the bodhisattva practice of the six perfections is accomplished, and the sought-after enlightenment can also be swiftly attained.
As the Sūtra says:

At that time, the World-Honored One, again relying upon the Tathāgata’s aspect of the Wisdom-Seal that Sustains All Buddhas’ Secret Dharma-Gates of All Tathāgatas, proclaimed for the sake of all Bodhisattvas the Vajra Dharma-Gate of the Profound Principle of the Wisdom-Seal Sustained by All Tathāgatas within the Prajñāpāramitā.
The praise says:
This second section, the Vajra Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s Wisdom Seal, reveals that the fruit of one's own essence is attained through two practices.
The text consists of three parts, all of which are explained as before.
This is the first title for the dharma-gate taught therein, which upholds all the profound dharmas of the Buddhas by means of the seal of sublime wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*).
Because the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the profound dharmas of the Buddhas is difficult to know, it is called "secret" (*guhya*).
By means of the single seal of wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*), one upholds all Buddha-dharmas; because all Buddha-dharmas enter into this, it is called "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*).
Now, this teaching is expounded so that one may diligently enter [it], and thus it is called a "gate" (*mukha*).
Because its essence of wisdom is firm and solid, capable of destroying all of birth and death, it is called "vajra.
The Sūtra says:
"One who possesses and receives the vajra-body seal of all Tathāgatas shall realize the dharma-body of all Tathāgatas."
If one fully embraces all the Vajra Speech Seals (*vāg-mudrā*) of all Tathāgatas, one shall attain mastery over all phenomena.
It is said in praise:
"By practicing the distinct seals of the causes—the three activities of the Tathāgata—while still within the causal state, one attains at the time of fruition results such as the Vajra Dharma-body."
The Sūtra says:
"If one fully embraces all the Tathāgatas’ Vajra-mudrās of Mind, one shall attain mastery over all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).
If one fully embraces all the Tathāgatas’ Vajra-mudrās of Wisdom, one will be able to attain the supreme and wondrous body, speech, and mind, which are like vajra—unmoving and indestructible."
The praise says:

Because one possesses the practice of the three karmas as the Vajra Wisdom Seal while in the causal stage, at the time of attaining the fruit, one is able to obtain the supreme and wondrous body, speech, and mind; that is to say, like a vajra, it cannot be moved by evil friends and cannot be destroyed by birth and death.

The meaning intended here is that the specific causes for the excellence of each of the three types of action performed separately result in their respective three fruits, whereas the collective superior causes of all three types of action performed together result in a single fruit.
The three karmas are firm and solid, like a vajra, unshakable and indestructible.
The Sūtra says:
After the Buddha had thus taught the Vajradharma of the Tathāgata-jñāna-mudrā-prajñā-pāramitā-naya, he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and the others, saying:

If there are those who hear this Dharma-gate of the Vajra Profound Principle of the Seal of Wisdom, and who believe, understand, uphold, recite, and practice it, they will be able to accomplish all undertakings, will always be in harmony with all superior matters, and all their desired practices of supreme wisdom and sublime meritorious deeds will be swiftly perfected.
The praise states:
"From this point on is the third section, extolling the virtues of this sutra.
'All undertakings are accomplished' refers to all blameless, principle-conforming, and virtuous deeds."

"One who is always in harmony with all superior matters" means that in the present life and in future births, they will always be in harmony and correspondence with superior matters; they will be entirely free from decline and other such adversities, and the merit and wisdom they cultivate will all swiftly reach fulfillment.
This explains the benefits attained during the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*).
The Sūtra says:

"One shall attain the most supreme purity of body, speech, and mind, which, like a vajra, is indestructible, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*)."
The praise says:
This explains the sublime and wondrous fruits of the stages to be attained in the future.
The Sūtra says:

At that time, the World-Honored One, further relying upon the marks of the Tathāgata of all dharmas free from conceptual proliferation, proclaimed for the sake of the bodhisattvas the profound principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Dharma-gate of the Wheel of Syllables.
The commentary states:
The preceding six sections of the sutra have clarified the sublime realms.
Next, there are six sections that should clarify the sublime practices, which are further divided into three parts:

The first two sections reveal the characteristics of severing and cultivating based on the true nature (*dharmatā*); the next two sections reveal the characteristics of severing and cultivating based on contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*); and the final two sections reveal the characteristics of universal cultivation based on both methods.
Regarding the first two sections, which reveal the characteristics of abandonment and cultivation based on the true reality (*dharmatā*), there are two parts:

first, the dharma-gate of the wheel of letters that transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), because by contemplating *tathatā* one abandons discursive discrimination; and second, the gate of the equality of the vast wheel, because by contemplating equality one realizes and attains the true reality.
From this point downward, the first section consists of three parts:
first, the title of the dharma-gate being taught is presented.
The middle part is further divided into two:
First, the characteristics of the Tathāgata as the basis are distinguished:

suchness and dharmatā are free from all conceptual discrimination; because they transcend the path of verbal expression, they are devoid of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and thus constitute the characteristic based upon the dharmakāya.
Regarding the Dharma-gate of the syllable *cakra* (wheel), the term "wheel" has two meanings:
first, the sense of being perfectly circular; second, the sense of crushing and destroying.
Because one contemplates that the nature of true suchness (*tathatā*) is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and pervades all phenomena, it is called "perfectly circular."
Because one observes this, one becomes free from conceptual attachment and destroys all clinging to birth and death; therefore, it is called "Destruction" (Cūḍāmaṇi).
The Dharma-gates that express the principles of this wheel are called the "Wheel-Syllable Dharmas."
Because the teaching is able to express and reveal [the truth], it is called a "gate.

By hearing this teaching, one subsequently gives rise to wheel-like activity; having given rise to wheel-like activity, one attains the fruit of the wheel; having attained the fruit of the wheel, one in turn turns it for others, thus continuing in succession.
The Sūtra says:
It is said that all phenomena are empty because they lack intrinsic nature;
all phenomena are signless because they are free from all signs.
All phenomena are wishless, because there is nothing to be wished for.
The praise says:
the following is the second section, which correctly presents what has been taught.
Within this, there are four points:
first, the objects of the three doors of liberation.
All that is conceptually imputed is empty; the perfected nature is signless; and the dependent nature is wishless.
Furthermore, these three types all pertain to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Moreover, there are only two [categories], namely the false and the true.
Both the true and the false pertain to [the three natures] because each comprises three types.
That which is devoid of "mine" is called emptiness; that which is free from the ten names is called signlessness; and that which does not aspire is called wishlessness.
As the Sūtra says:
"All phenomena are detached, because they are without attachment."
All phenomena are quiescent, because they are eternally extinguished.
The praise says:
This is the second [stage], free from attachment and free from birth.
The Sūtra says:
"All phenomena are impermanent, because their nature is eternally non-existent;
all phenomena are without bliss, because they are not to be enjoyed."
All phenomena are without self, because they lack autonomy;
all phenomena are without purity, because they are free from the marks of purity.
The praise says:
This is the third [point], which is free from the four inverted attachments.
The Sūtra says:
"All dharmas are unapprehendable, because when their nature is investigated and sought, it cannot be apprehended."
All phenomena are inconceivable, for their nature is non-existent when subjected to conceptualization;
all phenomena are non-existent, being merely provisional designations through the conjunction of various conditions;
all phenomena are free from conceptual proliferation, for their fundamental nature is empty and quiescent, transcending verbal expression.
All phenomena are pure by their very nature, because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is pure by its very nature.
It is said in praise:
"This is the fourth [point], free from all attachments."
Because there is nothing to be apprehended as it is grasped; because the mind of investigation and the discourse of speech are inconceivable;
and because phenomena are merely conventional designations, lacking any real existence.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is beyond words, for it is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
The nature of phenomena is fundamentally pure, because the nature of the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā*) is inherently pure.
Since this is the nature of phenomena, all phenomena follow their fundamental essence and are therefore all empty.
The Sūtra says:

After the Buddha had thus taught this Dharma-gate of the Wheel of Syllables for the Principle of Prajñā Free from All Proliferation (*prapañca*), he addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

"If there are those who hear this Dharma-gate of the Wheel of Syllables for the Principle of Prajñā Free from Proliferation, and who believe, understand, uphold, recite, and cultivate it, they will attain unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The eulogy says:
This is the third praise for the excellence of the sutra.
Because he has realized that the nature of phenomena is empty, he has attained unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena.
The Sūtra says:

At that time, the World-Honored One, again relying upon the Tathāgata’s mark of the wheel-comprehension of all Tathāgatas, proclaimed for the sake of the bodhisattvas the profound principle of the entrance into the vast wheel of the Prajñāpāramitā, the gateway of the equality of the *naya*.
The praise says:
This is the second entry into the gate of the equality of the vast wheel, because one realizes the truth through the cultivation of the contemplation of equality.
Within this there are three parts; this [line] indicates the name of the dharma-gate being taught.

Previously, the syllable *laṃ* was explained, but it did not clarify how all phenomena are subsumed; now it is clarified that all phenomena are subsumed within the Truth (*tathatā*), because they are perfectly complete and free from attachment.

Because this [Truth] pervades everywhere, it is called "vast"; because there is no phenomenon that is not subsumed, it is called "equality"; and because it is the fundamental essence of all phenomena, it is called "nature."
The Sūtra says:
It is called entering the equality of the vajra, because it can enter the nature-wheel (*dharmadhātu-cakra*) of all Tathāgatas;
it is called entering the equality of meaning, because it can enter the nature-wheel of all Bodhisattvas.
"Entering the equality of phenomena, because one is able to enter the wheel of the nature of all phenomena.
The commentary says:
From this point downward is the second section, which formally presents what is being explained.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the specific explanation of the wheel of nature; second, the general explanation of the wheel of nature.
Within the specific explanation of the wheel of nature, there are three further sections:

First, the wheel of the nature of the noble ones (*ārya-gotra*) is elucidated; second, the wheel of the nature of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu-gotra*) is elucidated; third, the wheel of the nature of sentient beings (*sattva-gotra*) is elucidated.
Within the first [section], there are three parts:
first, the wheel of Buddha-nature (*buddha-gotra*) is elucidated.
The fundamental nature of the Dharmakāya can destroy birth and death, for it is as firm and indestructible as a vajra.
Since the Dharma of the Bodhisattva is practiced, cultivated, and realized based on that which is expounded by the teachings, its meaning is equal; thus it is called the "Bodhisattva-nature."
The Buddha, too, must be this equality of meaning; for apart from the substantial meaning that transcends all designations, the specific name "Vajra" is not itself the meaning.
When Bodhisattvas realize this, they have not yet attained the perfect nature of the Vajra, and thus it is merely designated by the name "meaning."
The second is that which can express [the meaning], collectively termed "Dharma"; "Dharma" here refers to the teaching.

Because one wishes to reveal the sublime Dharma of cause and effect that is expressed, the expressive teachings are all subsumed within the wheel of the Dharma-nature; thus, while they are explained separately according to their functions, their nature is equally the ultimate reality.
The Sūtra says:
"By entering the equality of the aggregates (*skandha*), one is able to enter the wheel of the nature of all aggregates.
By entering the equality of the sense bases (*āyatana*), one is able to enter the wheel of the nature of all sense bases."
Entering the equality of the elements (*dhātu*), because one is able to enter the wheel of the nature of all elements.
The praise says:
From here below, the second section clarifies the wheel of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the specific dharmas; second, the general dharmas; and third, the dharmas of the stages.
Within the specific dharmas, there are seven sections; these [first] three constitute the initial category.
In terms of its distinct meanings, it is explained as threefold, yet its essence is the true *dharmatā*.
The Sūtra says:
"Entering the equality of the truths (*satya-samatā*), because one is able to enter the wheel of the nature of all truths."
They enter the equality of dependent origination, because they are able to enter the wheel of all natures of dependent origination.
They enter the equality of jewels, because they are able to enter the wheel of all jewel natures.
Entering into the equality of food, because one is able to enter the wheel of the nature of all food.
It is praised, saying:
These are four distinct dharmas.
The truths refer to the Four Truths; dependent origination has twelve links; the jewels refer to the Three Jewels;
and the nutriments refer to the four nutriments, namely: edible food, contact, volition, and consciousness.
Fragrance, flavor, and tangibility—these three are called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
Tangibility refers to the mental factor of contact (*sparśa*), which is associated with the sixth consciousness.
Volition refers to the mental factor of intention (*cetanā*), which is likewise associated with the sixth consciousness.
"Consciousness" refers to the aggregate of consciousness, which is exclusively the eighth [consciousness].
It is described as fourfold according to conditions, yet it is subsumed within the dharma-nature.
As the Sūtra says:
They enter the equality of wholesome dharmas, because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all wholesome dharmas;
they enter the equality of unwholesome dharmas, because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all unwholesome dharmas.
They enter the equality of determinate phenomena, because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all determinate phenomena;
they enter the equality of indeterminate phenomena, because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all indeterminate phenomena.
They enter the equality of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all contaminated phenomena;
they enter the equality of all uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all uncontaminated phenomena.
They enter the equality of conditioned phenomena, because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all conditioned phenomena;
they enter the equality of unconditioned phenomena, because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all unconditioned phenomena.
They enter the equality of worldly phenomena, because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all worldly phenomena.
They enter the equality of supramundane phenomena, because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all supramundane phenomena.
The praise says:
This is the second [section], clarifying the wheel of entering the dharma-nature through all the common dharmas.
Within this there are five parts; their meaning is as stated in the text.
These five supernormal powers pertain to both persons and phenomena.
The Sūtra says:
"They enter into the equality of the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all dharmas of ordinary beings."
They enter the equality of the Śrāvaka teachings, because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all Śrāvaka teachings.
They enter the equality of the Pratyekabuddha teachings, because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all Pratyekabuddha teachings.
They enter the equality of the bodhisattva-dharmas, because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all bodhisattva-dharmas;
they enter the equality of the Tathāgata-dharmas, because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of the Tathāgatas.
The praise says:
This is the third [section], clarifying the wheel of the dharma-nature that enters all stages and dharmas.
Within it there are five parts: first, ordinary dharmas; fourth, noble dharmas; these should be understood as appropriate.
The Sūtra says:
"One enters the equality of sentient beings, because one is able to enter the wheel of the nature of all sentient beings.
The Praise says:
This is the third [section], clarifying how sentient beings enter the wheel of their own fundamental nature (*prakṛti-cakra*).
The Sūtra says:
"By entering into all-pervasive equality, one is able to enter the wheel of all natures."
The praise says:
This is the second [section], which generally clarifies the wheel of nature.
Whether noble or ordinary, whether person or phenomenon, all enter the wheel of original nature.
To reveal that all things are subsumed within the vast wheel of the fundamental nature,
the Sūtra says:
After the Buddha had thus taught the principle of the entrance into the vast wheel of Prajñā-pāramitā and its equality, he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and the others, saying:

If there are those who hear such a profound principle of the nature of the wheel, the gateway to the equality of phenomena, and who believe, understand, uphold, recite, and practice it, they will be able to skillfully penetrate all states of equality and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Praise says:
This is the third [section] extolling the excellence of the sūtra.

By hearing this, one is able to skillfully enter into all states of equality in the present and future lives; through study, awakening, and realization, one skillfully enters them all, until finally attaining bodhi with swiftness.
The Sūtra says:

At that time, the World-Honored One, further relying upon the marks of the Tathāgata as the truly pure vessel-field for receiving all extensive offerings, proclaimed for the sake of the bodhisattvas the unsurpassed Dharma-gate of the profound principle of all offerings of the Prajñāpāramitā.
The commentary states:
Within the section on "Wisdom and Conduct," the following two segments reveal the characteristics of cultivation and abandonment based upon contemplative observation.
The first segment concerns the supreme Dharma-gate of true and pure offering, because one cultivates offerings by relying upon contemplative observation.
The latter section concerns the Dharma-gate of the Treasury of Wisdom for Skillfully Subduing, which arises from relying on contemplative observation to eliminate anger and other afflictions;
this is the first [section].
Within it, there are three parts:
First, the title of the Dharma-gate being taught is indicated.

Regarding "the true and pure field and vessel that extensively receives offerings": because the Buddha’s causal practices were endowed with true offerings and he was able to carry out all true dharmic practices, at the time of his attaining Buddhahood, all things were fully satisfied and his three karmas were purely clean; thus, he was capable of extensively receiving the offerings of sentient beings.
Being a true vessel of the Dharma and serving as a field of true purity for all sentient beings, it is therefore called "unsurpassed.
Although those of the two vehicles and so forth are indeed fields of merit, they are not unsurpassed.
The Sūtra says:
It means that one generates the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and extensively makes offerings to all Tathāgatas;
one upholds and protects the True Dharma, and extensively makes offerings to all Tathāgatas.
They practice all the pāramitās, making extensive offerings to all the Tathāgatas.
They practice all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas), making extensive offerings to all the Tathāgatas.
They practice all dhāraṇīs and samādhis, making extensive offerings to all Tathāgatas.
They practice all five eyes and six supernormal powers, making extensive offerings to all Tathāgatas.
They practice all meditative concentrations and liberations, making extensive offerings to all Tathāgatas.
They practice all loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, making extensive offerings to all Tathāgatas.
Practicing all the unique qualities of the Buddhas, he extensively makes offerings to all Tathāgatas.
He praises them, saying:
"From here on, the correct exposition begins."
By practicing correct offerings while in the causal stage, one subsequently establishes the pure cause.
Within this, there are three aspects:
first, the practice of cultivation; second, the practice of observation; and third, the practice of the Dharma.
This constitutes the first [section].
Within it, there are further three parts:
first, the practice of initial resolve; second, the practice of gathering and protecting; and third, the practice of cultivation.
"Among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is supreme. The *Devaparivarta* states:

"Two kinds of people remain far removed from what kings, thieves, and others cannot invade—the great treasury of jewels. Though the Dharma is difficult to hear throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, having heard it, they neither uphold nor bestow it."

Protecting the True Dharma with the great bodhicitta, practicing according to the teachings with a tranquil mind, and maintaining equanimity toward the benefit of oneself and others—this is called the true offering to the Buddha.
Regarding the Great Bodhicitta, the Buddha himself said:
"The meritorious fruit and retribution of even a single inferior thought of the initial resolve of the bodhisattvas cannot be fully described even in ten million kalpas, let alone over many kalpas."
For example, when the great ocean first begins to arise, one should know that it serves as the dwelling place for even priceless jewels, because all jewels are born from the sea.
When the trichiliocosm first arises, one should know that it serves as a place of reliance for all sentient beings within the twenty-five realms of existence.
It is the same with the bodhisattva’s generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*): when it first gradually arises, it universally serves as a place of reliance for all immeasurable sentient beings.

When a Bodhisattva resolves their mind, compassion is foremost; it is like space, which universally covers all without exception. Because space is immeasurable, sentient beings are immeasurable; because sentient beings are immeasurable, the Bodhisattva’s resolve is likewise so, for it is able to pervade all worlds and all living beings.

If a bodhisattva associates with spiritual friends, makes offerings to all Buddhas, cultivates and accumulates roots of goodness, aspires to seek the supreme Dharma, maintains a mind that is always gentle and pliant, is able to endure suffering when encountering it, possesses profound and sincere compassion, maintains a deep mind of equanimity, has faith and delight in the Mahāyāna, and seeks the wisdom of a Buddha—if a person can possess these ten dharmas, they are then able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, as explained at length in the sūtra.
Regarding "upholding the true Dharma": "upholding" (*saṃgraha*) means to embrace and maintain, which refers to the "embracing of the true Dharma" as taught in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
"Protecting" (*rakṣā*) means to guard and mindfully preserve, which refers to the mindful protection and entrustment of the true Dharma.
They embrace and protect [the teachings] as a fortress for the Dharma, offering worship without regard for their own bodies or lives.
From the *pāramitās* onwards are the practices of cultivation, which comprise seven categories:

*dhāraṇī* refers to total retention; *samādhi* refers to meditative concentration; *dhyāna* refers to the four meditative absorptions; *vimokṣa* refers to the eight liberations; and loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity refer to the four immeasurables.
Regarding the unique qualities of all Buddhas (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:

"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess one hundred and forty unique Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*). These are: the thirty-two marks of a great man (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Tathāgatas, the eighty secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), the four kinds of purity in every respect (*sarvākāraviśuddhi*), the ten powers (*bala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the three ways in which there is nothing to guard (*arakṣya*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharman*), the permanent destruction of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and the sublime wisdom of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). These are called the unique qualities of all Buddhas."
The thirty-two marks, the eighty secondary characteristics, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the quality of non-forgetfulness are all as previously explained.

Regarding the four kinds of purity in all aspects (*sarvākāra-viśuddhi*): first, purity of the basis in all aspects, because the heavy habitual tendencies (*dausthulya-vāsanā*) of the afflictions have been eternally exhausted.
Furthermore, with respect to one's own body, one dwells with mastery in the acts of assuming, maintaining, or relinquishing it according to one's own will.
Second, purity of the object of focus in all its aspects: this refers to exercising mastery over all objects of focus, whether they are emanated, transformed, or manifested in their various forms.
3. Purity of mind in all its aspects, because all mental heaviness (*dausthulya*) has been forever abandoned and all roots of goodness have been fully accumulated.
4. Purity of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), because the heaviness of ignorance has been forever abandoned.
Furthermore, the knowledge that pervades all that is knowable and the unobstructed knowledge function with mastery.
Regarding the three foundations of mindfulness (*trīṇi smṛtyupasthānāni*), it refers to the Tathāgatas’ aspiration throughout the long night:
"How may I cause all classes of sentient beings to dwell in accordance with reality within my well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, following them in their practice without error?"

Thus, regarding the desires and pleasures of the long night, when the Lord of Dharma transforms and guides the assembly, whether his aspirations are fulfilled or not, no defilement arises; this is because it is briefly revealed by means of the three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
These three are further distinguished by three types of groups:
first, those who practice exclusively correctly;
second, those who practice exclusively erroneously; [and third, those who practice both].
Third, regarding those who practice one part correctly and one part erroneously, he does not give rise to joy or distress, but gives rise only to great equanimity.
The three ways in which he is "unprotected" refer to the Tathāgatas' manifestation of the complete purity of the three karmas.

"Permanently destroying the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)" means that although the Tathāgatas may appear to engage in activities involving movement, gazing, speech, or remaining still as if they possessed afflictions, such actions generally do not manifest; all habitual tendencies have been severed without remainder.
The "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*) is, in brief, the non-erroneous knowledge regarding all phenomena.
The remaining qualities of a Buddha have already been explained as before.
The Sūtra says:
One contemplates that all phenomena, whether permanent or impermanent, are all unattainable, and thus makes extensive offerings to all Tathāgatas.
One contemplates that all phenomena, whether pleasant or painful, are all unattainable, and thus makes extensive offerings to all Tathāgatas.
One contemplates all phenomena, whether as self or as non-self, and finds them both unobtainable; one extensively makes offerings to all Tathāgatas.
One contemplates all phenomena, whether as pure or as impure, and finds them both unobtainable; one extensively makes offerings to all Tathāgatas.
The commentary states:
From here below is the second [section], the observation of the modes of activity (*ākāra*).
This, in turn, consists of three parts:
First, the practice of being free from the four inversions; second, the practice of the three gates; third, the practice of being free from attachment to arising and ceasing.
This is the first [category].

Ordinary beings mostly cling to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena as being pure, pleasant, self, and permanent; it is to subvert these views that the principle of the Four Noble Truths is taught.
Since there is no permanence, no bliss, no self, and no purity, this causes them to suppress the cycle of birth and death and seek the path of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Consequently, the followers of the two vehicles come to grasp at those four characteristics—impermanence and so forth—as being truly existent. Because they possess attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) and are bound to the minor fruits of their practice, they have no desire for the Mahāyāna.
The World-Honored One later taught the Great Parinirvāṇa—its permanence, bliss, self, and purity—to cause them to abandon the lesser fruits and seek the Mahāyāna.
Upon hearing this, they grew weary of and renounced [the lesser path], and subsequently attained the fruit of Buddhahood.
Both of these are merely provisional means for attracting and gathering [beings], and are not the actual principle.
All phenomena are truly neither of these two sets of four.
Therefore, it is said:
"The Buddhas sometimes speak of a self, and at other times they speak of non-self;
within the true reality of all phenomena, there is neither self nor non-self.
The same applies to the remaining three [marks].
Now, one establishes offerings by contemplating the true nature of reality; therefore, one contemplates that all phenomena—whether permanent or impermanent—are ultimately ungraspable.
As the Sūtra says:
"One contemplates that all phenomena, whether empty or non-empty, are all ungraspable, thereby extensively making offerings to all Tathāgatas."

One contemplates that all phenomena, whether possessing marks or being markless, are all unattainable, and thus makes extensive offerings to all Tathāgatas; one contemplates that all phenomena, whether possessing vows or being vowless, are all unattainable, and thus makes extensive offerings to all Tathāgatas.
The commentary states:
This is the second of the three gateways of practice.
If one belongs to the Two Vehicles, they contemplate suffering as empty because they practice the contemplation of emptiness and non-self.
Contemplating the entirety of the truth of origination and the path, as well as a portion of the truth of suffering, constitutes the practice of wishlessness;
contemplating the truth of cessation constitutes the practice of signlessness; thus the tasks of aspiration and revulsion are accomplished.

For those of the Mahāyāna, they contemplate the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) of real self and phenomena as the practice of emptiness; they contemplate the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) as the practice of wishlessness; and they contemplate the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) as the practice of signlessness.

Furthermore, all three—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—pervade [all phenomena], collectively destroying the deluded conceptualizations of ordinary beings, such as the grasping at a self and dharmas.
Therefore, non-emptiness is the grasping of ordinary beings; the same applies to having wishes and having signs.
These practices of emptiness and so forth are all gateways for entering [the path].

According to the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), it is neither empty nor non-empty, neither with vow nor without vow, and neither with marks nor without marks; yet, because we now contemplate this true nature, these cannot be apprehended.
By extending the preceding principle, one realizes all things.
Therefore, the treatise states: "Śūnyatā (the void) is called emptiness; the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is not empty, because it is the very nature of emptiness."
The Sūtra says:
"One contemplates all phenomena as neither detached nor non-detached, yet finds them all ungraspable; one extensively makes offerings to all Tathāgatas.
One contemplates all phenomena as neither tranquil nor non-tranquil, yet finds them all ungraspable; one extensively makes offerings to all Tathāgatas."
The praise says:
Ordinary beings, through their deluded thoughts, delight in and cling to the nature of birth and death, which is not tranquil; thus they possess non-detachment and non-tranquility.
