To destroy this, it is taught as detachment and tranquility. Because one destroys those afflictions by relying on the gates of detachment and tranquility, entering into reality is what is called detachment, tranquility, and so forth.

According to the reality of the essence of dharmas, it is neither distant nor near, neither tranquil nor untranquil; since states such as tranquility and non-tranquility are all merely gateways [into understanding], they are not the true nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*).
Because the essence of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) transcends the path of names and words and brings the way of discursive thought to rest, states such as "separation" are ultimately unattainable.
The Sūtra says:

To transcribe, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, contemplate, and cultivate the profound Prajñāpāramitā, and to widely proclaim and disseminate it for the sake of sentient beings; or to personally make offerings to it, or to bestow it upon others—these constitute making extensive offerings to all Tathāgatas.
The praise says:
From here below is the third section, the practice of the Dharma through the gate of practice.

First, writing; second, hearing; third, receiving and upholding—cherishing and valuing them so that they are never parted from the mind, for one vows that these majestic conducts shall accompany one throughout the cycle of birth and death.
Fourth, reading; fifth, reciting; sixth, reflecting; seventh, cultivating through practice according to what has been taught;
eighth, extensively proclaiming and disseminating it for the sake of sentient beings; ninth, making offerings to it oneself; tenth, bestowing it upon others.
These ten are called the practices of practicing the Dharma through practice.
Within these, one may perform them oneself, instruct others to do so, praise such actions, and rejoice in them with celebration and consolation.
Regarding the mention of "speaking for oneself" among the offerings, this is said because, in contrast to giving to others, one also speaks of doing it oneself.
To speak according to reality, making offerings oneself, teaching others to do so, praising, rejoicing in merit, and offering consolation all constitute making offerings.

Such acts as giving books to others, teaching them to transcribe them, and even teaching or encouraging others to praise [the Dharma] are all termed "Dharma-practice" (dharmacaryā) and are called "making offerings."

One who practices the ten dharmas attains an immeasurable and superior mass of merit because it is inexhaustible; this is due to the unceasing gathering of others, as explained at length in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*.
The Sūtra says:
After the Buddha had spoken this unsurpassed Dharma of the profound principle of the truly pure offering, he addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

"If there are those who hear this unsurpassed Dharma-gate of the Prajñā-principle of offering, and who believe, understand, uphold, recite, and practice it, they will swiftly fulfill all bodhisattva practices and quickly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The praise says:
This is the third [section] extolling the excellence of the sūtra.
Since making offerings of the Dharma is itself the practice of a bodhisattva, the bodhisattva’s practices will swiftly reach fulfillment.
The Sūtra says:

At that time, the World-Honored One, further relying upon the characteristics of the Tathāgata who is capable of skillfully taming all beings, proclaimed for the sake of the bodhisattvas the Dharma-gate of the Treasury of Wisdom, the Profound Principle for Taming Sentient Beings by Means of the Secret Wisdom Subsumed within the Prajñāpāramitā.
The praise says:

Within the section on the characteristics of practice based on clear observation, this is the second [sub-section], the Dharma-gate of the Treasury of Wisdom that Skillfully Subdues. This is because, by relying on observation, anger and other afflictions are eliminated.
The meaning of the text has three parts, which should be explained according to the preceding [section].
This is the first part, the general designation of the names of the dharma-gates being taught.
"Able to skillfully subdue" means being able to eliminate anger and other such afflictions, which is termed "skillful subduing."
Regarding "embracing the secret of wisdom to discipline sentient beings": the subtle wisdom of contemplative observation is called "secret.

This wisdom serves as a treasury; because it possesses the capacity to embrace all the merits of the qualities of all Buddhas, it is termed "embracing" (*saṃgraha*) and is also called the "treasury of wisdom" (*jñānagarbha*).
Because this treasury of wisdom can eliminate faults such as anger in oneself and others, it is called "subduing" (*dānta*).

The meaning of this gate reveals that through the wisdom of contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), one realizes the fundamental nature of phenomena, whereby both anger and evil dharmas are simultaneously subdued.
The Sūtra says:
"The equality of all sentient beings is the equality of anger; the disciplining of all sentient beings is the disciplining of anger;
the true dharma-nature of all sentient beings is the true dharma-nature of anger."
The *tathatā* (suchness) nature of all sentient beings is the *tathatā* nature of anger; the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) nature of all sentient beings is the *dharmadhātu* nature of anger;
the nature of all sentient beings being free from birth is the nature of anger being free from birth;
the nature of the *bhūtakoṭi* (limit of reality) of all sentient beings is the nature of the *bhūtakoṭi* of anger; the nature of the original emptiness of all sentient beings is...
Anger is fundamentally emptiness; the signlessness of all sentient beings is the signlessness of anger;
the wishlessness of all sentient beings is the wishlessness of anger; the detachment of all sentient beings is the detachment of anger;
the tranquility of all sentient beings is the tranquility of anger; all sentient beings...
The unattainable nature of sentient beings is the very unattainable nature of anger; the non-existent nature of all sentient beings is the very non-existent nature of anger;
the inconceivable nature of all sentient beings is the very inconceivable nature of anger;
the non-proliferative nature of all sentient beings is the very non-proliferative nature of anger; all sentient beings...
The nature of passion is the nature of the vajra; the nature of anger is the nature of the vajra.
The commentary states:
From here below is the second section, which formally presents what is to be explained.
The text contains two parts:
first, the exposition of the seventeen real marks (*lakṣaṇa*) which are themselves the real mark of anger; second, the explanation of the reasons for this.
This is the first part.
The text is divided into five parts.
First, by means of the three kinds of reality—non-duality, elimination of afflictions, and immutability—one should apply these to anger itself.
At the time of another's anger, one should form this thought:
Since phenomena (*dharma*) are equal, how can there be anger?
Since phenomena are free from defilement, how could anger discipline me?
Since phenomena are unchanging, the nature of anger is likewise so; why then must one engage in discrimination, seeing another as an object and giving rise to resentment?
Having performed this contemplation, all afflictions are thereby completely extinguished.
The subsequent sections should be understood accordingly.
Second, by means of the reality of permanence and the nature of extinction, one destroys the four kinds of real characteristics of the true object, which are identical to anger.
Third, by means of non-existence and detachment from characteristics, one does not seek the three kinds of real marks; this is identical to anger.
Fourth, by means of severing defiled phenomena and detachment from birth, there are two kinds; this is identical to anger.
The fifth consists of five aspects— non-attainment, non-artificiality, profundity, subtlety, and ineffable solidity—
which are applied one by one to anger respectively, in their proper order.
The dharma-gate herein has already been analyzed as before, and thus is not further explained.
Among the afflictions, hatred and anger are the most serious; these are singled out here, though in reality they apply to all other defilements as well.
Because anger is itself reality, one knows that fundamental defilement is exhausted.
When sentient beings give rise to anger, the original nature of sentient beings is identical to the original nature of anger.
The original nature of both persons and phenomena is none other than the true mark (*dharmatā*), for there is no duality between them.
Having realized this, one no longer perceives anger and the like; therefore, the fault of giving rise to afflictions should not occur.
The Sūtra says:
"For what reason?"

The true nature of the complete subduing of all sentient beings is itself unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; it is also the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and it is the omniscient knowledge (sarvajñājñāna) of all Buddhas.
The commentary states:
From this point downward is the second section, which explains the underlying cause.

Because sentient beings possess the fundamental nature of being to be tamed, the true mark (*dharmatā*) is itself the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

This explains that the true nature of reality is the original nature of bodhi; it is also the *prajñā* of contemplative observation, because the essence of the dharma-nature and the dharma-characteristics are not distinct, just as the sharpness of a blade is not separate from its substance.
From this, it is known that the fundamental nature of anger is also the omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*) of all Buddhas.
This has many interpretations; true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) and conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) each receive one of these names.
The second interpretation states:
"The Omniscient One is the Buddha.
It further says:
The wisdom of the wise is the wisdom accomplished by the Buddha.
This intrinsic nature of prajñā is itself the wisdom of the Buddha; because anger is itself suchness, it is also the wisdom of the Buddha.
Therefore, the nature of afflictions is identical to the factors of enlightenment, for there is no difference between them.
Furthermore, because one realizes that these are afflictions, they never arise again;
for the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally identical, as its function is not different.
Moreover, the nature of subduing is itself the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), and bodhi is likewise the true mark.
Prajñā is also the fundamental nature of the wisdom of all Buddhas; this fundamental nature is called "wisdom" because it is the source of wisdom.
Although these four names are distinct, they are identical in essence, and thus their characteristics are mutually inclusive.
Both wisdom (*jñāna*) and the locus of wisdom are termed *prajñā*, as their essential meaning is identical.
The Sūtra says:
After the Buddha had thus taught this Dharma-treasury of the wisdom of the profound principle of skillful subjugation, he addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

If there are those who hear this Dharma-gate of the Treasury of Wisdom on the Principle of Discipline through Prajñā, and who believe, understand, uphold, recite, and practice it, they will be able to discipline their own faults such as anger and resentment, and they will also be able to discipline all sentient beings.
The commentary states:
From this point downward is the third section, praising the superior virtues of the sutra.
The phrase "these defilements, such as the loss of patience and anger," refers generally to all types of afflictions.
The Sūtra says:
"One will always be born in the auspicious realms and experience various sublime pleasures; in this present life, all enemies will give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
The Praise says:
This is the second worldly superior fruit.
Anger is exclusively unwholesome; its arising inevitably brings about suffering.
Now, by being free from anger and the like, one is born in a happy realm and experiences the fruit of superior happiness, precisely because of the absence of anger.
Because he does not afflict others, he manifests a heart of loving-kindness toward his enemies.
The Sūtra says:
"One who is able to skillfully practice all the bodhisattva deeds will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The eulogy says:
This is precisely the supreme, virtuous fruit that transcends the world.
As the Sūtra says:

At that time, the World-Honored One, further relying upon the Tathāgata’s characteristic of the nature of all phenomena being perfectly established in equality, proclaimed for the sake of the bodhisattvas the most excellent Dharma-gate of the profound principle of the nature of all phenomena within the Prajñāpāramitā.
The commentary states:
Within the section on "Luminous Practice" there are six parts in total. From here down to the final two sections, the characteristics of practicing universally by relying on two dharmas are revealed.
This present section concerns the supreme dharma-gate of the equality of nature, because the true reality of meditative cultivation—the equality of persons and phenomena—is all-pervasive.

The latter section concerns the Dharma-gate of the Supreme Treasury Sustained by Sentient Beings; this is because when one practices contemplation and observes that all persons and phenomena are universally virtuous conditions.
Within this [section], there are three parts; this is the first, which provides a general title for the Dharma-gate being taught.

Regarding "being able to skillfully establish the dharma of the equality of nature": the dharma of the equality of nature refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*). Because it pervades both persons and phenomena, it is called the equality of nature.

This true nature cannot be established through verbal expression or conceptual discrimination; yet, because it is now provisionally designated as the "dharma of the equality of nature," it is termed "establishment."
Because it is the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is called "supreme.
Because it causes one to enter [into that nature], it is called a "gate.
As the Sūtra says:
Because the nature of all sentient beings is equal, the profound perfection of wisdom is also equal in nature.
Because the nature of all phenomena is equal, the profound perfection of wisdom is also equal in nature.
Because the nature of all sentient beings is disciplined, the profound perfection of wisdom is also disciplined by nature.
Because the nature of all phenomena is disciplined, the profound perfection of wisdom is also disciplined by nature.
Because all sentient beings possess a real meaning, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* also possesses a real meaning.
Because all phenomena possess a real meaning, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* also possesses a real meaning.
The praise says:
Below this is the second section, which formally presents what is to be explained.
This contains six parts:
First, the three—person, phenomena, and the truth of detachment from defilement—are all identical to the preceding gate in that they are *prajñā*.
The third is called "unchanging."
That which is called "Ultimate Truth" was previously termed "True Dharma," as it refers to the ultimate meaning (*bhūtārtha*).
Within the mundane and supramundane realms, there are no categories that exceed two kinds:
first, sentient beings; second, phenomena. To awaken to these two kinds is precisely the wisdom of the contemplative observation of Prajñāpāramitā.
These two kinds of intrinsic nature constitute the *prajñāpāramitā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*); therefore, they are mutually identical.
As the Sūtra says:
"Because all sentient beings are *tathatā*, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also *tathatā*."
Because all phenomena are suchness, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also suchness.
Because all sentient beings are the *dharmadhātu*, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also the *dharmadhātu*.
Because all phenomena are the dharma-realm, the profound perfection of wisdom is also the dharma-realm.
Because all sentient beings are the dharma-nature, the profound perfection of wisdom is also the dharma-nature.
Because all phenomena are the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also the very nature of phenomena.
Because all sentient beings are the very limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also the very limit of reality.
Because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also the limit of reality.
The commentary states:
"The second [section] establishes that the person, phenomena, reality, permanence, the nature of the dharmas, and the true essence of the dharma-realm—these four—are identical with *prajñā*."
The Sūtra says:
Because all sentient beings are fundamentally empty, the profound Prajñāpāramitā is also fundamentally empty.
Because all phenomena are fundamentally empty, the profound Prajñāpāramitā is also fundamentally empty.
Because all sentient beings are without marks, the profound perfection of wisdom is also without marks.
Because all phenomena are without marks, the profound perfection of wisdom is also without marks.
Because all sentient beings are wishless, the profound perfection of wisdom is also wishless.
Because all phenomena are wishless, the profound perfection of wisdom is also wishless.
The praise says:
The third [section] is because persons and dharmas do not exist; it is free from characteristics and does not seek the three kinds [of objects], as they are themselves *prajñā*.
The Sūtra says:
Because all sentient beings are themselves detached, the profound perfection of wisdom is also detached.
Because all phenomena are themselves detached, the profound perfection of wisdom is also detached.
Because all sentient beings are quiescent, the profound perfection of wisdom is also quiescent.
Because all phenomena are quiescent, the profound perfection of wisdom is also quiescent.
The praise says:
The fourth [perfection] consists of the two types—detachment from persons and dharmas, and detachment from birth—which are themselves *prajñā*.
The Sūtra says:
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, the profound perfection of wisdom is also unapprehendable.
Because all phenomena are unapprehendable, the profound perfection of wisdom is also unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are non-existent, the profound perfection of wisdom is also non-existent.
Because all phenomena are non-existent, the profound perfection of wisdom is also non-existent.
Because all sentient beings are inconceivable, the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable.
Because all phenomena are inconceivable, the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable.
Because all sentient beings are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also free from conceptual proliferation.
Because all phenomena (*dharma*) are free from conceptual proliferation, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also free from conceptual proliferation.
The praise says:
The fifth [section] consists of four aspects—non-attainment of person and phenomena, non-substantiality, profound subtlety, and transcendence of words—which are themselves *prajñā*.
The Sūtra says:
Because all sentient beings are limitless, the profound perfection of wisdom is also limitless.
Because all phenomena are limitless, the profound perfection of wisdom is also limitless.
Because all sentient beings possess functional activity, one should know that the perfection of wisdom also possesses functional activity.
Because all phenomena possess functional activity, one should know that the perfection of wisdom also possesses functional activity.
The praise says:
The sixth [section] concerns the two aspects—the person and the dharma—and their vast function, both of which reside within *prajñā*.
Because the object is vast, wisdom is likewise so.
Because the objective realm possesses the functional activity of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), and because Prajñā likewise possesses the function of observing the realm and eliminating it,
the Sūtra says:
After the Buddha had taught this most excellent Dharma— the profound principle of the equality of nature— he addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

If there are those who hear such a supreme dharma-gate of the principle of equality-prajñā, and who believe, understand, accept, uphold, recite, and practice it, they will be able to penetrate the profound prajñāpāramitā of the nature of equality.
The praise states:
This third section extols his virtues.
Regarding "the equality of nature": the true nature of reality (*tathatā*) is the essence of equality among all persons and phenomena; therefore, it is called "the equality of nature."

Thus, one is able to penetrate the equal nature of phenomena (dharmatā); by virtue of the majestic power of this equality of the nature of phenomena through hearing, faith, and so forth, one is therefore able to penetrate the equal nature of phenomena.
The equality of the dharma-nature is precisely the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. The meaning of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* comprises two aspects:
first, the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), and second, contemplative illumination (*vipaśyanā*).
Now, one attains the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) because one contemplates that the fundamental nature pervades both persons and phenomena.
That which was previously referred to as "profound prajñā" is precisely this contemplative observation.
Otherwise, how could the prajñā of the true mark also possess functional activity?
The Sūtra says:
"With a mind free from hindrance toward all sentient beings, one swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Praise says:

Since one is already able to penetrate the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) upon which [all things] rely, one is likewise unimpeded regarding the principles of the persons and phenomena that depend upon it.
"Hanging" (*guà*) means obstruction; "impeding" (*ài*) means being constrained.
To penetrate persons and phenomena without obstruction means that because one has penetrated that which is relied upon, one also penetrates that which depends upon it.
The Sūtra says:

At that time, the World-Honored One again, relying upon the marks of the Tathāgata Sarvadhāraṇīgarbhadharmatā, proclaimed for the sake of all bodhisattvas the profound principle of the supreme treasury of the Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is the pervasive sustenance of all sentient beings.
The praise says:

This second section is the Dharma-gate of the Supreme Treasury that Sustains Sentient Beings, for through the cultivation of contemplation and the illumination of observation, all persons and phenomena are universally perceived as having wholesome conditions.
Within this text there are three parts; this is the first, which indicates the name of the Dharma-gate being taught.
Within this, there are further two parts:
first, the explanation of the basis (*āśraya*), and second, the explanation of its name.

Regarding "that which abides and maintains the treasury of the Dharma" (*dharmagarbha-vihārin*): "abiding" (*vihāra*) means to dwell or remain; it refers to the Tathāgatagarbha upon which all sentient beings have depended from beginningless time, or that which has resided prior within all sentient beings.

"Upholding" (dhāraṇa) means to sustain; it refers to the tathāgatagarbha and so forth, which sustain sentient beings as their very foundation, and are likewise capable of sustaining all the seeds of the Buddha-dharma.

Regarding the "Dharma-treasury" (*dharmagarbha*): it refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is called a "treasury" because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and contains within itself the boundless qualities of a Buddha.

It is said that all sentient beings abide in and are pervaded by it; that is, the *tathāgatagarbha* universally pervades and dwells within the bodies and minds of sentient beings, capable of sustaining all the meritorious qualities of the Buddha-dharma. This is precisely the treasury of all supreme jewels.
The exposition of this teaching is termed a "Dharma-gate" (*dharmaparyāya*).
Since the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha* is the fundamental name, other names such as *vajragarbha* and so forth are not mentioned here.
The Sūtra says:
This means that all sentient beings are the Tathāgatagarbha, because the essential body of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is omnipresent.
The praise states:
"From this point downward is the second section, which correctly sets forth what is to be explained."
Among these, there are four [points], and this is the first.

Regarding the statement that "all sentient beings are the tathāgatagarbha": the term *tathāgatagarbha* refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*) while it is still within the state of bondage; when it emerges from bondage, it is called the *dharmakāya*.
"Treasury" (garbha) refers to a storehouse; because all the merits possessed by the Buddhas are contained therein, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Since the currently active merits have not yet arisen, it is not termed the *dharmakāya*.
Furthermore, this true nature, which is the perfectly real Tathāgata, is called the *tathāgatagarbha* when it is concealed within the *saṃkleśas*.
Since all sentient beings possess this ultimate truth, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "That which is birth-and-death is the *tathāgatagarbha*."

Regarding "Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s own essence is pervasive": "Bhadra" means virtuous and excellent. Because his entire being—encompassing all three karmas—is entirely virtuous and excellent, he is named Samantabhadra.

The Bodhisattva has realized this universally virtuous principle, and furthermore, his own essence is universally and entirely virtuous; thus, all phenomena of the three karmas and so forth are entirely virtuous.
Because the truth realized by this Bodhisattva can realize that the intrinsic nature of all conditioned phenomena and so forth are entirely compliant, disciplined, and virtuous;
and because this essential nature pervades the three types of action, enabling all three actions to be universally virtuous, he is therefore named Samantabhadra (Universally Good).

However, the original nature of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra is itself the Tathāgatagarbha; therefore, it is said that the essence of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra pervades the essence of all sentient beings, and thus all sentient beings are the Tathāgatagarbha.
By discarding function to manifest the essence, it is named the "Pervasive Samantabhadra.
As the Sūtra says:
"All sentient beings are the Vajragarbha, because they have been sprinkled by the Vajragarbha."
The praise says:
This is the second [point]: all sentient beings are the Vajragarbha.
Just as the Tathāgatagarbha is solid and indestructible, yet possesses the virtue of being able to shatter birth and death, it is named Vajragarbha.
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha is able to realize this principle of Vajragarbha and has also attained the wisdom of Vajragarbha; thus he is named Vajragarbha.

However, the fundamental nature of all sentient beings is itself Vajragarbha. By sprinkling their bodies and minds with the teachings of the Prajñā-Vajragarbha, they all attain solidity and shatter the firm laws of birth and death; therefore, one knows that all sentient beings are Vajragarbha.

"Consecration" (abhiṣeka) has the meaning of entering into body and mind; "sprinkling" (prokṣaṇa) means destroying the karma of birth and death, because when one is consecrated and sprinkled by the successive teachings of the Vajragarbha, birth and death are destroyed.
The Sūtra says:
"All sentient beings are the treasury of the True Dharma, for all follow the turning of the True Word.
The Praise says:
This is the third [point]: all sentient beings are the treasury of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).

The True Dharma is the authentic teaching of Prajñā, and "treasury" (*kośa*) refers to a storehouse; thus, all sentient beings are the storehouse of the True Dharma, because all sentient beings are capable of turning in accordance with the True Word (*samyag-vāk*).
"Right speech" refers to speech that accords with principle, which is precisely the *sūtra*.
This means that all sentient beings are able to proceed in accordance with right speech. "Proceeding" (*vartana*) means to move forward;
it signifies being able to act in reliance upon the noble teachings of right speech and thereby attaining the solid and substantial Dharma.
The nature and characteristics of sentient beings are both termed "sentient beings.
Because correct speech is initiated from all sentient beings, all sentient beings are called the "Treasury of the True Dharma" (*saddharmagañja*).
As the Sūtra says:
All sentient beings are treasuries of sublime karma, for they are the basis upon which all activities and applications depend.
The praise says:
This is the fourth [point], that all sentient beings are treasuries of sublime karma.
"Sublime activity" (*sukṛta*) refers to all the virtuous threefold actions of a bodhisattva; the meaning of "treasury" (*kośa*) is the same as before.
All sentient beings are the treasury of a bodhisattva’s sublime activity.

When a bodhisattva wishes to initiate various virtuous activities, they are all for the sake of sentient beings; whether it be to realize the fundamental nature of those sentient beings, or to initiate application (*prayoga*) in order to uproot their suffering and affliction within birth and death (*saṃsāra*), sentient beings are thus the basis upon which such application relies.
The basis is the treasury (*garbha*), for it gives rise to sublime karma from all sentient beings.
Of the four types mentioned above, the first is the essence of the Dharma, as it speaks of the fundamental treasury;
the second is the function of the Dharma, as it destroys birth and death.
The third is the basis of the teaching, for it is the foundation of non-erroneousness;
the fourth is the basis of qualities, for it is the foundation of all virtues.
If one cannot understand this, it will be contrary to these points.
The Sūtra says:

After the Buddha had taught this Dharma-door of the Supreme Treasury of the Profound Principle of Pervasive Prajñā for the sustenance of such sentient beings, he addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

"If there are those who hear this Dharma-door of the Supreme Treasury of the Pervasive Prajñā Principle, and who believe, understand, accept, uphold, recite, and practice it, they will be able to penetrate the nature of the supreme treasury of dharmas and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The commentary states:
From here below is the third section, praising the excellence of the sūtra.
The "excellent treasuries" (vicitra-kośa) refer to the four kinds of excellent treasuries, such as the *tathāgatagarbha*, because they are the fundamental nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Because of hearing [the teaching] now and so forth, one subsequently attains thorough penetration.
The Sūtra says:

At that time, the World-Honored One, further relying upon the Tathāgata’s mark of the ultimate, boundless dharma, proclaimed for the sake of all bodhisattvas the Dharma-gate of the Vajra of the Equality of the Ultimate Sustenance of the Meaning of Prajñāpāramitā.
The commentary states:
From here below is the third section, in two parts, which clarifies attaining the fruit through practice.
Within this, there are two divisions:

The initial "Dharma Gate of Boundless and Limitless Ultimate Reality" constitutes the merit of self-benefit, for at the time of attaining the two fruits, it is profoundly deep, of a single flavor, and supremely excellent.

The subsequent "Unsurpassed Dharma Gate of Profound Principles" constitutes the merit of benefiting others: having attained the two fruits, one becomes the sovereign of the three realms, fulfilling the aspirations of all sentient beings according to their wishes.
This constitutes the first section.
Within this first section, there are three parts;
this is the first, which provides a general title for the dharma-gate being taught.
Within this, there are further two parts:
first, the explanation of the basis; second, the discernment of its name.
"Ultimate" (niṣṭhā) means the most excellent meaning, the primary meaning, the unsurpassed meaning, and the sense of reaching the final limit.
"Boundless" (*ananta*) means broad; "limitless" (*aparyanta*) means deep.
This intends to describe the Buddha-body as the most supreme dharma of breadth and depth.

Regarding "ultimately abiding in and upholding the equality of the dharma and its meaning": "ultimate" is explained as before; "abiding" (*sthiti*) means relying upon; "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*) means maintaining; "dharma" refers to the teaching of the expressive words and letters; and "meaning" (*artha*) refers to the principle and intent expressed by those words.
"Equality" (samatā) means the sense of similarity and the sense of non-difference.
"Vajra" means the sense of solidity and the sense of being able to shatter.

This refers to the most excellent basis for abiding in and upholding the teaching and principles; it is the dharma-gate that does not differ from and yet destroys the phenomena of saṃsāra, because both the phenomena and their meanings are capable of being equal to the boundless limit.
Furthermore, it is the ultimate sustenance, for it sustains all the teachings of the Buddhas.
The meaning of the Dharma is characterized by equality, accord, and non-duality.
The Vajra Dharma is the gateway to the teaching that can shatter the solid reality of birth and death.
The Sūtra says:
"Because the profound Prajñāpāramitā is boundless, all Tathāgatas are also boundless.
The Praise says:
The following is the second section, which formally presents what is being explained.

Within the previously mentioned supreme dharma-gate of the equality of natures, it was stated that because all sentient beings are boundless and so forth, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise boundless.
Since Prajñā-pāramitā penetrates the five aspects of the true mark, contemplation, and letters, the Tathāgatas of the three bodies are likewise infinite accordingly.
The principle of the true mark is the boundless Dharmakāya; the wisdom of contemplation is the boundless Saṃbhogakāya.
Relying on these two kinds of transformation bodies to respond to sentient beings, they manifest according to conditions with infinite karmic functions.
"Infinite" means that their vast measure is difficult to fathom.
Each of the sense organs and the marks and signs of excellence is individually infinite, as they are produced by the guidance of limitless roots of goodness.
The Sūtra says:
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is boundless, all Tathāgatas are also boundless.
The Praise says:

"Boundless" (ananta) refers to the fact that it is profound and subtle, difficult to know; furthermore, because it is attained through cultivation over three *kalpas*, the profound *prajñā* is called "boundless," and its accomplishment as the three bodies (*trikāya*) is likewise called "boundless."
Because this is not something that can be known by those of the two vehicles, ordinary beings, or even Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.
The Sūtra says:
"Because the profound Prajñāpāramitā is of a single flavor, all dharmas are also of a single flavor."
The praise says:
Because these five factors—the observing subject, the observing illumination, the observed principle, the skillful means, and so forth—are all of one single flavor, they are called "equality.
"One flavor" has the meaning of "one characteristic," which refers to the meaning of the non-dual union of signlessness and the meaning of non-conceptuality.
Furthermore, "of one flavor" means that because it is solid and substantial, it is free from the characteristics of suffering and pleasure, and thus devoid of both joy and grief.
All phenomena—whether their teachings or their meanings—are likewise of one flavor, for they do not conflict with the two kinds of *prajñā*.

The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "For example, as long as the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven have not entered the Grove of Mixed Delights (*miśravana*), they are ultimately unable to enjoy objects or sensations in a manner that is free from the notions of 'I' and 'mine';
once they enter the Grove of Mixed Delights, they enjoy them at will without conceptual discrimination."

Because the Grove of Miscellaneous Delights possesses such virtues, it enables all the devas who enter this grove to experience and enjoy the various fruits of their karmic retribution—whether as objects or as sensations—in perfect harmony, without the need for any deliberate thought.

Thus, if a bodhisattva has not yet realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they can never attain an impartial mind or impartial equanimity; consequently, they remain no different from all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas because they still possess the notion of duality. Therefore, they are unable to abide in the wisdom of the single flavor of integrated experience.

If one has already realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one attains a mind of equality by dispelling the two notions; thus, one becomes distinct from the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. By means of this mind of equality, one is able to abide in equanimity and experience the unified wisdom of phenomena as a single flavor.
That treatise states: "In the Heaven of the Thirty-three there is a Grove of Miscellaneous Delights (*miśravana*), produced by the combined power of the merit of all the devas.

It causes the various classes of devas who are not in this grove to differ in their palaces and other matters, as well as in their experiences of pleasure and pain; they experience these with distinctions of 'I' and 'mine'."

Whether in this grove, whether in terms of activities or experiences, there is no distinction of superior or inferior; all are equally sublime, being enjoyed through the harmonious integration of non-self and the absence of "mine.
Because it enables such equal and harmonious enjoyment, it is called the Grove of Mixture (Miśrakāvana).

This is due to the predominant power of the various devas each cultivating meritorious karma that is equal and harmonious, which causes their fundamental consciousnesses to manifest as phenomena of the same location, the same time, and the same characteristics.

By the predominant power of that Forest of Intermingled Trees (*miśrakāvana*), those evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) likewise manifest in the same way; although each experiences [the environment] individually, they perceive it as being without distinction.
In this manner, the distinctions and non-distinctions between Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and those who have attained the stages are also like this.
"Because it is produced by being led by both the dual characteristics and the characteristicless, and because it has not yet attained non-arising and has attained distinctions.

That same sutra says: "Furthermore, just as various large and small streams, before entering the great ocean, each have their own distinct basis; their waters differ, they are meager, and the water increases or decreases. According to the functions of those waters, what they produce differs, and they sustain the lives of aquatic creatures only to a limited extent."

If one enters the great ocean, there is no other basis; the water is without distinction, the water is without limit, and the water neither increases nor decreases. Its function is singular: it is a vast support for the lives of aquatic creatures.

In this way, as long as bodhisattvas have not yet entered the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, they possess distinct bases, diverse cognitions, and limited cognitions that undergo increase and decrease; according to their respective cognitive activities, their functions differ, and they serve as the basis for maturing the roots of goodness of only a small portion of sentient beings.

If one has already entered the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, there is no separate basis; wisdom is immeasurable and wisdom neither increases nor decreases. One partakes in the unified, single-flavored wisdom of activities, which serves as the support for the maturation of the roots of goodness of immeasurable sentient beings.
That treatise states: "Water has various locations as its basis, because it relies upon diverse places.
The Bodhisattva’s basis consists of individual Tathāgatas, because he relies upon distinct Tathāgatas."
Diverse waters differ in being clear, turbid, or ashy, due to the distinctions among fine waters.
Bodhisattvas who possess diverse wisdoms differ because they have achieved their cultivation through various distinct resolute understandings (*adhimukti*).
The remaining metaphors for the dharmas may be understood according to their respective meanings.
Since the Bodhisattva has thus practiced, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, the three bodies and ten thousand virtues each possess but a single flavor.
As the Sūtra says:
"Because the profound Prajñāpāramitā is ultimate, all dharmas are also ultimate."
The praise says:

This contemplative observation, its object, the syllables, and so forth—these five most excellent things are called the ultimate first; the phenomena and their meanings follow after Prajñā in the same way.

The intent here is to reveal that through the cause of profound *prajñā*—namely, its textual expressions, its retinue, its objective sphere, and its boundless, limitless, single-flavored culmination—the practice undertaken attains the fruit of the three bodies (*trikāya*). The meaning of the Dharma taught accords with these bodies in the same way; thus, all phenomena possess the fundamental nature of profound *prajñā*.
Since the fundamental nature is ultimately of a single flavor, so too are all phenomena.
The Sūtra says:
After the Buddha had taught this adamantine Dharma of the ultimate principle that is boundless and limitless, he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and the others, saying:

If there are those who hear this ultimate *prajñāpāramitā* principle of the Vajra Dharma-gate, and who believe, understand, uphold, recite, and cultivate it, all obstructive dharmas will be entirely eliminated; they will certainly attain the nature of the Tathāgata-Vajradhara and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The praise states:
This is the third eulogy of the sutra’s supreme virtues.

Having heard that the dharmas and meanings pertaining to Prajñāpāramitā and the Buddha’s three bodies are boundless and so forth, all obstructive phenomena are completely eliminated, and one will certainly attain the nature of the Tathāgata-Vajradhara.

That is to say, by realizing this true nature of reality—the *tathatā* and *dharmadhātu*—which is capable of destroying birth and death, one swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This [realization] possesses two kinds of supreme virtues: the elimination of evil and the gathering of good.
The Sūtra says:

At that time, the World-Honored One again, relying upon the aspect of the Tathāgata Samantaprabha, proclaimed for the sake of all bodhisattvas the Vajradharma-gate of the Great Bliss Vajra-Āmoghā Mantra of the Secret Dharmatā of All Tathāgatas and the Non-conceptual Nature of All Dharmas within the Prajñāpāramitā—the supreme, foremost, and most profound principle of the initial, middle, and final stages, the unsurpassed Dharma-gate.
The praise states:

Having attained the two fruits through this second stage, the unsurpassed dharma-gate of the profound principle, one becomes the sovereign of the three realms for the benefit of self and others; fulfilling the aspirations of all sentient beings according to their wishes constitutes the fruit-virtue of benefiting others.

The "Omnipresent Illuminator" (Samantaprabhāsa-jñānin) refers to all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā); it is like awakening from sleep or the blooming of a lotus.
Having attained penetration into all phenomena and being able to fully accomplish both self-benefit and the benefit of others, it is called "Omnipresent Illumination."
"Attaining the secret nature of the dharmas of all Tathāgatas" means to obtain and realize them; that is, this Dharma-gate is able to attain the secret and so forth.
It is called "secret" (*guhya*) because it is precious and worthy of veneration; it is called "mysterious" (*guhya*) because it is profound, hidden, and difficult to know.
This refers to all conditioned phenomena that are supreme and subtle, namely, bodhi;
as well as the non-conceptual nature of all phenomena, which is the true dharmadhātu, because it is free from all names, expressions, and conceptual discrimination.
Great bliss is the attainment of untainted bliss (*anāsrava-sukha*).
There are five kinds of bliss: first, the bliss of the cause;
second, the bliss of sensation; third, the bliss of the remedy for suffering; fourth, the bliss of the cessation of sensation; and fifth, the bliss free from affliction and harm.
Within this, there are four types:
first, the bliss of renunciation; second, the bliss of seclusion; third, the bliss of awakening; and fourth, the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Now, having attained these five as well as the latter four, it is called "great bliss," because they pervade the entire dharmadhātu and are all of the nature of bliss.
"Vajra" means that which can shatter; because it is able to shatter all obstructing phenomena, it is so called.
"Amogha" (Not Empty) means that this wondrous Dharma is not empty and without fruit; because it necessarily possesses efficacious power and extraordinary, superior fruits, it is named "Amogha."

Regarding "divine mantra" (*shenzhou*): "divine" (*shen*) refers to the mastery over the principles and phenomena of noble virtue; "mantra" (*zhou*) refers to *dhāraṇī*. This means that the noble virtue shared by the Buddhas of the ten directions is designated as "divine."
In brief, it possesses all the merits of every Buddha-dharma and destroys all enemies of birth and death.
Because it comprehensively contains all virtues, it is called "dhāraṇī" (total retention); this is what is meant by "mantra."
The vajra-dharmatā is the wisdom (*prajñā*) of all Buddhas that consolidates all phenomena; as this is the foremost, it is called dharmatā.
This is the dharma-gate explained above.
That which is attained through practice and below constitutes, in its entirety, the dharma-gate of attainment.

Regarding the stages of beginning, middle, and end: this refers to the three positions of initial teaching, intermediate teaching, and final teaching within this sutra; or alternatively, the three positions of generating the resolve, practicing, and realizing; or the three positions of hearing, practicing, and becoming free from desire.

This is the most supreme, non-dual, foremost, and unsurpassed practice of the Dharma; because this dharma-gate is the most preeminent, one is able to realize the secret nature of the Tathāgata’s dharmatā.
The Sūtra says:
"It is called the supreme accomplishment of great desire and so forth, which brings about the supreme accomplishment of great bliss for the great Bodhisattvas.
The Praise says:
From here below is the second section, which formally presents what is being explained.
This section contains two parts:

first, three successive cycles explain the fruits and benefits obtained from the causes of a bodhisattva’s practice of the ten paths of unwholesome action; second, three successive cycles explain the dhāraṇīs.
The beginning and middle [sections] each contain three repetitions.
Within the first repetition, there are two parts:

first, it clarifies the benefits obtained as fruits resulting from unwholesome courses of action with greed and so forth as the causes; second, it clarifies the benefits obtained as fruits resulting from wholesome courses of action with *prajñā* (wisdom) as the cause.
In the section explaining that desire and so forth serve as causes, the first part clarifies the fruit of self-benefit and the latter part clarifies the fruit of benefiting others.
Within the clarification of the fruit of self-benefit, it is shown that by taking desire and so forth as causes, one successively attains four kinds of fruits:

first, great bliss is attained with desire and so forth as the cause; second, great awakening is attained with great bliss as the cause; third, the ability to subdue the four māras is attained with great awakening as the cause; and fourth, mastery is attained with the subduing of the four māras as the cause.
What is meant by the "supreme accomplishment of great craving" and so forth?
It refers to the Bodhisattva, within the causal stage, reversing the ten paths of unwholesome action of saṃsāra and personally practicing the ten paths of supramundane non-virtuous action:
first, the ability to take life, which means severing the flow of sentient beings' transmigration in saṃsāra; this is the meaning of "killing."

Second, taking what is not given: there is no one who gives, yet one naturally takes it up; this signifies the meaning of seeking nothing from others and benefiting oneself through self-appropriation.
Third, sexual misconduct: clearly understanding that desire is deviant, one cultivates right conduct.
If one discriminates desire and knows it to be truly only false, as a verse says: "The Buddha taught that greed, anger, and delusion all arise from discrimination;
the inversions of purity and impurity likewise arise conditioned by these."
"Those things that arise conditioned by the inversions of purity and impurity lack intrinsic nature; therefore, they are revealed as not being real.
Regarding the fourth false speech: if, within falsehood, one is able to speak of it as false.
As it is said in a verse: "The Blessed One has spoken of all false phenomena as they truly are;
among false phenomena, conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are the most false.
Regarding the five types of divisive speech (*paiśunya*), what is *bheṣaṇī*?

This means "always dwelling in the most excellent. The term *śūnyapauṣṇī* (空貝戍尼) explicitly refers to divisive speech (*paiśunya*), while its hidden meaning signifies "ever-victorious emptiness" (*nitya-jaya-śūnya*).
*Pau* represents the meaning of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), *ṣṇī* represents the meaning of emptiness (*śūnya*), and *nī* represents the meaning of permanence (*nitya*);
here, the hidden meaning is taken.
Regarding the sixth [unwholesome path of action], harsh speech (*pāruṣya*): what is meant by *pāruṣya*?
It refers to being well-established in the "other shore" (*pāra*) of that which is to be known.
This term *pāruṣya* explicitly denotes harsh speech, while implicitly it signifies abiding on the other shore.
The "other shore" (*pāra*) is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); because the Buddha is able to dwell securely within it, he is called the *Parasariya*.
Regarding the seven types of frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*), if one correctly explains the distinctions among their categories, [it is not frivolous].
Regarding the eight types of desire, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "If there is a repeated desire to personally realize unsurpassed meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
This intention refers only to that which is induced from a state of distraction; it speaks merely of craving for concentration.
This refers to the arousal of great desire for unsurpassed bodhi;
desiring to deliver sentient beings from birth and death is called "desire.
Ninth is "anger": if one can, within the mind, rightly loathe and harm all afflictions so that they are severed and extinguished, this is the meaning of "loathing and harming."

Regarding the ten types of wrong views, if one perceives the pervasively operating nature of wrongness in all instances as it truly is, one then sees that all deluded conceptualizations have the nature of erroneous confusion.

Although Bodhisattvas may secretly engage in the ten paths of unwholesome action, here the mental karma of great greed is cited as the foremost; in reality, however, all three types of karma serve as the causes.

Because Bodhisattvas accomplish these ten causes through their most supreme conduct, they experience the first five kinds of happiness, which surpass all the happiness found in the stage of ordinary beings; therefore, they are called "supreme."

Furthermore, "Great Bliss" refers to the fruit of the five cultivations; it is the attainment of the joy of the Dharma-garden by being free from various conceptual signs, as has already been explained.
The Sūtra says:
"The supreme accomplishment of Great Bliss causes the Great Bodhisattvas to achieve the supreme accomplishment of the Great Enlightenment of all Tathāgatas."
The praise says:
Because one realizes the five kinds of blissful dharma-gardens, one is able to attain great awakening regarding both principle and phenomena for oneself and others.
In the stage of a bodhisattva, one attains all the causes of Buddhahood; in the stage of a Buddha, it is called the attainment of the perfection of great awakening.
The Sūtra says:
"The supreme accomplishment of the Great Enlightenment of all Tathāgatas brings about the supreme accomplishment of subduing all great Māras for the sake of the Mahābodhisattvas.
It is praised as follows:
Because one awakens to the principles and facts regarding what is erroneous or correct for oneself and others, one is able to forever sever the four kinds of great māras.
The Sūtra says:
"The most supreme accomplishment that subdues all great māras; the most supreme accomplishment that causes the Great Bodhisattvas to universally attain mastery over the three great realms."
The praise says:
Because he has subdued the four māras and transcended the three realms to attain the fruit of the exalted state, he is universally great throughout the three realms.
Because he cannot be destroyed by the four māras of birth and death, he is called "Sovereign."
Briefly stated, there are ten kinds of mastery: mastery over life, mastery over the mind, and mastery over requisites; these three result from the perfection of the pāramitā of generosity.
Mastery over karma and mastery over birth are perfected through the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Mastery over resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) is perfected through the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Mastery over aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) is perfected through the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Mastery over supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vaśitā*) is perfected through the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
Mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*) and mastery over phenomena (*dharma-vaśitā*) are perfected through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*),
as explained in the ninth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts.

These ten masteries are described as the fruit of self-benefit from the perspective of their essential nature; since there are also specific stages at the time they are realized, the Buddha’s mastery is universally and vastly greater than that of the triple world.

Thus, there is a verse that says: "In heaven and earth, in this world, in the Hall of the Learned, in the abodes of the departed, or in the celestial realms throughout the ten directions—nowhere is there a man, a bull-king, or a Great Śramaṇa equal to him; he has searched the earth, the mountains, and the forests, and found none his peer. Therefore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, pervades the entire great triple-world.

In brief, because it comprises the pure dharma-realm and the four wisdoms—the great mirror-like wisdom, the wisdom of equality, the wisdom of wondrous observation, and the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done—along with the two kinds of adornments of merit and wisdom, it is the most supreme.
The Sūtra says:

"The supreme accomplishment of universal greatness and mastery over the three realms enables great Bodhisattvas to extract sentient beings from the realm of existence without exception, bringing benefit and peace to all sentient beings through the supreme accomplishment of ultimate great bliss."
The commentary states:
The preceding section clarifies self-benefit; the following section clarifies benefiting others.
Within this, there are two parts:
The first part clarifies the practice of benefiting others through the vast and supreme mind;
from "Why is this so? onwards, the latter part clarifies the practice of benefiting others through the constant mind and the non-erroneous mind.
"Those who are able to uproot the realm of sentient beings without exception" refers to all living beings.

Encompassed within the category of sentient beings are those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; whether they possess form or are formless, whether they have perception, lack perception, or are neither with nor without perception—all of these are to be uprooted from suffering and granted happiness.
There is not a single sentient being who is not within the sphere of compassion and wisdom; therefore, there is nothing left behind.
"Left behind" (*yi*) carries the sense of being dropped or lost;
"remainder" (*yu*) carries the sense of being a leftover or something that has not been fully exhausted.
"Extraction" (ba) means to rescue.
It refers to extracting all sentient beings so that not a single being is left behind, lost, or submerged, nor remains as a mere stump or remnant of a thicket without being pulled out.
Because this intention pervades the ten directions, the three realms, the five destinies, and the four modes of birth, it is called the "vast mind."
Regarding "the supreme accomplishment of benefit, happiness, ultimate great bliss": there are ten types of benefit, as stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:

(1) exclusive benefit, (2) shared benefit, (3) benefit consisting of welfare, (4) benefit consisting of happiness, (5) benefit subsumed under causes, (6) benefit subsumed under results, (7) benefit in this life, (8) benefit in future lives, (9) ultimate benefit, and (10) non-ultimate benefit.
There are five kinds of peace and happiness (*sukha*), as previously explained.
Furthermore, the gathering of wholesome qualities is termed "benefit" (*hita*), while the avoidance of unwholesome qualities is termed "peace and happiness.
There are ten such pairs, the explanation of which is found in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-ṭīkā*.
Ultimate great bliss is what is called nirvāṇa; as the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "I shall cause all to enter nirvāṇa without remainder.
While that [teaching] applies to all three vehicles, it speaks only of nirvāṇa and does not mention anything else.

Now, taking up the bliss of awakening and nirvāṇa means possessing all conditioned and unconditioned, untainted merits, which cause all sentient beings to be joyful, harmonious, and compliant, without any violation or harm, and without any oppression or affliction; therefore, it is called "Great Bliss."
This is the first mind; because it intends to cause sentient beings to abide in the most supreme state, it is called "the first.
The Sūtra says: "Why is this so?"
As long as there are superior wise ones remaining within the abodes of the cycle of birth and death, they shall constantly benefit sentient beings through peerless dharmas and not enter into nirvāṇa.
The Praise says:
Why is this so? To investigate its origin:
what is it that enables all sentient beings to be led, without exception, to the realm of nirvāṇa? What indeed is this?

As for "the abodes where one wanders through birth and death until the very end," this refers to the infinite duration of future time, following the cycles of birth and death of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions at every moment and season.
The locations where the worlds of the ten directions abide manifest the vastness of place and the vastness of time.
Those with superior wisdom are those capable of collectively relinquishing both "I" and "mine."

One who is called a "superior knower" because they have abandoned the clinging to persons and phenomena is one for whom both the wisdom regarding persons and the wisdom regarding phenomena are fully perfected; this is precisely what is meant by having a mind that is not inverted.
One is called a "superior knower" because they are free from these two types of clinging.

Throughout this constant ability to benefit sentient beings with peerless dharmas without entering nirvana—extending across the realms of the ten directions and throughout the limits of future birth and death—they are always able to bring benefit and joy to sentient beings through these foremost, most excellent, and peerless dharmas.

Sentient beings are infinite, for the period until they enter nirvāṇa can never be exhausted; therefore, those of supreme wisdom do not enter into quiescent extinction in accordance with the needs of sentient beings. Why is this?

Because they lack attachment to phenomena and attachment to sentient beings, and because they are devoid of the distinction between self and other, their benefit for sentient beings is constant and inexhaustible.

Just as worldly parents rescue their sons and daughters, giving rise to a mind of compassion that lacks the distinction between self and other and does not shrink from toil, they are thus able to long maintain the intention to generate compassion and provide salvation.
The Bodhisattva is likewise; therefore, it is called the "Eternal Mind.

Once the four minds within the causal stage have been perfected, they reach the state of Buddhahood and are able to benefit sentient beings without end, constantly rescuing and delivering all within the dharma-realm of the ten directions until every single one has attained liberation.
This refers to the attainment of the four fruits by means of the four types of vajra-mind.
As the Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, through the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the Prajñāpāramitā, one establishes supreme wisdom, skillfully accomplishes all pure activities, and is able to bring all states of existence (*bhava*) to complete purity."
The praise says:

In the first section, the aforementioned [passage] concerns the benefits obtained with greed and so forth as the cause; this [section] concerns the benefits obtained with *prajñā* (wisdom) as the cause.

Skillful means (upāya) refers to the manifestation of activities such as preaching the Dharma at the appropriate time, in accordance with the illnesses, behaviors, capacities, and inclinations of sentient beings through the power of wisdom; therefore, it is called skillful means.
To act in accordance with the requirements of the occasion as a preliminary practice for entering the Path is called *upāya* (skillful means).
It is like walking along a road and seeing someone chasing a rabbit; if another person asks whether you saw it, you should remain seated and answer, "I truly did not see it."
To protect against the act of killing, one immediately manifests the appearance of sitting and says, "I did not see it," rather than saying, "I did not see it while standing.
Thus, one does not commit the offense of lying, and the purpose of protecting against killing is accomplished.

The Bodhisattva is likewise: desiring to cause sentient beings to abandon the false and enter the true, he speaks of nameless dharmas by means of names; according to their gravity, the appropriate timing, and what is suitable for their capacity, he teaches them so as to lead them into the Way.
Using an elephant to represent the non-elephant, and using words to represent the wordless—because these do not directly designate the ultimate reality, they are called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Because one wondrously attains the essential principle and responds to things according to the occasion, never failing in the midst of managing affairs, it is called "skillful means" (*kauśalya*).
One establishes superior wisdom; because skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) serves as its cause, the result—superior wisdom—is attained.
This superior wisdom is precisely the perfection of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyapāramitā*), which is subsumed within the two types of wisdom.
There are two distinctions of wisdom:
first, dedication; second, deliverance. This is dedication, because it ultimately leads to omniscience.
"Skillfully discerning all pure undertakings" refers to the three types: supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Through these, the two causes of merit and wisdom, as well as the two benefits of self and others—all virtuous deeds—are skillfully discerned.

Regarding the phrase "able to cause all realms of existence to attain purity": when the causes and effects of the three realms of existence and the nine states of existence are both extinguished, and the defilements of birth and death are entirely eliminated, it is therefore called "purity."
Thus, all evils are completely eliminated.
Although the preceding [stages] with greed and so forth as their causes possess two benefits, the primary aim lies in benefiting others by giving rise to the four types of mind;
this [stage], however, takes Prajñā as its cause, being able to exhaustively cultivate all that is wholesome and exhaustively eliminate all that is unwholesome.
Since the bodhicitta is of three kinds, the fruits and benefits obtained are likewise threefold.
Although the preceding section explained that desire and so forth serve as causes, their essence is in fact prajñā, described here under different names;
all of them have prajñā as their intrinsic nature.
The above constitutes the first sequential explanation.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, by means of greed and so forth, he tames the world universally and at all times, even to the point that all states of existence are made pure and naturally subdued."
The commentary states:
From here below is the second section, which further explains the fruits and benefits obtained from greed and the other [afflictions].
Within this, there are two parts:
The first part clarifies benefiting others, and the latter part clarifies benefiting oneself.
This is the section on benefiting others.

Regarding the phrase "taming the world through greed and so forth," this means that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas observe that sentient beings are largely obscured by stinginess; although they possess precious wealth, they are unable to cultivate merit with it, nor do they use it for themselves, feeling as much deep pain and regret as if their own flesh were being cut.
The Bodhisattva, knowing that those obscured by stinginess increase their evil karma and will consequently fall into the miserable realms with no prospect of escape,
gives rise to great desire for wealth and gathers treasures so as to cause them to abandon their parsimony and refrain from committing evil deeds.

In reality, it is through the great compassion arising within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that Bodhisattvas give rise to these forms of desire and so forth; they do not do so for their own personal fame, profit, or the veneration of their retinue. Therefore, by giving rise to a single instance of desire, they increase hundreds of thousands of virtues.
Thereupon, as Sudhana sought a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), he encountered a king who was executing, binding, flogging, and whipping immeasurable sentient beings.
Sudhana felt remorse in his heart, and the king said to him:
"These sentient beings are dull-witted, stubborn, and resentful; if they were not subjected to such suffering and punishment, they would never be tamed."
"Therefore, I suffer for it.
Only then did Sudhana understand.
It is just as when King Śrīghoṣa increased his merit even further by killing five hundred brāhmaṇas; this case is exactly like that.
All karmic paths of the ten non-virtues should be understood according to this principle; therefore, when greed arises, it constitutes a great benefit for a bodhisattva.
As the Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, just as a lotus flower is pure in its color, form, and radiance, and is not defiled by any impure substances."
In this way, although greed and the like benefit the world, they cannot defile one who dwells in transcendence and possesses transcendence.
The praise says:
"This clarifies the practice of self-benefit through greed and the like."

When a bodhisattva gives rise to these afflictions such as desire within body and mind, their physical form becomes radiant and pure, remaining unstained by any defilements or afflictions; therefore, they retain these afflictions to assist their vows for rebirth and to exercise great mastery.
If one is a Buddha, it is as if through those very afflictions such as greed that one benefits sentient beings.
Even if one abides in a mind characterized by the faults of the afflictions, or abides in other tainted minds—whether wholesome or neutral—it is called "having faults."
This refers to the meaning of "outflow" (*āsrava*).
Within these three natures, [the mind] cannot be defiled at any time.
Just as a lotus flower and the like, though emerging from the mud, cannot be stained by it, so too is the mind of a Bodhisattva.
The Sūtra says:
Furthermore, great greed and the like can attain pure great bliss and great wealth, sovereignty over the three realms, and the constant ability to steadfastly benefit sentient beings.
The commentary states:
This is the third successive re-explanation.

Furthermore, regarding "great greed" and so forth: "greed for self" and so on refers to what is called "greed for attachment," which arises from the fear that by committing evil deeds with the body, one will fall into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Taking greed as one's own self, one cultivates the path to leave suffering behind.

Thus, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "It is better to give rise to a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to a view of emptiness even as small as a hair," because a false view of emptiness prevents the severance of cultivation.

If one has greed for a self, fearing that it will increase ill repute, one then increases the cultivation of the path; through causes such as [the transformation of] greed and so forth, the fruit is the attainment of great bliss.

Possessing the seven kinds of noble wealth—the precious wealth of the *dharmadhātu*—one becomes the lord of the three realms. Being undefiled by transgressions, one attains the ten masteries (*vaśitā*). At all times, in all places, and regarding all matters, one steadfastly benefits all sentient beings; this benefit to sentient beings is precisely the benefit of the Bodhisattva.

Among these three types, because they were able to cultivate [the path] by taking desire and so forth as causes—either during former causal stages or at the stage of fruition—they attain boundless fruits upon reaching that stage of fruition.
The first is actual practice; for the sake of turning back from evil, one speaks of counterfeit greed.
The second is spoken of counterfeit greed because one is impelled by great compassion.
The third is spoken of counterfeit greed for the sake of seeking one's own benefit.

However, when one correctly initiates practice, birth-and-death, afflictions, and evil karma are all extinguished; thus, all defiled greed and the like vanish entirely. How, then, can it be said that they arise?
The Sūtra says:
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke this divine mantra:
Namo bhagavate pralambabāhuye bhaṭṭārakāya.
(1) Namo bhagavate pralambabāhuye.
(2) Namo bhagavate pralambabāhuye. (3)
4. Āpārimatīrṇāya | 5. Sarvadharmatīrṇāya | 6.
Sarvadharmatīrṇanuttarāya tīrṇāya ||
Tadyathā: sapta pratyekam, mahāpratyekam.
10. *Pratyarpaṣakare* 11.
*Pratyarogakare* 12. *Ādhakāravitanmani*
Siddhi (13), Susiddhi (14),
Siddhyantu me bhagavati (15).
