Saṃmūḥ śvāsakare (19) | Bhūrbhūḥ (20) | Sītsīdha (21) ||
Kyan-pa kyan-pa (22),
Zhe-ra zhe-ra (23), Ha-ra-ba ha-ra-ba (24).
Akece akece (25), bhagavati (26), māvilambha (27).

“Svāhā. This divine mantra has been proclaimed by all the Buddhas of the three periods of time and is collectively protected and sustained by them. For those who can receive and uphold it, all obstacles shall be extinguished; whatever they desire shall be accomplished without fail, and they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Tathāgata further spoke this divine mantra:
“Namo bhagavate pralambabāhuye.”
Tadyathā: 3.
munidame, 4. saṃghalokadame.
6. Aṭṇugrahadaṃye | 7.
Vimudridaṃye | 8. Satvānugrahadaṃye |
9. Vaiśravaṇadame, 10.
Caṇḍānuparivartitana-dame, 11. Kūṭa-saṃghāṭa-dame.
*Sarvakālapratipannadaṃ me svāhā.* (12) *Svāhā.* (13) This divine mantra is the mother of all Buddhas.

Those who can recite and uphold it shall have all their sins extinguished, shall constantly behold all Buddhas, attain the knowledge of past lives, and swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Tathāgata further spoke this divine mantra:

*Namo bhagavate | Pratyamitāye | Tadyathā | Śrīye | Śrīye | Śrīye | Śrīye śive | Svāhā.* This divine mantra possesses great majestic power. Those who can receive and uphold it will have their karmic obstructions eliminated; they will maintain all the True Dharma they hear through dhāraṇī and never forget it, and they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The praise says:
From here below is the second section, consisting of three successive recitations of mantras;
this is the first mantra.
The praise of his virtues is as stated in the text.
All Buddhas speak of him with one voice, and their minds all protect and keep him in mind.

"Protecting" means bestowing empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); "keeping in mind" means remembering. The minds of all Buddhas empower him so that they never forget him; according to his heart's desires, all evils are eliminated and all wholesome aspirations are fulfilled.
Within the second incantation for extolling virtues, it is said that she gives birth to all Buddhas and is thus called their "mother," because all Buddhas are born from her as their source.

Regarding the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*): wherever one is born, one attains wondrous wisdom, knowing matters such as past abodes and eons; being able to fully comprehend the causes and effects of good and evil is precisely the knowledge of past lives.
Within the third incantation praising his virtues, it says: "Possessing great majesty, he is adorned with all virtues and is revered by all.
As for his power, he is able to subdue all."

Regarding "those who maintain the sublime Dharma they have heard without forgetting": this refers to attaining the retention of the meaning of the Dharma through mindfulness and wisdom, and thus one should never forget it.
Therefore, the explanation provided here follows the wording of that specific verse of praise; the remaining different phrasings may be understood by analogy with this meaning.
The Sūtra says:
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken this mantra, he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and the others, saying:

"If there are sentient beings who, every morning, with a sincere mind, listen to and recite this most supreme Dharma-gate of the profound principle of the Prajñāpāramitā without interruption, all their evil karmic obstructions will be extinguished, and all sublime joys and pleasures will constantly manifest before them."
The praise states:
From this point downward is the third section, extolling the excellence of the sutra.
This is divided into two parts:
The first section provides a specific praise of this particular Dharma-gate; the second provides a general praise of the merit of the entire sūtra.
Within the first section, there are three parts:

first, praising the merit of extinguishing evil and gathering good; second, praising the merit of encountering [this teaching] through the planting of causes; and third, praising the merit of the place where it resides as being worthy of veneration.

Within the initial praise, the first part is a general praise for the virtue of abandoning evil and attaining goodness, while the latter part is a specific praise for the cultivation and production of various wholesome virtues.
This constitutes the beginning.
The Sūtra says:

This Great Bliss Vajra Amogha Divine Mantra will, upon its manifestation, surely bring about the ultimate fulfillment of all Tathāgatas’ vajra secret supreme accomplishments; before long, one shall attain the state of a Great Vajradhara and the nature of a Tathāgata.
The praise says:
From here below, there is a specific eulogy of the various virtuous qualities that are induced and produced.
Within this, there are three parts:
First, the mantra of the Great Bliss Vajra that is fully perfected;
second, the accomplishment of the secret vajra dharma, which is the immediate attainment of the jewels of the teachings, practices, and principles;
third, the attainment of the nature of the Tathāgata Vajradhara, which refers to the Great Vajradhara at the stage of Buddhahood—that is, the true wisdom of a Buddha.
The nature of the Tathāgata is precisely the Jewel of the Dharma-body, which is the fruit.
These latter two fruits are not accomplished during the stage of the cause; therefore, it is said that they "shall be attained," as they are attained upon reaching Buddhahood.
The Sūtra says:

"If there are classes of sentient beings who have not planted many roots of goodness under numerous Buddhas, nor long since made great vows, they will be unable to hear, write down, recite, copy, honor, revere, contemplate, or practice this profound principle and most excellent Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā."
The praise says:
From here below is the second type of cause for encountering virtue.
In all that one cultivates, practice and vows must be pursued together.
If these two did not previously exist, one would be unable to give rise to the ten dharma-practices within this [teaching].
Among them, there are seven: first, hearing; second, copying;

third, reading; fourth, reciting; fifth, making offerings and showing respect; sixth, reflecting; and seventh, cultivating. The remaining three dharma-practices are likewise: namely, giving to others, upholding, and expounding—these three kinds.
In this regard, even the mere act of transcribing [the scriptures] depends on encountering the necessary causes, let alone such things as receiving and upholding them.
All of these clearly demonstrate that they will not be encountered in the absence of the requisite causes.
As the Sūtra says:

Only those who have planted various roots of goodness under many Buddhas and long since made great vows are able, regarding this most profound principle and supreme Dharma-gate, even to hear a single phrase or a single word; how much more so could they fully read, recite, and uphold it?
The commentary states:
From here on, the formal treatise contains the causes for its eventual encounter.
The text is intelligible, and its meaning may be understood by reference to what precedes.
It is impossible to describe all ten cases in full.
As the Sūtra says:

"If sentient beings were to make offerings, show respect, honor, and praise as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in eighty *gaṅgā* rivers—each numbering in the hundreds of millions (*koṭi*), hundreds of billions (*nayuta*)—only then would they be able to hear this profound principle of the *prajñāpāramitā* in its entirety."

The commentary states: The preceding section clarified that even a single phrase or a single word still relies upon prior causes; this section clarifies that [the practice] extends from beginning to end, and thus depends upon manifold practices.

When the four bases of service are gathered together, it is termed "offering"; when the three karmas are reverently upheld, it receives the name "veneration"; when carried upon the crown with earnest devotion, it is further called "reverence"; and because the preceding discussion is not yet exhausted, it is also termed "praise."
"Ganges" is the name of the goddess Gaṅgā; "equal" means similar. The number of Buddhas is as uniform as the sand.
Within this river there is pure sand and no stones, just as the Wei River today has no stones, only sand.
*Koṭi* means one million; *nayuta* means ten million. One grain of sand constitutes one *koṭinayuta*.
It is only by making offerings to as many Buddhas as eighty times ten million times ten million *Gaṅgā* sands that one can fully hear this profound sutra.
It is not so; otherwise, none would be able to hear the profound meaning in its entirety.
Because the deep principles of the sutra are not what can be known by those of small wisdom or inferior folly, great causes were provisionally employed.
Now, at last, we cultivate and encounter it—how joyful that today we have fortunately encountered this numinous text!
The Sūtra says:
"If this sūtra circulates in other regions, all devas, humans, asuras, and so forth should make offerings to it as they would to a stūpa of the Buddha;
those who place this sūtra upon their bodies or in their hands should be saluted and honored by all devas and humans."
The praise says:
From here below is the third section, concerning the venerability of his station and virtue.
He is honored wherever he is and esteemed among all people; this may be understood according to the text.

A *buddha-caitya*—formerly called a *zhiti*, meaning a stupa or temple—is worthy of reverence and solemnity even when it enshrines the physical remains of the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*); how much more so this Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*), which cannot fail to receive offerings?

The Sūtra says: If there are sentient beings who receive and uphold this sūtra, they will attain knowledge of past lives for many *koṭi* kalpas; they will constantly and diligently cultivate all wholesome dharmas; evil Māras and non-Buddhists will be unable to detain them; the Four Great Heavenly Kings and the other hosts of devas will constantly follow and protect them, never abandoning them for even a moment; they shall never die an untimely death nor suffer unjust calamities; all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will constantly provide protection and support, causing virtue to increase and evil to diminish at all times; they will be reborn in various Buddha-fields according to their vows, and until they reach Bodhi, they shall not fall into the evil realms.
The Praise states:
From here below is the second section, which generally extols the supreme virtues of this one-fascicle sūtra.
Within this, there are two parts:
This consists of a brief, specific praise at the beginning and a summary praise at the end;
this is the former.
Within it, there are ten virtues:
First, attaining the knowledge of past lives over one or many kalpas;
second, constantly practicing virtue with diligence throughout all births;
third, not being detained by Māra and his like.
Fourth, the various devas will constantly provide protection;
fifth, one shall never meet with an untimely death;

sixth, there shall be no unjust misfortunes or afflictions—where "misfortune" refers to calamities arising that ruin the family or destroy the person, and "affliction" refers to contracting a disease—and in the end, none of these things shall occur.
Seventh, they are constantly protected and remembered by the seven Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas;
eighth, they cause evil to be extinguished and goodness to arise;
ninth, they are born in Buddha-lands according to their vows.
From this day forward until the attainment of enlightenment, one shall not fall into the three evil destinies.

The term "evil destinies" here comprehensively includes the three types of evil destinies within the human realm, from which one shall likewise not fall: namely, the formless eunuch, the hermaphrodite, and the woman.
The Sūtra says:
"All classes of sentient beings who receive and uphold this sūtra will certainly obtain boundless benefits and merits.
I shall now briefly explain a small portion thereof."
The Praise states:
This is a summary of the eulogy.

The ultimate truth elucidated exhausts the profoundness of the fundamental nature; the teaching that elucidates it is supremely wondrous because it accords with the profound principle. The boundless benefits gained by those who receive and uphold it cannot be fully described; therefore, only a small portion has been stated here.

Therefore, practitioners who wish to realize this virtue should diligently cultivate and train until they attain ultimate realization; only then will they know that the benefits of this sutra are inexhaustible.
The Sutra says:

When the Bhagavan had finished speaking this sutra, Vajrapāṇi and the other great Bodhisattvas, as well as the assembly of devas, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Praise states:
This is the third section, on Awakening through Practice.

The great Bodhisattvas who have gathered in the Reward Land, as well as the other celestial assemblies and the great beings who have manifested transformation bodies, were all moved by the Tathāgata’s profound exposition of the grand principle for awakening to tranquil cessation; they respectfully received the instructions for practicing with a deep resolve and departed from the assembly.
On an auspicious day in the tenth month of the year of Bingshen during the Kyōhō era,
by Kiyoshi Yoshida Gennobu.
